In June 1985 the CIA set down its requirements and reporting rules for the prisoner and missing mission. The paper covers what collectors had to gather and how findings moved back up the chain. Routine as it sounds, this paperwork kept a far-flung search organized.

Dated February 1954, this CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Bolivia. The revolution of 1952 had brought the MNR party to power, with land reform and mine nationalization in its train. Washington watched the experiment with open unease.

The paper assesses where the Bolivian revolution might go next and what risks it posed. Bolivia was a test of whether a poor, landlocked country could remake itself without falling under communist sway. For readers, the forecast records the agency's early judgment on one of Latin America's deepest social upheavals. It was written while the revolution's own leaders were still deciding how far it should run.
cia-0000124310: A July 1951 CIA document covers North Korean treatment of prisoners at Manpojin. The northern camps ranked among the Korean War's grimmest stories, and Manpojin sat near the Yalu River, far from witnesses. The paper records the treatment there as it was reported to the agency. Manpojin lay in the far north near the Chinese border, a place whose distance from the front made outside checks on camp conditions nearly impossible then.

Pierre Smeesters, Anne Vergison, Dioclécio Campos, and co-authors compared the same germ in two very different places in 2006. Group A Streptococcus is the bacterium behind strep throat and, at its worst, rheumatic fever. Its strains vary by region. The team charted that variation in Belgium and in Brazil.

Their epidemiologic landscape compares which strep types circulate in each country and how common each one is. cia-0000136610: Dated only to 1961 in the catalog, with that year marked as estimated, this Spanish text comes from the 2506 Brigade papers. An earlier summary described London and Washington coordinating a war against Hitler; that belongs to another era and is dropped. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, and 1961 was its year of action. The document survives in Spanish in the declassified release, its month and subject not recorded.
cia-0000137310: Dated 1960, NSC Briefing — Cuba is a declassified CIA paper prepared for the National Security Council. Briefings of this kind gave the president's senior advisers a shared, current picture; this one's subject, by its title, was Cuba during the year of rupture with Castro's government. The catalog records no specific topics for it, and several sibling briefings with the same title and year are held in these files. It survives as released through the CIA Reading Room, one installment in a standing briefing series.
cia-0000137410: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. un-sc-res-10: Security Council Resolution 10 was adopted on November 4, 1946, in the council's first year, when its members were still learning how the new body would work. The record in this catalog names no subject, and the resolution's topic should be taken from the official text rather than guessed at. It stands as one of the early formal decisions of the council, preserved in the UN's official record. It dates from the season when the wartime alliance was being recast as a peacetime system for settling disputes.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d10: Paired with a letter to Stalin the same day, President Roosevelt's note to Prime Minister Churchill of June 18, 1943 is Document 10 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two messages went out together as the president kept both partners in step. The record supplies date, sender, and receiver, and no topic. In the Foreign Relations series it stands early in the chain of papers that produced the Cairo and Tehran meetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d110: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the date November 9, 1943, and it stands as Document 110 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The day's traffic also held letters from Chiang, Harriman, and Bohlen, a fair sample of the summit's whole cast. The record for this note gives the date and the names only. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that crowded day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d210:
Foy Kohler of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs wrote a secret memorandum on 11 November 1943. It records fresh British Embassy reports on the Cairo talks between Anthony Eden and Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu, adding two later meetings in Ankara on 7 and 8 November.

Numan, the memo shows, grew somewhat warmer in the final talk. He admitted the Moscow decisions were better than expected, yet he resented Eden's threatening tone and felt Eden spoke for Russia as much as Britain. He wanted to know exactly what Turkey must do, what Allied help she could count on, and what the political results would be. The Balkans now worried Ankara as much as the Straits once did.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d310:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, on command of British and American forces operating against Germany. It is the full American case for a single commander over the whole European war, pressed at the Sextant Conference.

Operations fall into three linked groups: the Mediterranean, northwest Europe, and the strategic air war on Germany's interior. Since events in each group shape the others, the chiefs argue, one commander must direct all three under the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and his appointment is most urgently necessary. Even named at once, he could not be organized before the end of January 1944. The paper ends with the bombing war, where it calls unified command imperative if lives and planes are to be saved.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d410:
A third draft of the Tehran communiqué is printed here with its handwritten changes shown, Roosevelt's apart from three by Hopkins. An editorial headnote presumes this was the draft discussed and put into final form at the dinner meeting of 1 December 1943.

Hopkins' hand inserted the heading Communiqué, changed Soviet Russia to the Soviet Union, and added the place and date, Tehran, Iran, 1 December 1943, at the foot. Roosevelt's changes tighten the text throughout. The leaders have shaped and confirmed our common policy. Their concord will win an enduring peace. The conferences are now friendly, a word glossed in Russian and English at the margin. A note under the signatures, in the President's papers, reads: as corrected, this becomes the final draft.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d510: Document 510 is an editorial note placed by the volume's historians. It appears in the Cairo-Tehran volume of the Foreign Relations series. Such notes fill gaps between papers with background and cross-references. They keep names, dates, and earlier decisions straight for the reader. The conferences documented here met in late 1943. Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin used them to plan the war's next phase. Read the note as part of that official record's apparatus.
frus-1944-quebec-d10:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 4, 1944, the day Allied troops entered Rome and two days before D-Day. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

June 4 was a hinge date: Italy's capital fell even as the invasion fleet sailed for France. Churchill, whose strategy had always prized the Mediterranean, marked the moment in his correspondence with Washington. For readers, a letter from that crowded day shows the war's two Western campaigns peaking together, and the Prime Minister keeping his hand on both through his channel to Roosevelt.
frus-1944-quebec-d110:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt this long memorandum on September 8, 1944, ahead of the Quebec Conference. Its title names the subject: lend-lease and economic relations with Britain in "Phase 2," the period after Germany's defeat but while the Pacific war went on. Britain's weakened finances frame the whole paper.

Hull urged helping Britain enter the postwar period on sound footing, with trade and finance run on Bretton Woods principles. He tied aid to full British effort against Japan and to a British reconversion program matched with America's. Done right, he argued, lend-lease could continue during the Pacific war without breeding later disputes. It set out the American position going into the Quebec talks on aid.
frus-1944-quebec-d210:
No official memorandum survives for this luncheon, and the editors again lean on Mackenzie King's notes. King lunched with Roosevelt, Churchill, and Eden, and the talk turned to timing the proposed world organization conference for October 30. That date fell just a week before the American presidential elections, which sharpened every political calculation around it.

King warned of opposition from small countries, Canada included, to any appearance that the great powers were seeking to control the world through the new organization. Churchill described the disagreement with Stalin over the council's powers, especially a Soviet veto in disputes where the Soviet Union was itself a party. Eden's diary adds that Churchill explained why Eden could not accept Roosevelt's Hyde Park invitation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d10: General John Deane, who headed the American military mission in Moscow, reported to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 17 October 1944. His message is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta. Deane dealt daily with Soviet officers, so his reports gave Washington a soldier's view of cooperation with an ally whose help the war effort still required.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d110:
Acting Secretary Stettinius sent the President a German control agreement on 25 November 1944 and asked for a quick answer. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards a photostatic copy of the deal reached in the European Advisory Commission. The commission's minutes of 14 November, when the agreement was signed, came with it.

The agreement sets up the Allied control machinery for Germany during the surrender period. Stettinius stresses that it grew from close consultation with the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the War and Navy Departments. Approval from the President would let Ambassador Winant tell the commission that the United States accepts. Copies were also going to the Secretaries of War and the Navy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d210:
France asked outright for a seat at the Big Three conference, and Stettinius sent the request to the President on 18 January 1945. His covering note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, transmits Ambassador Caffery's telegram with the French text in full. The note is dated from Paris on 16 January.

The Provisional Government says it learned from public reports of the planned meeting of the three allied powers. That meeting will fix the terms of their cooperation in the war. Paris then sets out its standing. The fighting in the West runs on French soil or hard by her frontiers. France is straining to the full extent of her present strength. The claim to be heard, the enclosure argues in effect, follows from where the war is being fought.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d310:
Supplying friendly forces in freed Europe is the subject of a United States Chiefs of Staff memorandum written at Malta on February 1, 1945. It deals with gear for Allied and liberated forces, with Greece at the front of the queue. A new Greek army was to take over guard duty inside Greece, and its needs had been spelled out in a theater message.

Most items, the memo notes, could come from British stocks in the Mediterranean or on the way there. But every issue made for this purpose would need replacement later. The paper shows supply, not strategy, filling much of the chiefs' working day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d410:
Matthews sent Stettinius a suggested reparations paper on February 9, 1945, with this covering note. The draft, meant for Molotov and Eden, rested on the Russian proposal of basic principles. Its first two sections followed the Soviet text almost word for word. Eden had suggested added words in the first paragraph.

Matthews also advised a question for Molotov: at what prices — that is, prices of what year — would the total of reparations be fixed? The attached draft itself has not been found, the editors note. A handwritten tag credits "Doc" Matthews as author. The cover note shows how technical points hid inside the grand reparations fight.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d510:
Matters on Poland have reached a dead end, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on April 7, 1945 — and laid the blame on the Western ambassadors. In his view, Harriman and Clark Kerr, the American and British members of the Moscow Commission, had departed from the principles of the Crimea Conference. They had introduced new elements the conference never provided.

At Crimea, Stalin argued, all three leaders had treated the functioning Polish Provisional Government as the kernel of the new government of national unity. It was subject to reconstruction, not replacement. The ambassadors, he charged, now read the bargain differently. The letter, given in translation, is the alliance's Polish quarrel stated by its strongest party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d10:
Churchill decided to risk a snub in this short telegram to Truman of May 15, 1945. Your number 39 has just arrived, he writes. I agree with what you say. I will take a chance of getting a snub from Stalin by sending him a telegram urging a friendly tripartite meeting.

The editors note the risk was real. In March, Churchill had ended a message to Stalin hoping their difficulties would be swept away if only they could meet. Stalin's reply had ignored the sentence entirely. This three-line wire thus records a deliberate gamble: the Prime Minister would ask plainly, and take the answer he got.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d110:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied reparations commission, cabled President Truman from Moscow on June 29, 1945. The top secret telegram is document 110 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Pauley was working in Moscow with his Soviet and British counterparts on how much Germany should pay for the war.

Pauley says he is bending every effort to have a proposed reparations plan ready to lay before the three heads of government at their meeting. Soviet negotiator Maisky and Britain's Monckton expect to attend, and Pauley hopes to be there too, as Truman had discussed with him before he left the United States. He asks that the Army be told to arrange places for himself, Dr. Lubin, and four others.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d210:
Secretary Byrnes answered Justice Jackson from aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945. The brief telegram is document 210 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Jackson had reported from London that the war crimes trial talks were slow and technical, and that he dreaded the Big Three debating the subject.

Byrnes appreciates the report and agrees with Jackson: the subject is too technical for detailed discussion by the Big Three. But if he finds discussion unavoidable, he writes, he will try to let Jackson know in time for a consultation with the President and himself. The reply kept the war crimes charter where Jackson wanted it, in the hands of the lawyers in London, while the leaders dealt with it only in broad terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d310:
Barnes took up the Soviet plan for Bulgaria's Control Commission on July 12, 1945, and set it against an older promise. He quoted Ambassador Winant's letter of October 22, 1944, to the Soviet side. That letter said the commission would work under instructions from all three allied governments.

Against that standard, Barnes measured the new Soviet talk of mere consultation. Consultation, he argued, was not joint control. The cable asks Washington to see the gap between the armistice promise and Soviet practice in Sofia. It reached the Department days before the Potsdam conference opened, capping a month of warnings from Sofia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d410:
A sudden Soviet shift is reported in Winant's cable from London of July 10, 1945. He thanks the Department for its prompt action of July 8, which was meant to ease the French zone agreement to completion. Yet after a long discussion the night before, the European Advisory Commission still could not complete the agreement.

Gousev, the Soviet representative, now said he did not know whether his government would approve postponing the fixing of France's Berlin area. Moscow might wish the French area described within the agreement itself, and he must consult his government. Winant assumed the shift came on instructions from Moscow, since Gousev had known the proposal since June 29.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d510:
Poland's frontiers frame an extract from the briefing book paper on suggested American policy toward Poland, dated June 29, 1945. The Crimea Conference, it recalls, settled Poland's eastern frontier by adopting a slightly modified Curzon Line as the Polish-Soviet boundary. It also recognized that Poland should receive substantial additions of territory in the north and west.

The new Polish government was to be consulted on their extent, but final delimitation of the Polish-German frontiers was to await the peace conference. Meanwhile, the paper notes, the Lublin government had taken over almost at once all the territory of pre-1939 Poland, as the German population withdrew. With Soviet consent and help, it then took over German lands in the east as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d610:

The extract's weight sits in one quoted passage from the U.S. paper under review. Among the added tasks to aid the grand strategy is this one. The Allies should encourage Russian entry into the war against Japan. They should also give Russia such aid to her war-making power as is needed and practical in that link. The British note that they agree in full with the U.S. memo, subject to their earlier remarks. None of those remarks touched this passage on Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710:

The first entry follows the party out of Washington that night. Truman left the White House by motor car at 9:40 p.m. with a small staff group. At Union Station the special train waited on Team Track No. 2. Secretary Byrnes came aboard at 10:15 p.m., while Admiral Leahy and others had boarded earlier. At 11 p.m. the train rolled for Newport News, Virginia. There the heavy cruiser Augusta waited to carry the President across the Atlantic. The next morning's entry notes the same pier had served President Roosevelt's Crimea trip that year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-10:

Cohen has Truman stress the urgency of preparing for the European settlements. The first concrete proposal was the draft for a Council of Foreign Ministers. Churchill suggested it be referred to the foreign secretaries. Stalin agreed to that procedure, but voiced his doubt over China in a council for the European peace. Truman then stated the U.S. policy toward Germany in his own words. The Control Council, he thought, should start to function at once under the agreement already made. His draft of principles for that council was laid before the meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-110:
Another set of Thompson minutes records Potsdam talks on July 25, 1945. The conference often ran several meetings in a day, and note-takers split the load. Thompson's sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form a near-daily spine for the American record. This set covers a further session from a crowded day.

Readers meet the session's flow: topics in order, speakers in turn, points left hanging. Minutes like these let later readers test claims about who agreed to what. They also catch the strain of the schedule itself. By late July the talks had run a week with the largest questions still unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d810:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 23, 1945, in document 810. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His post stood inside a control commission where the Soviet voice ruled. The report entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Barnes's mid-conference report carries the pressure of his position. He reported facts his hosts would rather have hidden. Readers gain a clear sense of Bulgaria's slide from the Western orbit. The document shows reporting as a form of resistance: to write the truth home was to keep a claim alive. His letters remain a key source on the Balkans' turning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d910: American staff drafted this short memorandum on July 22, 1945, as one response to the Soviet definition of war booty. It quotes the Soviet text in full. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1010: Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations, sent this short telegram from Babelsberg on July 26, 1945. That body selects captured craft, including tugs. The chosen officer must be fit to pick tugs suited to American purposes. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1110:

The translators added notes to guide readers through names and customs. The middle volume holds the epic's long arc together, linking the heroes of myth to the shahs of record.
berkeley-principles-human-knowledge-1710:
George Berkeley published A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge in 1710 in Dublin. Berkeley, an Irish clergyman and philosopher, was only twenty-five. His claim was bold: matter does not exist, and reality consists of minds and their ideas alone.

Berkeley argued that to be is to be perceived, esse est percipi in his Latin phrase. A tree exists because a mind perceives it, and God's mind holds all things when no human watches. He attacked abstract ideas and the physics of his day. Readers have argued over the Principles ever since. It remains the central text of British empiricist metaphysics and a standing puzzle in philosophy.
goldman-anarchism-other-essays-1910:
Emma Goldman published Anarchism and Other Essays in 1910 in New York. Goldman, a Russian-born lecturer and publisher of Mother Earth magazine, was then the best known anarchist in America. The essays gather her talks on the subjects that filled her halls.

Goldman defined anarchism as freedom from government and from the dead weight of church and property. Other essays treat patriotism as a threat to peace, marriage as an economic bargain, and the traffic in women as a product of poverty. She wrote in a direct, urgent voice for working readers. The book stands as the American anarchist manifesto of its era and the clearest short statement of her thought.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol2-:
Paul Ehrlich won wide fame for his work on immunity and for the first drug made to target a single disease germ. Charles Bolduan translated this second volume of his studies into English. It appeared in 1910 as part of the second edition of the set.

In his preface Ehrlich says the volume gathers most of his recent immunity studies with his collaborators. The papers measure toxins and antitoxins with great care, building what he called quantitative serology. He argues his theory rests on a huge mass of experimental data. The volume completes a core record of early immunology.
bennett-clayhanger-1910:
Arnold Bennett set his Clayhanger novels in Bursley, his fictional version of a Staffordshire pottery town. Clayhanger, published in 1910, opens the series and draws on Bennett's own youth. It follows a printer's son across the last decades of the 1800s.

Edwin Clayhanger dreams of becoming an architect, but his stern father pulls him into the family printing business. The novel tracks Edwin's slow growth under that pressure, through work, illness, and a first serious love. Bennett fills the story with exact detail of pottery-town life. It is the start of his Potteries epic, which later volumes carry forward into Edwin's middle age.
conrad-secret-sharer-1910:
Joseph Conrad wrote The Secret Sharer in late 1909, drawing on an old story from his own years at sea. The novella was published in 1910. Conrad had been a merchant sailor for twenty years before he turned to fiction, and the sea fills this tale.

A young captain, new to his ship, finds a naked swimmer clinging to the ladder at night. The man, Leggatt, has killed a sailor on his own ship and fled. The captain hides him in his cabin for days, risking his command. The two men mirror each other so closely that helping the fugitive escape feels like saving himself.
forster-howards-end-1910:
E. M. Forster published Howards End in 1910, and it became his first widely praised novel. Forster, a Cambridge graduate, wrote about the England he knew: cultured liberals, rich business families, and the clerks caught between them. A country house gives the book its title.

Two Schlegel sisters, Margaret and Helen, befriend the wealthy Wilcox family and a poor clerk named Leonard Bast. Margaret marries into the Wilcoxes, while Helen's rash choices pull Bast toward ruin. The house, Howards End, passes slowly toward the person who understands it best. Forster's famous plea, only connect, sums up the novel's hope for bridging class and feeling.
jonson-alchemist-1610:
Ben Jonson, Shakespeare's great rival and friend, wrote The Alchemist for the King's Men in 1610. Jonson set the comedy in a London emptied by plague. A master has fled the city, leaving his house to a scheming servant.

The servant Face joins the fake alchemist Subtle and the prostitute Dol Common to run a confidence shop. Gullible visitors pay for lucky charms, magic metals, and astrological advice, each greedier than the last. Jonson's plot spins faster and faster until the master returns at the worst moment. The play is a brilliant machine of greed, disguise, and comic justice, still a favorite on stage.
robinson-town-down-the-river-1910:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Town Down the River in 1910, returning to the Tilbury Town portraits that had made his reputation. By then Robinson had won powerful admirers, including President Theodore Roosevelt, who found him a government job. This volume is the essential middle collection of his career.

New townsfolk join the gallery: failures, dreamers, and quiet sufferers rendered in exact, ironic verse. Robinson also includes poems on larger themes, among them a notable piece on the painter George Crabbe. His sympathy never turns soft, and his endings often twist the knife gently. Readers who want Robinson beyond the famous anthology pieces should start with this book and its haunted New England streets.
pascal-pensees-trotter-1910:
Blaise Pascal, the French thinker and scientist, died in 1662 leaving behind bundles of short notes. Friends published the notes in 1670 as the Pensées, or Thoughts. W. F. Trotter translated the book into English in 1910, and his version long served as the standard one.

The fragments argue that reason alone cannot settle the deepest questions of life. Pascal's famous wager urges the doubter to bet on God's existence. He calls man a thinking reed, weak in body yet great in mind. Other notes treat custom, boredom, pride, and the hidden God. Few books of fragments have been quoted so often or read so closely.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol1-1910:
Romain Rolland began his long novel Jean-Christophe in 1904, telling the life of a German composer. Gilbert Cannan translated the work into English, and volume one appeared in 1910. It holds the first four books: Dawn, Morning, Youth, and Revolt.

Young Jean-Christophe Krafft grows up in a small town on the Rhine, poor and gifted. Music becomes his refuge from a drunken father and a narrow world. He fights the stale taste of his elders and starts to find his own voice. Rolland wrote the cycle as a hymn to art, freedom, and the kinship of peoples. The full work later helped earn him the Nobel Prize in literature.
bunin-the-village-1910:
Ivan Bunin published The Village in Russian in 1910, and Isabel Hapgood translated it into English in 1923. Two brothers, Tikhon and Kuzma Krasov, rise from peasant stock in a poor Russian village. Tikhon grows rich and hard, while Kuzma teaches himself letters and sinks into despair.

Between them Bunin paints village life without the pity or hope other writers added. Drink, violence, ignorance, and rare kindness fill the long, plotless days. The book split Russian critics, some hailing its truth and others its bleakness. Bunin later became the first Russian to win the Nobel Prize in literature. The Village shows the harsh ground from which his polished art grew.
rilke-malte-laurids-brigge-1910:
Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Rilke's only novel, appeared in German in 1910. The text here is the German original; the first English translation came in 1930 and is not in the public domain. Malte, a young Danish nobleman without money, lives in a cheap Paris room and writes what he sees.

Fear walks with him through hospitals, crowds, and streets full of the poor. Memories of his childhood home in Denmark break into the Paris notes without warning. Rilke breaks the tale into fragments, more diary than plot. The book became the first great German novel of modern city consciousness. Its dread and pity still feel new.
art-of-war-giles-1910:
Lionel Giles translated Sun Tzu's Art of War into English in 1910, with a long introduction and critical notes. Sun Tzu, a Chinese general of deep antiquity, is credited with the oldest military treatise in the world. Giles's edition introduced the work properly to the English-speaking world for the first time.

Thirteen short chapters treat ground, supply, spies, deception, and the cost of war. Sun Tzu prizes winning without battle above every bloody triumph. His maxims favor knowledge of self and enemy over force alone. Giles set the Chinese scholarship in order and answered earlier, weaker versions. Business and strategy readers later adopted the book far beyond armies. The Project Gutenberg text is ebook number 132.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-10:
Volume ten, published in 1885, closes the main body of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night. Shahrazad's storytelling ends, her pardon is granted, and the frame tale completes its long arc. Burton then adds his famous Terminal Essay, a wide survey of the book's history, sources, and the societies behind it.

The essay treats the geography, folklore, and private life of the East with a scholar's range. With it, Burton's ten volumes stand as both translation and reference work. Later editors plundered the essay even when they bowdlerized his tales. Six supplemental volumes followed with further stories from other manuscripts. The main set, though, ends here, on the thousand and first night.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume ten completes Penzer's Ocean of Story, the ten-volume edition of Tawney's Kathasaritsagara begun in 1924. Somadeva's frame closes as Naravahanadatta wins his fated place among the Vidyadharas. The ocean of story, gathered in eleventh-century Kashmir from centuries of Indian tale, comes to rest at last.

Penzer's final apparatus rounds out a comparative index of motifs unmatched in its day. Tawney's translation, honored here in full, had waited forty years for such an edition. Scholars of folklore treat the set as a working library in itself. General readers finish with the sense of having sailed a whole literature. No English story collection of the age attempts this scale and completes it.
hicks-stoic-and-epicurean-1910:
R. D. Hicks wrote Stoic and Epicurean in 1910 as a clear English guide to the two great schools that led Greek thought after Aristotle. Both schools taught in Athens, drew loyal bands of pupils, and shaped Roman life for centuries. Hicks treats each school on its own terms and in plain terms.

He walks through their views on nature, logic, and knowledge, then gives most space to their rival ways of life. The Stoics taught calm in the face of fate. The school of Epicurus taught quiet pleasure and freedom from fear. Hicks wrote for the general reader, and his survey long served as the first book students were handed on these schools.
bernard-clairvaux-on-loving-god-1910:
Bernard of Clairvaux was the Cistercian abbot whose words moved kings and launched a crusade. He wrote On Loving God, De Diligendo Deo, for a cardinal who asked him why God should be loved. The English edition here dates to 1910, printed at London with the translator unnamed in the scan. Bernard's answer became the classic of affective mysticism.

He sets out four degrees of love. Man loves himself for his own sake, then God for his gifts, then God for God's own sake. At last he loves even himself only in God. The prose burns with scripture and with a monk's plain speech. Bernard asks for the whole heart, not a measured share. The short book has guided prayer for nine centuries.
scheible-das-kloster-vol10:
Band ten of Das Kloster, cells thirty-seven through forty, appeared in 1848 from Johann Scheible's Stuttgart house. Ten bands of complete reprints had made Scheible the keeper of Germany's folk print past. His rule never changed: print the whole text, however odd, however feared.

So the grimoires come entire, Faust books and Höllenzwänge among them, with nothing struck out. Folk charms hold their place beside works of high ritual, and chapbooks fill the gaps between. For the student of German magic, such fullness is the point. A cut text hides what its makers believed; Scheible's pages hide nothing, and band ten keeps that faith.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-2-:
Volume two of Maudslay's translation of Bernal Díaz's True History appeared in 1910, covering Books Five to Nine. The years are 1519 and 1520, when Cortés's small force entered the Aztec world and met Moctezuma. Díaz, an old soldier writing long after, had served in the ranks through all of it.

His history insists on the view from the ground: marches, councils, gifts, and growing dread. He wrote against the official story told by Gómara, which he thought stole credit from the men who fought. The siege of the great city still lies ahead in later volumes. Here the wonder and the danger rise together, page by page.
ricardo-high-price-bullion-1810:
David Ricardo made his name with The High Price of Bullion, a pamphlet of 1810. Britain's Bank Restriction had freed the Bank of England from paying gold for notes. Bullion prices rose, and Ricardo blamed paper money issued in excess. His tract applies the quantity theory of money to the case.

Too many notes, he argues, cheapen each one against gold and goods. The cure was a return to cash payments under strict rule. The pamphlet's clarity won him a hearing among statesmen and thinkers. It set the terms of the great bullion debate. Economists still cite it as a model pamphlet. Ricardo the theorist enters history here.
spr-proceedings-vol23-1909-1910:
Volume twenty three binds parts fifty eight and fifty nine, for 1909 and 1910. The Society for Psychical Research carries its record into the years before the Great War. Thought transference trials appear with new statistical checks. The census tradition still governs how spontaneous cases are gathered.

Trance sittings with Piper and her successors in the files fill long sections. Investigators try proxy sitters and other guards against hidden knowledge. Apparition reports continue, each tied to named witnesses. Volume twenty three sustains the primary archive of the evidential debate. Its tone is sober where its subject is strange. That contrast defines the whole Proceedings run.
flaubert-temptation-st-anthony-hearn-191:
Saint Anthony sits in the Egyptian desert while wonders and horrors crowd his night in Flaubert's Temptation of Saint Anthony. Lafcadio Hearn's 1910 translation renders the work Flaubert called his life's own, rewritten across thirty years. Gods, heretics, monsters, and Death itself parade before the hermit's eyes.

Each vision tempts the saint with a different offer: power, pleasure, knowledge, rest. The book reads more like a vast stage dream than a novel, rich with the lore Flaubert loved. Odilon Redon's dark images, noted in this edition, suit a text where faith wrestles every phantom it can name.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol10:
Volume X of the Journal of Discourses rounds the first ten of the set, printed at Liverpool in 1863. Stenographic reports carry the voices of Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and other speakers of the day. A full decade of Utah preaching now stood in print, sermon upon sermon, for readers everywhere.

The talks range across belief and behavior, from God's nature to the care of orchards, homes, and families. That breadth is the record's charm and its use: a whole society thinks aloud in these pages. Volume X closes the set's first stretch, with sixteen volumes of the same record still to come.
shaker-testimony-christs-second-appearin:
The Shakers set out their whole faith in the Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing, first printed in 1808 and reissued in 1810. The United Society of Believers speaks here as one voice. Mother Ann Lee, their foundress, is presented as the vessel of Christ's second appearing, the hinge of their system.

Celibacy, shared goods, and confession of sin flow from that claim, and the book argues each from scripture. It is systematic, dense, and meant to answer critics who saw only dancing and strangeness. As the charter theology of American Shakerism, it remains the movement's fullest statement of itself.
wattles-science-getting-rich-1910:
Wallace D. Wattles promised a method, not a mystery, in The Science of Getting Rich, printed in 1910. His New Thought classic teaches thinking in the Certain Way. Hold the picture of what you want, act with faith, and give every person more than you take. Gratitude keeps the channel open, in his scheme.

The short book speaks to clerks and strivers who felt the age's wealth passing them by. Its plain chapters made it the most cited prosperity text of the whole movement in time. A century of success literature drinks from Wattles and his Certain Way, often without knowing his name at all.
wattles-science-being-well-1910:
Wattles turned his Certain Way toward the body in The Science of Being Well, the 1910 companion to his prosperity book. Health, he argues, follows the same law as wealth: think health, act as the well act, and trust the life principle within. Worry and gloomy images count as real dangers here.

Eating, bathing, breathing, and sleep all get chapters shaped by his mental-science rules. The tone stays practical, closer to a handbook than a sermon. Together with its sister volume, the book shows New Thought at its most confident, promising readers command over fortune and flesh alike.
aucassin-nicolette-lang-1910:
Aucassin loves Nicolette, a Saracen captive raised in a French castle, and their story survives in one manuscript. Aucassin and Nicolete, from about 1200, is the only surviving French chantefable, a tale alternating prose and verse. Andrew Lang's classic 1887 translation appears here from the 1910 David Nutt edition.

The tale parodies the romances of its age: the hero weeps, sulks, and bungles while Nicolette acts with sense and daring. Captures, escapes, and a kingdom where roles reverse keep the comedy bright. Lang's version carried the little masterpiece to English readers, where its charm has kept it in print ever since.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
In 1910 Tome III carried the French Sahih of al-Bukhari toward its close in Les Traditions Islamiques. Houdas and Marçais kept their steady pace through the later books of the collection, where reports treat campaigns, virtues, and the Prophet's companions. The Imprimerie nationale edition aimed at completeness, and this volume honors that aim.

Al-Bukhari's method, testing every chain of transmission, made his Sahih the most authoritative hadith book in Sunni Islam. French scholars gained, through these tomes, a full view of the tradition's inner workings. Tome III stands one volume from the end of a translation that took eleven years to finish.
seligman-melanesians-of-british-new-guin:
Charles Gabriel Seligman led the Cambridge expedition's work in The Melanesians of British New Guinea, published in 1910. The volume reports on the Papuan coast: sorcery, secret societies, and mortuary ritual among the peoples studied. A chapter by F. R. Barton adds his own years of local knowledge to the team's findings.

Seligman's party worked village by village, recording custom before deep change reached the coast. Masks, feasts of merit, and the handling of the dead pass in careful detail. The book stands as a standard early ethnography of Papua, exact and humane in equal measure.
pound-provenca-1910:
Provença, published in Boston in 1910, is Pound's early collection of translations and originals drawn from the troubadours of medieval Provence. Before Pound was a modernist leader, he was a scholar of these twelfth-century love poets, and this book shows why.

He renders Arnaut Daniel, Bertran de Born, and others into English verse that strains to keep their music and difficulty. Original poems in the same manner stand beside the translations. Pound believed modern poetry had to pass through this medieval discipline. The book is the record of that apprenticeship, and of a young poet finding his masters.
james-moral-equivalent-war-1910:
The Moral Equivalent of War began as an address and was published in 1910; it is James's most famous short piece. A pacifist who honored soldiers, he asked how a society could keep the virtues war breeds, discipline, loyalty, and sacrifice, without the killing.

His answer is a conscription of youth into peaceful service: an army enlisted against nature, sent to mines, roads, and fisheries to earn civic honor by labor. The proposal influenced later service programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps. James admits the scheme's difficulty and presses it anyway. The essay remains the classic statement of his moral imagination.
russell-philosophical-essays-1910:
Philosophical Essays, published in 1910, collects Russell's early papers from the decade when analytic philosophy was being invented. The subjects are truth, knowledge, and ethics, treated with the new logical tools he was forging with Whitehead.

The volume includes his essay on the elements of ethics and his engagements with pragmatism, whose theory of truth he resisted. Russell's prose here is already the famous instrument: lucid, cool, and quietly devastating. These papers bridge his Leibniz book and the Principia then in press. For readers of Russell, this is the workshop where the mature voice was made.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-1-1910:
Principia Mathematica, published in three volumes between 1910 and 1913, was Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell's attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic. This first volume lays the foundations: propositional logic, classes, and relations.

Working in a dense forest of symbols, the authors build number and proof from a handful of primitive ideas. One famous proof, that one plus one equals two, arrives hundreds of pages in, with a note that the proposition is occasionally useful. The labor took a decade and changed both fields. Logicism, the program it founded, shaped a century of thought.
bates-naturalist-river-amazons-1910:
Henry Walter Bates spent eleven years, from 1848 to 1859, collecting on the Amazon. The Naturalist on the River Amazons, first published in 1863 and reprinted in the 1910 edition here, is his classic account. Darwin urged him to write it, and praised the result.

Bates shipped home some 14,000 species, most of them insects, and many new to science. He noticed harmless butterflies copying the bright warnings of harmful ones, a pattern now called Batesian mimicry. River towns, forests, floods, and festivals fill the narrative between the science. The book founded the study of mimicry and remains beloved travel writing.
plos-pone-0003410:
Walter R. J. Taylor and colleagues tested a flu drug delivery route in this 2008 study. The drug oseltamivir is the standard oral treatment for severe H5N1 bird flu. Very sick patients often cannot swallow pills safely. Doctors can give the drug through a nasal feeding tube instead.

The team measured drug levels in the blood of adult patients in Vietnam. Levels after tube dosing reached the range judged adequate for treatment. No injected form of the drug existed at the time. The result backs tube dosing when severe flu patients cannot swallow.
plos-pone-0003510:
Martin Löwer and co-authors catalogued secreted enzymes of the ulcer bacterium in this 2008 paper. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach and causes lasting inflammation. Its exported proteases may drive that damage and even cancer risk. Proteases are enzymes that chew through proteins.

The team screened the bacterial proteome for proteins likely to be exported. Several candidate proteases emerged from that sequence screen. One, called HtrA, showed real proteolytic activity in tests. The inventory names suspects behind a very common chronic infection. This germ infects about half the world, though most carriers never feel it.
plos-pone-0003610:
Murali Krishna Ghatkesar and co-authors measured molecular binding with tiny beams in this 2008 paper. When two molecules bind, two physical changes occur. Their masses combine into one larger mass. The structure of at least one partner also changes, causing mechanical stress.

Their nanomechanics method reads those changes on a small cantilever. Bending beams thus report binding without labels or dyes. The approach characterizes molecular interactions more completely than mass alone. Such label-free tools serve drug screening and basic biology. Binding strength decides whether a drug works at all in the body.
plos-pone-0003710:
Jens M. Nygren and David Bryder published this blood study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lifelong blood production rests on rare stem cells in the bone marrow. These hematopoietic stem cells were long viewed as mostly idle next to their fast-dividing offspring. Older tools could not count their divisions inside the body.

The authors built a new assay that traces a cell's division history in vivo. It showed that stem cells which divide faster lose their self-renewal power sooner. The trade-off helps explain how the blood system balances renewal across a lifetime.
plos-pone-0003810:
Marie Thibonnier, Jean-Michel Thiberge, and Hilde De Reuse published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bacteria rescue ribosomes stuck on broken messages through a quality control system called trans-translation. It needs a small RNA, SsrA, and a partner protein, SmpB, to free the ribosome and tag the faulty protein.

In Helicobacter pylori, the ulcer bacterium, the team found this rescue system is essential for life. The protein tagging step is also required for resisting stress and for taking up DNA. Such an essential step is a potential weak point for new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0003910:
Charlotte Lahoute, Athanassia Sotiropoulos, Marilyne Favier, and co-authors studied muscle aging in mice in 2008. Aging muscle loses mass and gains fat and scar tissue, a decline called sarcopenia. Many genes shift with age in muscle, yet the drivers stay unclear. One candidate is serum response factor, a gene switch called SRF.

The team studied skeletal muscle that lacks SRF. Such muscle showed signs of aging ahead of schedule. The result names SRF as one guard against early muscle decline. It offers a lead for research on keeping strength later in life. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004010:
Roosa Leimu and Markus Fischer pooled studies of local adaptation in plants in a 2008 meta-analysis. Local adaptation means populations thrive best in their home conditions. The idea matters for evolution, conservation, and climate change work. How general it is in plants had not been systematically judged.

Their PLOS ONE article combines results from many plant studies. They also ask which species, population, and habitat traits shape adaptation. A pooled view shows where home advantage is strong or weak. That guides seed transfer and planting choices under climate change. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004110:
Jeremy R. Haag, Olga Pontes, and Craig S. Pikaard studied two plant-specific polymerases in 2009. Plants have five nuclear RNA polymerases, more than other eukaryotes. Polymerases IV and V are found only in plants. They drive small-RNA-guided DNA methylation, which silences genes.

Their PLOS ONE article tests the metal-binding sites of Pol IV and Pol V. Both metal A and metal B sites proved required for silencing. Without them, siRNA-dependent methylation failed. The result confirms these polymerases work as true enzymes in the pathway. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004210:
Han-Jun Jin, Chris Tyler-Smith, and Wook Kim published this population genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Koreans are generally classed as a northeast Asian group based on geography. Yet Y-chromosome studies had shown that the Korean population carries lineages from both southern and northern East Asia.

To untangle that history, the team analysed mitochondrial DNA, inherited from mothers, alongside Y-chromosomal markers inherited from fathers. Comparing the two sides of ancestry sharpens the picture of how Korea was peopled. The study weighs how much of the population came from each direction.
plos-pone-0004310:
Sarah Louie and colleagues published this signalling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wnt signals guide cell fate, proliferation, polarity, and movement as vertebrate embryos grow, acting through beta-catenin-dependent and independent pathways. Wnt signals are among the oldest in animal life. Dishevelled is a scaffold protein required for this signalling, gathering other proteins around it.

The team studied Hipk1, a protein that associates with Dishevelled. They report that Hipk1 tunes the beta-catenin signalling pathway. A modulator attached to the central scaffold can tune one of the embryo's most important signals up or down. Tuning it changes how cells read Wnt messages.
plos-pone-0004410:
Two opioid receptors push impulsivity in opposite directions. Mary Olmstead, Abdel-Mouttalib Ouagazzal, and Brigitte Kieffer report that split in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Impulsivity is a primary feature of many psychiatric disorders, including ADHD and drug addiction.

Impulsivity covers failing to delay rewards and failing to withhold a motor response. Using a signaled nose poke task, the authors show mu and delta receptors regulate motor impulsivity oppositely. That contrast could guide drugs that tune one receptor but not the other. It refines models of addiction and self-control. Motor impulsivity is the urge to act, distinct from choosing delayed rewards.
plos-pone-0004510:
Two typhoid-causing Salmonella types arrived at the same deadly trick by different roads, show Wei-Qiao Liu, Ye Feng, Yan Wang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. More than fourteen hundred Salmonella types cause gut illness that usually passes on its own. A few, including Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi C, cause typhoid, a whole-body infection that can kill.

It was not known whether the typhoid agents came from one common ancestor or evolved separately. Comparing their genes, the team found paratyphi C diverged from a gut relative, Salmonella choleraesuis. Its disease style converged with typhi's. In plain terms, nature invented typhoid more than once. That matters for vaccines, which may need to cover separate lineages.
plos-pone-0004610:
Thyroid hormone switches genes in the developing cerebellum, and Hongyan Dong, Carole Yauk, Andrea Rowan-Carroll, and co-authors mapped where it binds, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thyroid hormone is critical to normal brain development, but the mechanisms operating in this process are poorly understood. Without enough of it, a child's brain development suffers lasting harm.

The team used a method called ChIP-on-chip, which fishes out DNA regions bound by a protein and identifies them on a chip. They sampled the cerebellum of mice fifteen days after birth and captured regions bound by the thyroid receptor beta. The resulting list of binding sites and target genes shows, concretely, which genes the hormone throws its switches on during a key window of brain growth.
plos-pone-0004710:
Chehani Alles and colleagues compared gene activity in breast cancers that lack the estrogen sensor, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Such cancers tend to have worse outlook, higher grade, and distinct traits under the microscope. Within them, one subgroup stands out for its own gene pattern and course.

The team merged many studies and ran gene set tests split by sensor status. They found raised activity of two growth drivers in the basal subgroup. Clear driver maps can help split breast cancer into truer types. That split guides which drugs to test for each type. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
crabbe-borough-1810:
George Crabbe, who lived from 1754 to 1832, shaped The Borough in 1810 as a set of verse letters. Each letter paints part of a Suffolk seaport town and the people who live and work there. The first letter gives a broad view of the river, the quay, the shipping, and the shipyards.

Fishermen, smugglers, the poor, the pious, and the proud all pass through his steady portraits. Crabbe refused the soft glow of pastoral verse and showed hard labor and hard winters as they were. That plain truth, told with real pity, is why many readers call The Borough his finest work.
garland-other-main-travelled-1910:
Other Main-Travelled Roads came from Harper as a sunset edition, with rights dates of 1892, 1899, and 1910. Garland opens with verses on prairie folks, starting with the pioneers. They rise, he writes, to mastery of wind and snow, and go like soldiers into strife.

Nearly twenty years after his first farm tales, Garland returns to the same ground here. The farms look familiar, and the struggles have not vanished. Time has passed, though, and the tone grows riper and more thoughtful. With the first volume, the book forms a full portrait of rural life in the Middle West at the century's turn.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-10:
Hedda Gabler burns a manuscript, manipulates her circle, and courts ruin out of boredom and pride. The Master Builder follows Halvard Solness, an aging architect who climbs his own tower toward doom. Archer's tenth volume, from 1908, pairs Ibsen's two most fascinating self-destroyers.

Hedda remains the role great actresses measure themselves against, brilliant and trapped at once. Solness fears the young, clings to his fame, and hears a younger woman knocking at the door. Ibsen's psychology cuts deepest in these late plays. Fear of decline and hunger for freedom drive both plots. The volume shows a master in his sixties outwriting everyone younger.
bancroft-history-us-vol-10:
George Bancroft brings the American Revolution toward its triumph in the tenth volume of his History of the United States, from 1860. The war's later years test the young republic's money, arms, and will. Victory, long in doubt, draws steadily nearer.

Bancroft, often called the father of American history, writes with democratic fervor. For him, the Revolution proves liberty to be the world's great hope. His pages honor farmers and soldiers beside generals and statesmen. The volume stands near the crown of a vast work that taught Americans to read their founding as a providential march toward freedom.
froude-history-england-vol-10:
Spain sends its great fleet against England in the tenth volume of Froude's History, from 1865, covering the Armada year. Drake and Howard lead the sea fight in home waters. Storms then scatter the Spanish ships along wild coasts, completing England's deliverance.

Froude treats the victory as the climax of his whole Tudor epic. Protestant England, in his telling, survives by courage, seamanship, and God's weather. The fate of a nation hangs in the balance through the summer's fighting. His account reads as patriotic pageant, done with great narrative skill, and it crowned his reputation with the reading public of his day.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-10:
Brébeuf's long study of the Huron people crowns Volume 10, from 1897. Thwaites devotes the book to the Huron mission in the year 1636. No writer of the age left a fuller account of Iroquoian life in print.

Towns, councils, feasts, dreams, and beliefs unfold in Brébeuf's calm prose. He explains kinship, healing rites, and the great feast of the dead. His respect for Huron thought sets the text apart from its time. Scholars still call it study of a culture before that field had a name. It was written in a bark mission house, by firelight.
journal-of-discourses-vol-10:
Plural marriage meets open defense in Volume Ten, published in 1863. Young argues the doctrine from the Tabernacle pulpit without flinching. The nation, deep in civil war, is dared to object if it will.

Sermons ground plural marriage in scripture and in claimed revelation. Speakers frame the practice as a test of faith and obedience. The prophet stands at his most defiant in these bold discourses. Outsiders read such pages to grasp what made Utah so distinct. The volume remains key for anyone studying the doctrine's public face in Utah. Its frankness sets it apart from later, more guarded treatments.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol4-1910:
The fourth volume of Bakunin's collected works, edited by Guillaume, came out in French in 1910. It centers on the open war between Bakunin and Marx inside the First International. That fight, fought through congresses, letters, and pamphlets, ended with Bakunin's expulsion in 1872 and the split of the workers' movement.

Bakunin's texts accuse Marx's party of seeking power for itself under the name of the working class. He defends a loose federation of free groups against any central committee. Guillaume prints documents from both sides of the quarrel, which keeps the volume useful even for readers who side against Bakunin. These pages are the primary record of socialism's great schism, told by one of its two main actors.
cia-0000008010:
September 1955 gave analysts a deadline to work toward: July 1956, when Vietnam's future was due for key choices. The Geneva Accords had split Vietnam in two and promised nationwide elections by that date. In the south, Diem's government resisted holding the vote.

A CIA estimate for the period weighs Diem's grip, northern intentions, and the odds of renewed war. Such forecasts tried to give policymakers warning, not certainty. This one captures the moment when division hardened into two rival states. Its judgments help explain why the later war found roots so early in the decade that followed.
cia-0000008710:
Future Soviet moves in Vietnam drew a CIA forecast in March 1965, as American combat troops began landing. Moscow backed North Vietnam with aid and weapons, but it also feared a wider war with Washington. Analysts had to judge how far Soviet support might go.

The paper weighs aid levels, diplomacy, and the rivalry between Moscow and Beijing for Hanoi's ear. Its judgments fed choices about bombing, escalation, and signaling to the USSR. Readers can see the Vietnam War framed as one board in a global contest. The estimate shows superpower caution studied at close range.
cia-0000009910:
An American pilot died while held near Ban Na Kay, and two other Americans were moved, a November 1966 item records. Ban Na Kay sits in the Laotian uplands, in cave and mountain country. Death and movement in one report show captivity's two constant motions.

One man's file closes as two others' files gain a new location. Analysts split the item three ways and filed each part under a name. The movers' new place, if named inside, reset the search around them. This entry preserves the combined report before that splitting, as the news first arrived.
cia-0000012310:
Helms again, this time in a memo whose date is unknown and only estimated as 1962, addressed to the Director of Central Intelligence. The floating date sets the letter among the Penkovsky file's crisis-year papers. In 1962 the colonel's case ran toward its climax, and summit mail on it piled up faster than clerks could always date it.

Uncertainty about a date is a small fact that tells a larger one: haste ruled the bureaucracy that year. The files keep these loose pages without apology. For readers, the memo shows the great case's paperwork at its most hurried and human.
cia-0000012410:
Meeting number twenty-eight survives without a firm date, its year estimated as 1961. The undated record drifts through the file like a loose page. It stays valuable despite its lost place in the chronology. By the high twenties, the numbering itself tells the story. No Western service had ever debriefed one source at this length, this depth, or this level of danger.

The record's missing date is part of the file's honesty. Files kept under pressure have gaps, and the gaps remain visible. For readers, the session shows the operation's scale, counted in sittings rather than claims.
cia-0000013610:
Venezuela's young democracy under Rómulo Betancourt is surveyed in a CIA paper from October 1961. Betancourt had won the presidency after a decade of dictatorship. He governed an oil-rich country while gunmen tried to kill him and rebels tried to topple him. Trujillo's Dominican regime even backed an attempt on his life, yet the voting and the building went on around him.

The paper takes the measure of that battered democracy in its third year. It weighs the parties, the oil money, and the plots together. For readers, it keeps the watch on a rare experiment: a Latin democracy taking hits and holding.
cia-0000014710: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, espionage, and a block of following information fill a CIA file dated July 1, 1952. The title promises detail the open line does not show. By mid 1952 the couple sat in prison under death sentences. Files like this gathered fresh facts while their appeals ran through the courts.
cia-0000015310: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It takes up Berkner's letter of April 21, the title oddly notes. The dates clash, a common slip in clipped file titles. Either way, the Berkner thread ran on into 1958, long after the first panel had closed its work.
cia-0000015410: Air Force officers met CIA staff on April 5, 1958, to talk about the report of the Scientific Advisory Panel on flying objects. Little in the title hints at detail, and the record stays at that level.
cia-0000021510: Sightings of pilots are discussed in an untitled CIA record dated in 1967. The pilots in such files were usually Americans lost over Laos or Vietnam. Each rumored sighting raised hope that a missing man still lived. Staff had to weigh those rumors with care, since families waited on the same news and false hope carried its own cruelty.
cia-0000022810: A dead American pilot was sighted in Snuol District, in Kratie Province, Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Kratie sits on the Mekong River in the country's east. cia-0000023010: What followed an attempt on the life of Trujillo is covered in a CIA record dated in 1967. The heading can also be read as the aftermath for Trujillo's assassin, and the catalog leaves it tangled. Rafael Trujillo, the Dominican strongman, was in fact killed in 1961. Either reading places the entry in the long shadow of that shooting and its reprisals.
cia-0000039010:

The record preserves a political demand: a sitting president put on trial. Such demands showed how killings and drug-era scandals shook Honduran public life. The file captures a moment when opposition parties used the language of the courts. Their target was a sitting president. Honduras was caught between its own politics and the wars around it.
cia-0000042810:

Inside, the suspects are identified as the president announced them. Naming soldiers broke the army's long shield of silence. It also bound Cristiani's own standing to the case's outcome. The file preserves the moment the accusation became official. The accused were no longer a rumor in the press. They were names spoken aloud by their own commander in chief.
cia-0000045210:
Venceremos reported a rift in the government over the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A rift at the top was exactly what rebel radio liked to report. Divisions over talks ran between the palace and the armed forces.

Inside, the rebels' account of the government's split is preserved. Exposing an enemy's quarrels is a classic aim of wartime radio. True or stretched, the story served the guerrillas' daily campaign. The file lets readers weigh their version against the government's own statements in this same set, and judge where the boasting ended and the real friction began.
cia-0000049010: A CIA item from 1981 names individuals assassinated by unidentified killers in El Salvador. The list form is the point: victim after victim, each with a name, each killer unknown. Lists like this one became raw material for the Truth Commission, which had to turn names into cases and cases into findings.
cia-0000049110: American support for the embassy's work on the Sheraton murder case is recorded in a CIA item from 1985. Two American labor advisers and a Salvadoran land-reform official were shot dead at the Sheraton hotel in 1981. The case became a test of whether killers in uniform, or beside it, could ever be tried.
cia-0000049310: El Salvador: Growing Rightist Dominance is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049310, dated October 6, 1980, and marked for the Truth Commission. It stands as an early agency reading of Salvadoran politics, kept in the declassified record under its original subject line.

It is a brief declassified review item whose heading frames a standard early-term check on a Salvadoran leader.

plos-pone-0004810:
Stefan Koestler and colleagues measured F- and G-actin concentrations in lamellipodia of moving cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells protrude by polymerizing monomeric G actin into polymeric F actin at the tip of the lamellipodium. Filaments depolymerize toward the rear in a treadmilling process, supplementing the G actin pool for new rounds of polymerization at the advancing front edge.

Direct concentration measurements test that classic model. Values show how much building material is available locally. Quantitative data constrain models of cell crawling. Crawling underlies wound healing, immunity, and cancer spread. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0005410:
Antibodies against two malaria parasite surface proteins, MSP3 and MSP6, help a protective mechanism that stops parasite growth. Both proteins share a small signature section at one end. Singh and colleagues extended that story to a whole gene family in PLOS ONE in 2009.

A conserved multi-gene family in Plasmodium falciparum induces cross-reactive antibodies. Cross-reactive means the antibodies hit several family members, not just one variant. Broad coverage is precious in malaria, where the parasite often escapes by varying its surface. Parts of this parasite stay the same while the rest of its coat shifts,. Those fixed parts are the spots where one vaccine might guard a child in Mali and a man in Brazil at the same time.
plos-pone-0005510:
Svenja Günther, Kai Matuschewski, and Sylke Müller knocked out a malaria gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Lipoic acid is a helper that lets key enzymes in cells handle fuel. The malaria parasite must attach this helper to its enzymes to keep growing in blood.

The team removed a parasite gene for one attaching enzyme and watched what happened. The parasites fared poorly in the blood stage, the stage that makes people ill. A step the parasite cannot do without is a promising target for new malaria drugs. The blood stage is also the stage that spreads back to mosquitoes, so weakening it could cut transmission as well.
plos-pone-0005610:
Adeel Safdar and co-authors studied small RNAs in mouse muscle after hard exercise in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. MicroRNAs tune gene activity after genes are read, and a few are known to guide muscle cell growth. What a single bout of endurance exercise does to them was less clear.

The team ran mice through acute endurance exercise and measured microRNAs in their skeletal muscle. The profile shifted with the workout, pointing to which genes muscle adjusts first. That helps explain how one exercise session starts the body's adaptation to training. Endurance exercise reshapes muscle over weeks, and this early response is where that reshaping begins.
plos-pone-0005710:
Heather Miller and colleagues sorted out the true job of a helper protein in HIV in 2009. The protein, Tat-SF1, was thought to help HIV's Tat switch on viral genes. It was found through lab mixes that rebuilt viral gene reading step by step.

Careful tests showed Tat-SF1 is not needed for Tat's switch-on work after all. Instead, it sets the balance between two forms of HIV RNA, cut and uncut. That balance decides which viral proteins get made. Correcting an old assumption keeps HIV research aimed at the right targets for drugs.
plos-pone-0005810:
Philip Liu and co-authors untangled in 2009 how two immune signals converge to arm human cells against germs. When a sensor on monocytes detects germs, the cell mounts a vitamin D dependent attack. A cytokine called IL-1 beta is part of that same defense web.

The team showed the IL-1 beta path and the vitamin D receptor path meet and reinforce each other. Together they drive the antimicrobial response triggered by the sensor. That meeting point helps explain why vitamin D status affects infection risk. It also suggests combined ways to boost innate defense.
plos-pone-0006410:
Maps of protein interactions grow faster than anyone can test them by hand. Hua Li and Shoudan Liang showed that local network topology in human protein interaction data predicts functional association, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. High-throughput techniques generate huge interaction volumes, needing methods that suggest functional relationships automatically.

In yeast networks, neighbourhood patterns had already hinted at shared functions. The human analysis extends that principle. Proteins whose local map positions resemble each other often work together. Automated hints let experimentalists spend bench time on the likeliest pairs. Such maps help labs choose which pairs of proteins to test first at the bench.
plos-pone-0006510:
Catherine Dostert and co-authors linked a leftover of malaria to fever and immune alarms in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria brings back fever attacks again and again. The germs that cause it feed on blood. As they feed, they leave behind a dark crystal waste called hemozoin. The team asked what this waste does to the body.

Their title says the crystal acts as a danger signal that sets off an immune alarm called the Nalp3 inflammasome. That alarm may help drive the fever and harm of the disease. The waste thus keeps the body on alert even as germs are cleared. Blocking that alarm could be a new way to treat severe cases.
plos-pone-0006610:
Corinne Berthonneche and co-authors charted cardiovascular traits across mouse strains in PLOS ONE in 2009. They report characterization of many cardiovascular-related traits in twenty-three inbred mouse strains. Mice were phenotyped either in response to chronic administration of a single drug or at baseline. The drugs blocked or activated beta-adrenergic signaling, a core heart control pathway.

Strain differences show how strongly genes shape drug responses. Such a panel helps researchers choose the right strain for a study. It also models human variability in response to beta blockers. The dataset is a resource for cardiovascular genetics.
plos-pone-0009410:
Yali Hou and co-authors published this dog breeding study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Canine hip dysplasia is a common inherited fault that cripples hips and burdens owners. A screening program for breeding dogs began in the United States in the 1960s. The team asked whether decades of screening actually improved hips.

They analyzed records of Labrador retrievers born from 1970 to 2007. The long cohort lets genetics separate steady improvement from year-to-year noise. Breeding programs are often run on faith; this audit checks the payoff. Its lessons reach any breed where inherited joint disease is selected against.
plos-pone-0009510:
Rita Guerreiro and colleagues examined a gene tied to Alzheimer's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Large genome scans had just flagged a gene called CLU as a risk factor. Such scans give a first hint, not a full account. The team read the gene in detail in patients and in controls. They hunted for variants that change risk.

Their work refined which parts of CLU matter for the disease. Confirming a scan hit with close reading helps separate true signals from noise. Each firm risk gene adds a clue about how the disease starts. CLU is thought to help clear harmful proteins, so its variants may point to new care ideas.
plos-pone-0009610:
Richard Gardner studied the first cell divisions of mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body's left and right sides are set very early in development. In mice, the young embryo normally rotates in a set direction as it grows. Gardner asked what decides that direction. His work points back to the embryo during its earliest cleavages. At that stage it is still a small ball of cells, and their makeup matters.

The way those first cells are composed biases which way the embryo turns. So a basic body pattern may be seeded before any organs form. The finding links the chemistry of the egg to the anatomy of the adult. It gives developmental biology a very early handle on left right patterning.
plos-pone-0010410:
Marcel Schmidt am Busch, Audrey Sedano and Thomas Simonson tested whether computer-designed proteins can help recognize protein shapes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recognizing a protein's fold usually relies on statistics from natural examples of that fold. The authors tried a different supply of examples: sequences invented by computational design. Designed sequences follow the same physics but are not found in nature.

If designed sets work as well, they could fill gaps where natural examples are scarce. The study validated the design method against known cases. It also weighed uses in searching for similar proteins and spotting folds. Protein shape predicts protein job, so better recognition speeds biology broadly. The work treats design as a way to learn, not just to build.
plos-pone-0010510:
Erbin Dai and colleagues blocked a chemical attraction system in donor tissue to protect mouse transplants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Immune cells home to grafts using chemokines, chemical beacons stuck to sugars called glycosaminoglycans. That binding builds the gradients cells follow. Most research targets chemokine receptors on cells. This team instead broke the beacon-to-sugar link inside the donor tissue itself.

Treated grafts suffered less vessel disease and less rejection. Protecting the graft before transplant is attractive, since the recipient's whole immune system stays untouched. Vessel disease in grafts is a leading cause of late transplant failure. A treatment applied once, to the organ, could have lasting benefit. This study demonstrates that strategy in mice.
plos-pone-0010610:
Joshua Cohen, Maria Staroselsky Dibner, and Andrew Wilson checked whether new drug money for neglected diseases was working, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Earlier studies blamed low funding for the lack of treatments. Funding then rose sharply, and the authors asked what it bought.

They tracked products in development and whether finished drugs reached patients. More projects had started, but access in poor countries still lagged. Price, delivery, and local health systems blocked many finished products. The lesson is blunt: funding research is only half the job if medicines never arrive.
plos-pone-0010710:
Casey Richardson and colleagues questioned gene labels in the model plant Arabidopsis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some listed genes are orphans with no known relatives or clear job. The team suspected some were wrongly labeled as protein-coding genes at all.

Genome-wide chips measured RNA read from both strands of DNA. Silencing tests then checked which readings were real. Several orphan genes matched antisense patterns, not true protein messages. Mislabels waste years of follow-up work across the field. Cleaning the catalog is slow, unglamorous labor that makes every later plant study more reliable.
plos-pone-0010810:
Stephanie Adams and colleagues studied how two forms of the tau protein interact, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tau normally supports the cell's internal tracks. In several dementias it piles into tangled filaments. The protein comes in three-repeat and four-repeat forms, named for a repeated segment, and diseases differ in which form piles up.

In test systems, the three-repeat form blocked the four-repeat form from building filaments. Mixing the forms thus slowed the very process that defines these diseases. The balance between forms may decide whether tangles form at all. Therapies that nudge that balance, even slightly, gain a clear rationale from this result.
plos-pone-0010910:
Atsushi Niida, Seiya Imoto, Rui Yamaguchi and co-authors published this bioinformatics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Each human tissue runs a different program of gene activity, written partly in regulatory codes near the genes. Earlier tools hunted those codes by comparing one tissue against all others, or by grouping genes that share a code, but both miss programs active in only some samples.

Their new method, BEEM, starts from gene sets sharing common regulatory motifs and then extracts tight expression modules across many tissues at once. Niida and colleagues designed it to catch programs switched on in a subset of tissues, exactly the blind spot of older tools. Decoding these shared codes helps explain how the same genome produces a liver cell and a neuron, and where that control breaks down in disease.
plos-pone-0011010:
Nelson Cuamba, John Morgan, Helen Irving and co-authors published this malaria vector study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anopheles funestus is a major African malaria mosquito, hard to breed in laboratories, so resistance in wild populations is under-studied. The team collected and reared thousands of larvae from Mozambique's Chokwe District to test the adults against insecticides.

Standard susceptibility assays showed extreme pyrethroid resistance: no deaths after the normal exposure time and under half even after more than double it. Resistance to a carbamate insecticide also appeared, but the mosquitoes stayed fully sensitive to DDT, ruling out one classic resistance mechanism. Cuamba and colleagues document a population that front-line bed net insecticides barely kill. Such field evidence is what malaria programs need before resistance turns into failed control.
plos-pone-0011110:
Lehmann, Lafferty, Garzino-Demo and colleagues studied HIV patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. They focused on a rare immune cell type that makes large amounts of interferon alpha, an alarm signal. In people with HIV, these cells were found gathering in the lymph nodes.

There, the cells kept releasing their alarm signal over time. Constant alarm may wear down the immune system instead of protecting it.
