That pattern helps explain why HIV causes lasting immune stress even as the virus attacks defenses. The finding may point to ways to calm harmful arousal while keeping real defense intact.
plos-pone-0011210:
Verde, Ruiz, Santiago and colleagues built a dosing tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. A blood thinning drug related to warfarin needs exact dosing: too little invites clots, too much risks bleeding. Two genes are known to shift how much drug a person needs.

The team combined variants of both genes into a single algorithm that predicts the right dose. Gene guided dosing could prevent dangerous bleeding events in new patients. It replaces early trial and error with a test based starting point. That is a concrete example of medicine tailored to a patient's DNA.
plos-pone-0011310:
Lindberg, Wijbrandts, Van Baarsen and colleagues profiled joint tissue in arthritis for PLOS ONE in 2010. A biologic drug helps many rheumatoid arthritis patients, but not all. The team read gene activity in the inflamed joint lining, called synovium, before treatment and tested whether that profile predicts who responds.

Gene patterns in the tissue did carry predictive signal for clinical response. A tissue based forecast could spare non responders months of ineffective treatment and side effects. It moves joint care toward matching drugs to patients in advance. Biopsy guided choice is demanding, so the study also motivates a search for simpler blood based versions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1210: On 29 July 1945 the Acting Secretary of State in Washington wrote to the Secretary of State at Potsdam. It is a home-office message between the department's two leading men, sent in the summit's final days. Joseph Grew held the acting post while James Byrnes led the team in Germany. Word between them kept the department's two halves in step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1310:
Stimson wrote to Harrison on 23 July 1945. The war secretary's replies kept the Interim Committee's work aligned with the summit's course. By that date the American leaders were settling how the new weapon would enter the war's endgame.

A note on this channel carried the atomic file's direction from the man who owned it. Stimson's hand guided both the committee in Washington and the brief at Potsdam. This message is his guidance at the second week's start. It belongs to the small set of papers through which the bomb's use was shaped, far from any public eye.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1410:
Caffery sent a fifth cable to Secretary Byrnes on 6 August 1945, part of the densest single-day run in the volume's French papers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Five cables in a day from one post is close to a paper siege. Caffery knew Washington's habits and pressed his case while the Potsdam results were still fresh and open to shaping. Each cable in the run takes its own file or point, so readers should not expect repeats. Together they show an ambassador using the cable room as an instrument, and they give the French section of the volume its driving rhythm.
frus-1945-50-intel-d10:
Tamm sent Hoover another inside memorandum on 17 September 1945. The FBI's leadership was tracking the intelligence reorganization plans day by day that month. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff papers like Tamm's kept Hoover briefed on moves by the White House, the Budget Bureau, and the military services. Each report sharpened the bureau's sense of where the new central agency might cut into FBI ground. For readers, the value is in the accumulation: the volume prints the bureau's watch in near-real time. This memorandum is one tick of that clock, three days before the president dissolved the OSS and redrew the map.
frus-1945-50-intel-d110:
Souers wrote to Hoover of the FBI on 19 April 1946. The new director of central intelligence addressing the FBI's chief opened the most delicate channel in the volume. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The CIG and the FBI divided the world between them in theory. Foreign work went to the group. Home work and Latin America stayed contested, by wartime claim. Every letter between their chiefs walked that border. Readers can read Souers's approach to Hoover as diplomacy between sovereigns, which, in bureau terms, it was. The exchange that follows in the volume, letters and counter-letters through 1946, decided how America's two secret empires would share a hemisphere.
frus-1945-50-intel-d210:
Dated 14 March 1947, this memorandum runs from George M. Elsey to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford). The State Department prints it as document 210 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d310:
On 1 June 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Members of His Staff. It stands as document 310 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was settling into its shape, while the Dulles Report's advice worked its way through office after office.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d410:
Fisher Howe, deputy special assistant for research and intelligence at the State Department, wrote to Sheppard on 9 January 1950. Sheppard served as a special assistant to the Secretary. The memo is document 410 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The note moves from the intelligence bureau to the Secretary's inner office in one step. Such short links mattered, since the bureau's reports did no good if they sat unread. Readers can see how State Department analysts kept a path open to the top of their own house. Sheppard's desk was a gate through which many such notes had to pass to reach the Secretary.
frus-1861-d10:
Joseph Wright wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1861. The dispatch is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

By late June both sides were in the field, and Europe watched for a quick result. Wright's reports kept his corner of that watch. The letter shows the plain, dated rhythm by which far posts fed a capital that could not see events for itself. Each dated page added one more fixed point to a map Washington drew from afar. Fixed points like this one let later readers chart the war's foreign course.
frus-1861-d110:
A letter of 24 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons at the British legation.

The matched dates show the machine in motion: the Navy chief reports, the State chief answers abroad. Seward's note to Lyons carries the product of that inner talk. It is a small, clear case of how the Union turned sea power into diplomacy. Such matched dates let readers watch the inner talk become foreign policy in a day. One day from inner talk to foreign note was swift work for the age of sail and steam.
frus-1861-d210:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Wood on 22 August 1861. It was printed as Document 210 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d310:
Writing on 7 September 1861, Mr. Dryer sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 310 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d10:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 January 1862. It was printed as Document 10 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d110:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 25 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 110 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d210:
Lord Lyons replied into the file on 21 February 1862 with a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 210 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both men wrote on the same day, a sign of active business between them.

Same-day exchanges usually mean a matter was moving fast or a deadline pressed. Lyons wrote as Britain's eyes in Washington as well as its voice, reporting home on all Seward said and did. A note from his hand in February belongs to the routine that kept a hard relationship workable through the war's first full winter. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d310:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the September Paris mail with a dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 15 September 1862, printed as Document 310 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-September found Lee's army in Maryland and the Union's foreign standing at its lowest point of the year. France had drafted a plan to propose a truce, and Britain was considering it. Seward's letter to Dayton that day went out two days before Antietam, into the most dangerous fortnight the Union faced abroad during the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d410:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry in Madrid on 15 September 1862. It is Document 410 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Mid-September 1862 was a hinge of the war: Lee's army was in Maryland, and Lincoln waited on a victory before issuing his emancipation order. Foreign courts held back, waiting on the same news. Seward's letters in these days armed his agents with the Union's reading of events. For the Madrid legation, that meant pressing Spain to see a government that meant to win, and to keep its ports closed to Confederate use.
frus-1862-d510:
On 23 July 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote again from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous report. The dispatch is Document 510 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reports in a bad month had a hard job. They had to be truthful. Yet they must not give Washington fresh cause for worry it could not act on. Pike's July letters did that job plainly, recording Dutch steadiness while Union arms regrouped. He also tracked the war's naval fringe, where Dutch colonial ports had rules to enforce. The letter continues a correspondence notable for its regularity. In the whole of 1862, few American posts wrote home as often as Pike's. Fewer still wrote as frankly.
frus-1862-d610:
Thomas Corwin received the year's closing Mexican order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 21 October 1862. It is Document 610 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

October's instruction reached Mexico as the French settled in for a long war and as Washington, steadied by Antietam, took stock of its foreign position. The policy Seward repeated to Corwin had not changed in a year: friendship for Mexico's republic, refusal to accept the European enterprise, and patience. Within two years a freed Union army would stand on the Rio Grande and the patience would end. The letter is a fitting close to the volume's most principled American file.
frus-1862-d710:
On 13 September 1862, Andrew B. Dickinson wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second day in a row. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 710 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Two reports on two days point to a post with much to tell. From Nicaragua, an envoy tracked the transit route, the local government's acts, and the safety of Americans passing through. Dickinson's letters fed that watch. Kept in the volume, they show the pace of a small legation's work when events moved fast and mail home was slow.
frus-1863p1-d10:
On 8 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. A second letter to Adams bears the same date in the volume. This one is document 10 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote as the year turned, with the war at a grim point and Europe still weighing its course. His letters told Adams what to say and what to hold back in talks with the British. Paired sheets like these show the secretary working a brief in parts. This letter belongs to that pair, and to the long chain that bound Washington to its London post.
frus-1863p1-d110:
On 6 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 110 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Early March found the legation deep in the ship question, as Southern warships took shape in British yards. Adams's mail pressed the facts on Washington and, through his talks, on the British themselves. This letter is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the post in its spring rhythm: watch, report, and press, week after week.
frus-1863p1-d210:
A dispatch dated 5 June 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 210 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d310:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 October 1862. His note is document 310 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Seward answered the legation knowing London would read every word. Even routine notes carried weight, because each answer set a precedent for the next dispute. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d410:
On 5 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 410 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d510:
The date 13 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d610:
The letter printed as document 610 was written on 13 August 1863 by Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
plos-pbio-0020110:
Vincenzo Costanzo, Tanya Paull, and Max Gottesman examined a DNA damage alarm protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mre11 gathers with partner proteins where DNA breaks. The team found that Mre11 can also line up short, straight DNA pieces and build signaling groups on them.

Those groups switch on the cell's damage response, the system that pauses growth and starts repair. Showing that Mre11 can assemble them on simple DNA helps explain how the alarm starts so fast. Faults in this system cause human disorders with high cancer risk. A clear view of the first steps gives researchers firm ground for studying those diseases.
plos-pone-0000110:
K. P. Arunkumar and Javaregowda Nagaraju surveyed insect and worm DNA in PLOS ONE in 2006. A palindrome in DNA reads the same forward and backward. The control region of the mitochondrial genome, which manages how that genome is copied, turned out to hold unusually long palindromes in insects and nematodes.

Long palindromes can fold the DNA into hairpin shapes, which may help or hinder copying. Finding them concentrated in the control region hints they do a job there rather than sitting as clutter. The survey spans many species, so the pattern is broad. It gives genome readers a feature to check when they sequence new mitochondrial genomes, and a clue about how those genomes run.
plos-pone-0000210:
José Fayos and Carolina Fayos published this applied computing paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It uses Kohonen neural networks, a type of self-organizing map, to mine wind data. Data mining here means sorting large wind records into patterns that forecasters and engineers can use.

Wind patterns drive weather forecasts, wind farm output, and building safety. A neural network that groups wind behavior into clear types can make those records easier to read. The paper shows the approach at work, an early example of machine learning applied to routine meteorological data.
plos-pone-0000310:
Isaias Glezer, Ariel Chernomoretz, Samuel David, and colleagues published this neuroimmunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inflammation in the nervous system can save neurons or kill them. The authors identify genes involved in the balance between neuronal survival and death during inflammation.

Which way inflammation tips decides outcomes in stroke, injury, and diseases like multiple sclerosis. A gene list for that balance gives researchers defined targets to push toward survival. The work maps the molecular side of a long-observed clinical puzzle. The pattern also offers a way to test drugs meant to protect neurons during brain inflammation.
plos-pone-0000410:
David Bressler, Nicole Spotswood, and David Whitney reported a surprising brain signal in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In fMRI scans, most active brain areas show a stronger blood signal, but some show a negative one, a dip called the negative BOLD response. It was often treated as noise or as mere shutdown. The team tested what the dip in the visual cortex actually carries.

The authors found that the negative response holds precise, stimulus-specific information about what the person was seeing. That makes the dip a signal worth reading rather than discarding. Brain imaging studies that use it could extract more detail about how the visual system represents the world.
plos-pone-0000510:
Maxence Vieux-Rochas and colleagues used vitamin A's active form to probe how vertebrate jaws arose, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Retinoic acid can cause craniofacial malformations when its levels are wrong during development. The team studied the molecular dynamics of those malformations, drawing implications for the origin of gnathostome jaws, the hinged jaws of most vertebrates.

Jaws were a revolution in animal evolution, and their origin from gill arches is a classic problem. A chemical that predictably reshapes the face exposes the gene circuits that pattern it. Linking those circuits to the jaw's first appearance connects a birth-defect mechanism to one of evolution's biggest inventions.
plos-pone-0000610:
Enikö Sonkoly and colleagues asked whether tiny RNA regulators help drive a common skin disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that fine-tune gene activity. The paper was titled MicroRNAs: Novel Regulators Involved in the Pathogenesis of Psoriasis? It examined their role in psoriasis. In that disease, skin cells multiply too fast and inflammation persists.

If microRNAs are mis-set in psoriatic skin, they could explain changes across many genes at once, a pattern single-gene studies struggled to unify. The question mark in the title was honest for 2007. MicroRNA research was young. The paper was among the early tests of its reach into skin disease.
plos-pone-0000710:
Eleanor M. Weston, Adrian E. Friday and Pietro Liò measured faces for evidence that mate choice shaped human evolution. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study considers sex differences in facial structure in the context of development. At puberty, the height of the upper face, between lip and brow, develops differently in males and females. Those differences, they show, are not explicable by simple size or growth accounts alone.

Biometric evidence of that kind supports sexual selection as the shaping force. Faces carry signals used in judging mates, so selection could sculpt them directly. If so, the hominin face records social and mating pressures, not just diet, climate, and ancestry.
plos-pone-0000810:
Lucia Regales, Marissa N. Balak, Yixuan Gong and colleagues built mice whose lung tumors carry a drug-resistance mutation, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The EGFR T790M mutation confers acquired resistance to kinase inhibitors in human lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR mutations. It is occasionally detected before treatment, and may also confer genetic susceptibility to lung cancer. Studying its role in tumor formation needed a living model.

The team developed mice with lung tumors expressing the T790M mutant. Such models let researchers watch resistance arise, and test next-generation inhibitors against it in a whole animal. Lung cancer drugs often fail exactly at this mutation, so a faithful model is strategic ground for drug development.
plos-pone-0000910:
Nicola Viebig, Emily Levin, Sebastien Dechavanne and colleagues disabled a malaria gene and watched what changed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Malaria in pregnancy is a major cause of illness and death for mothers and newborns. Much of the harm comes from infected red blood cells sticking in the placenta in huge numbers.

The sticking depends on a parasite gene called var2csa. The team disrupted that gene and report that the placental adhesion trait was impaired. A result like this matters for vaccine hopes: a protein needed for sticking is a natural target. It also confirms, by removal, what var2csa actually does.
plos-pone-0001010:
Tara Young, Michael Tsai, Bin Tian and colleagues showed that ordinary gene messages can free a stalled transcription engine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A factor called P-TEFb is a key regulator that lets gene reading run at full length. It first drew wide notice as a factor HIV needs to copy itself.

P-TEFb is often held back by a small RNA called 7SK. The team report that cellular messenger RNA can activate transcription elongation by displacing that 7SK RNA. In other words, the products of gene reading help release the brake on further reading. The finding adds a feedback loop to a central control in gene expression.
plos-pone-0001110:
Cedric Laguri, Rabia Sadir, Patricia Rueda and colleagues characterized a new variant of a cell guiding signal, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CXCL12 is a chemokine that steers cell migration and tissue homing for many cell types. It works through its receptor CXCR4 and through heparan sulfate, a sugar chain on cell surfaces.

An alternative splicing route produces a gamma isoform with an extra piece. The team show that piece is an unstructured, positively charged domain that regulates the signal's activity and its binding to both partners. A tail that changes grip changes where cells are sent. Migration signals guide development, immunity and cancer spread alike.
plos-pone-0001210:
Histones are the spool proteins DNA wraps around, and chemical marks on them help control gene activity. Kangling Zhang and colleagues catalogued those marks in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Studies in mammals and yeast had found some marks conserved at the same positions and others unique.

The authors report distinctive core histone post-translational modification patterns in Arabidopsis. Post-translational modifications are chemical tags added after a protein is built. A plant-specific map of these tags supports work on gene regulation in crops and in the field's favorite model plant.
plos-pone-0001310:
Therapeutic antibodies are often built as chimeras: mouse variable regions, which grab the target, joined to human constant regions, which the body tolerates. Marcela Torres and colleagues asked whether the constant regions are truly interchangeable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They exchanged murine and human immunoglobulin constant chains and measured the consequences.

The authors report effects on the kinetics and thermodynamics of antigen binding, and on chimeric antibody autoreactivity. In other words, the supposedly passive half of the antibody changes how the working half behaves. Antibody engineers need to know that the scaffold is not neutral.
plos-pone-0001410:
Aurore Schneider, Jonathan Garlick, and Christophe Egles wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gel that may speed wound healing. Skin wounds that fail to heal cause lasting harm and high care costs. The team used tiny self building protein fibers as a scaffold for repair. They combined this nano scale tool with skin care methods.

In their tests, the fiber scaffold sped the closing of the wound surface. New skin grew over the wound at a faster rate. A scaffold that the body takes well could help chronic wounds that now resist care. The work is an early step toward dressings built at the level of molecules.
plos-pone-0001510:
Ashverya Laxmi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on light and a plant hormone carrier. Light steers many steps of plant growth. Root growth is shaped by light sensed in the shoot, with the hormone auxin as the courier. The team asked how light moves a key auxin carrier inside root cells of Arabidopsis.

They show light is vital for where the carrier, called PIN2, sits in the cell. That seat sets the flow of auxin through the root. A light to carrier link helps explain how shoots and roots grow in step. It also matters for crops grown under changed light.
plos-pone-0001610:
Melanie Sekeres and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on gaps in trial registers. Since 2004, top journals have asked that all trials be logged in a public register at the start. World and journal bodies set what each log should hold. The team checked how well logs report who leads each trial on the science side.

They found leadership facts are oft left poor or blank in the logs. That gap hides who is in charge and who to hold to account. Registers can only build trust if their fields are filled with care. The study gives register keepers a clear fix list.
plos-pone-0001710:
Jing Huang, Qini Gan, Limin Han, and their co-authors studied a lifespan-linked protein in aging human cells for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Sir2, a protein that uses NAD to remove chemical tags from other proteins, modulates lifespan in yeast, worms, and flies. Its mammal counterpart is SIRT1, which also helps cells survive stress.

The team asked whether extra SIRT1 can fight ordinary cellular senescence, the state where old cells stop dividing. They report that SIRT1 overexpression antagonizes senescence, with the ERK and S6k1 pathways switched on. The full text gives the fibroblast tests and the pathway data. The work adds molecular detail to the long-running question of whether sirtuin-boosting drugs could slow cell aging.
plos-pone-0001810:
Chia-Chyi Liu, Shiang-Chi Lee, Michael Butler, and their co-authors compared vaccine production cells for dengue virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dengue has four serotypes, DEN-1 to DEN-4, and a vaccine must grow all of them stably. The team investigated replication kinetics of the four serotypes in Vero cells and MRC-5 cells grown on Cytodex 1 microcarriers. One virus, DEN-4, was recovered from an infectious cDNA clone.

They report high genetic stability of dengue virus propagated in MRC-5 cells compared with Vero cells. The full text gives the growth curves and mutation counts. A production cell line that keeps the virus unchanged is valuable, since drift during manufacture can weaken or alter a vaccine.
plos-pone-0001910:
Annalisa Grimaldi and co-authors used treated mats to draw stem cells out of tissue in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Stem cells take their cues to become a given cell type from signals around them. Though research is intense, how this shaping works at the base level is still not fully clear.

The team placed mats soaked with growth factors into living tissue, then gathered the cells that moved in. The trapped cells showed a range of traits, giving the lab many cell types to study from one pull. A simple way to harvest stem cells where they live could aid both basic study and future repair work.
plos-pone-0002010:
Zhong-jin Yang and co-authors tested an artificial oxygen carrier's effect on brain blood flow in rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The carrier, Oxycyte, is a perfluorocarbon emulsion that carries oxygen far better, volume for volume, than blood. The brain guards its own blood flow tightly to meet its need for fuel.

The team thinned the rats' blood to a set volume with the emulsion and measured regional flow in the brain. If a blood substitute starves or floods the brain, it is not safe, however well it carries oxygen. Flow data of this kind are a needed safety check before human use.
plos-pone-0002110:
Agata Kolodziejczyk and co-authors catalogued signal chemicals in the first relay of the fly's visual system, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The lamina is the most peripheral synaptic region of the fruit fly's visual system, and its wiring has been comprehensively described. It is used as a model for how synapses develop and adapt, yet its neurotransmitters were less fully mapped.

The team charted components of signaling by glutamate, GABA, and acetylcholine, three main nerve messengers, in lamina cells. A chemical parts list completes the wiring diagram: form plus chemistry is what a circuit model needs to predict behavior.
plos-pone-0002210:
Nicole Cameron and co-authors studied how a rat mother's care shapes her daughters' later reproductive life, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In humans, early family life predicts the age of puberty, teen sexual activity, and the age of first pregnancy. Like patterns appear in other species, where mothers pass effects to offspring without changing DNA.

The team examined how varied maternal care in rats programs sexual behavior and the hormone system that runs reproduction, the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Their work shows early care can set lifelong patterns in the brain and body. Findings like these frame how early life gets under the skin.
plos-pone-0002310:
Ayelet Di Segni, Keren Farin, and Ronit Pinkas-Kramarski reported a new binding partner for a family of cancer receptors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The ErbB receptor family sits on cell surfaces and drives growth signals. These receptors are major contributors to malignant change and are overproduced in many human cancers.

The authors identify nucleolin, a protein best known from the nucleus, as a new interacting partner of ErbB receptors. A partner can change how a receptor signals, how long it stays active, and how drugs reach it. Each new connection in the ErbB web offers another point where cancer signaling might be interrupted.
plos-pone-0002410:
A research team led by Zhang reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jingxian Zhang, Balasubramanyam Addepalli, Kil-Young Yun, and others. Its subject is a Polyadenylation Factor Subunit Implicated in Regulating Oxidative Signaling in Arabidopsis thaliana. Plants respond to many unfavorable environmental conditions via signaling mediated by altered levels of various reactive oxygen species (ROS).

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002510:
Work from Edwards and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Albert O. Edwards, Sung J. Lee, Brooke L. Fridley, and others. Its subject is density of Common Complex Ocular Traits in the Aging Eye: Analysis of Secondary Traits in Genome-Wide Association Studies. Genetic association studies are identifying genetic risks for common complex ocular traits such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

The subjects used for discovery of these loci have been largely from clinic-based, case-control studies. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002610:
In 2008, Hiroi and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Makoto Hiroi, Teiichi Tanimura, Frédéric Marion-Poll, and others. Its subject is hedonic Taste in Drosophila Revealed by Olfactory Receptors Expressed in Taste Neurons. Taste and olfaction are each tuned to a unique set of chemicals in the outside world.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002710:
Catriona M. Harris led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was evaluating the influence of epidemiological parameters and host ecology on the spread of phocine distemper virus through populations of harbour seals. The catalog record names Catriona M. Harris first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Outbreaks of phocine distemper virus (PDV) in Europe during 1988 and 2002 were responsible for the death of around 23,000 and 30,000 harbour seals. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002810:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Mariana Gil and colleagues addresses does an insect's unconditioned response to sucrose reveal expectations of reward?. Authorship is credited in the record to Mariana Gil and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. We asked whether and how a sequence of a honeybee's experience with different reward magnitudes changes its subsequent unconditioned proboscis extension response (PER) to. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002910:
James Doroghazi and Daniel Buckley examined how soil bacterial communities are spread out in 2008. Ecologists describe such patterns with a species abundance distribution, which shows how many kinds are common and how many are rare. For microbes, the shape of that pattern had been hard to pin down.

Using a fingerprinting method called GC-TRFLP, the PLOS ONE study found evidence that soil bacterial communities follow a lognormal pattern. In that pattern, most kinds sit at middling counts with a long tail of rare ones. The result helps soil ecologists compare communities on a shared footing.
plos-pone-0003010:
Adam Coleman, Xiuli Yang, Manish Kumar and co-authors tested a Lyme disease protein long thought to aid immune evasion in 2008. Borrelia burgdorferi cycles between Ixodes ticks and mammal hosts. It makes at least five surface proteins that acquire complement regulators, thought to help it resist host defense.

One of them, CRASP-2, does not contribute to complement resistance or host infectivity, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, a clean negative result prunes the list of true evasion factors. Vaccine and drug efforts against Lyme disease can focus on proteins that actually matter. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003110:
Andreas Martin Lisewski applied information theory to protein folding errors in 2008. Transmission of genomic information from coding sequence to protein structure during synthesis is subject to random errors. Shannon's noisy channel theorem, from communication theory, sets limits on reliable transmission despite noise.

Random amino acid mutations and protein misfolding lead to a Shannon limit in sequence-structure communication, the title claims. Published in PLOS ONE, the framing treats the cell as a channel with a capacity limit. That view may explain why error rates in translation sit where they do. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003210:
Szymon M. Kiełbasa and Martin Vingron study self-regulating genes across vertebrates in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Feedback loops are the simplest building blocks of transcriptional regulatory networks, so their behaviour over evolution is of prime interest. The authors address whether the number of autoregulatory feedback loops is enriched in higher organisms. They begin by analysing such loops in available data.

The title reports that transcriptional autoregulatory loops are highly conserved in vertebrate evolution. Readers see a basic circuit kept across long spans of time, which suggests it does essential work. Conservation maps like this help separate core control design from lineage-specific extras.
plos-pone-0003310:
Lidia De Filippis, Daniela Ferrari, Laura Rota Nodari and colleagues immortalize human neural stem cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human neural stem cells represent an essential source of renewable brain cells for both experimental studies and cell replacement therapies. Their relatively slow rate of proliferation and physiological senescence in culture make their use cumbersome under some experimental conditions.

The team use the c-Myc mutant T58A to immortalize the cells. Readers get a method to expand brain stem cells without the usual slowdown. A stable supply is needed before cell therapy or drug screening with human neurons can scale up.
plos-pone-0007410:
Xi-Qin Ding, Alexander B. Quiambao, J. Browning Fitzgerald, and colleagues tested eye gene delivery safety in mice in 2009. Delivery under the retina of compacted DNA nanoparticles produces efficient gene expression in retinal cells. The nanoparticles use a polyethylene glycol substituted peptide to compact DNA into tiny particles that cells can take up.

The authors evaluate ocular safety of those compacted nanoparticles. They report delivery does not elicit toxicity in the mouse retina. Safety is the gate for retinal gene therapy, because the eye cannot tolerate inflammation well. Their result supports further development of non-viral eye treatments.
plos-pone-0007510:
Ildefonso De la Fuente and colleagues published a theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the stable core of cell chemistry. Studies of single-celled organisms show a set of enzymes that stays active at all times. That set is called the metabolic core. Around it, other reactions switch on and off. The team asked what makes such a core appear in the first place.

Their models point to the number of catalytic elements as the crucial factor. When enough reacting components are present, a stable core emerges on its own. Below that threshold, the chemistry stays unsettled. That rule of thumb could help predict how real cells organize their metabolism. It also speaks to deeper questions about how orderly chemistry arises from many simple parts. The core is an outcome of numbers, not design.
plos-pone-0007610:
José López-Bao and colleagues published a field study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was the Iberian lynx, one of the world's most at-risk wild cats. Teams that guard such animals sometimes leave out extra food. The food may be meant for cats whose lives or litters are most at risk. Whether cats of each sex and age use that food in equal shares was not known. The team watched who ate at the feeding sites.

The strongest lynx took over the extra food. Access skewed by sex and age, so the gains were not shared alike. A plan meant to help the neediest may instead feed the strongest. That warning holds for feeding plans aimed at many kinds of wildlife. Good aims need checks on who truly gains. The study shows a care tool can widen gaps inside the very group it aims to save.
plos-pone-0007710:
Nobuaki Kono and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It introduces a web tool called Pathway Projector for viewing biochemical pathways. Pathway maps give context for the flood of data from modern experiments. They show how the parts of a cell work as a system.

The tool builds on the KEGG Atlas maps and the Google Maps interface. Users can zoom and pan across huge pathway charts, much like a street map. Layers of experimental data can be placed on top. The browser aims to do for pathway research what genome browsers did for DNA sequences.
plos-pone-0007810:
Dian-Bing Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It develops a fast test for the anthrax bacterium, Bacillus anthracis. The germ can be used as a biological threat agent. Quick, simple detection is vital for defense and for medicine.

Anthrax exists as hardy spores and as growing vegetative cells. Most tests catch one form or the other. The team raised monoclonal antibodies that detect both forms with the same reagents. They report three antibodies with high affinity and specificity. A single test for both forms would speed field screening in an emergency.
plos-pone-0007910:
Marjo den Broeder and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It creates a zebrafish model of fragile X syndrome. Fragile X is one of the most common known causes of inherited intellectual disability. The mutated gene, FMR1, is conserved from humans to fruit flies.

To study FMR1 during vertebrate development, the team knocked the gene out in zebrafish. They describe the generation and characterization of the mutant fish. Zebrafish develop fast and can be watched under a microscope. A fish model lets researchers screen drugs cheaply. It also tests what FMR1 does as a body is being built.
plos-pone-0008010:
Jeroen Pennings and colleagues mined data for better pregnancy screening markers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Screening for Down syndrome uses proteins in the mother's blood, drawn from the placenta or the baby's liver. The current set misses some cases and flags others wrongly.

Rather than test proteins one by one in the lab, the team sifted gene and protein data for strong candidates first. Their short list gives labs a focused set to check. Better markers would mean fewer mothers sent for risky follow-up tests and fewer cases missed before birth.
plos-pone-0008110:
Kwadwo Kusi and colleagues mixed several forms of a malaria protein to widen a vaccine's reach in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, AMA1, helps the parasite break into red blood cells. Its shape varies by strain, so a vaccine built on one form may miss others.

Animals given the mixed vaccine made antibodies that knew all the forms in the mix, not just one. Breadth is the whole game against a shape-shifting foe. The result backs the cocktail approach for malaria vaccines, even though mixing raises the work of making and testing them.
plos-pone-0008210:
Paola Sebastiani and colleagues studied genes linked to extreme old age in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Living to very old ages runs in families, which suggests genes play a role. Most genes found so far act in fat metabolism or insulin signaling. Many more longevity genes likely remain undiscovered. The team looked in an unexpected place: RNA editing genes.

They linked these genes both to extreme old age in humans and to lifespan in roundworms. Using two species strengthens the case for a real effect. RNA editing changes RNA after it is copied from DNA. The findings open a fresh angle on the biology of aging.
plos-pone-0008310:
Kanae Iijima-Ando and colleagues modeled Alzheimer's disease in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Amyloid-beta 42 is thought to play a central role in the disease. How it causes neuronal dysfunction and degeneration remains elusive. Mitochondrial problems are seen in Alzheimer's brains. Whether those problems cause the damage was an open question.

In the fly model, mitochondria ended up in the wrong places within neurons. That mislocalization underlay the dysfunction caused by amyloid-beta 42. Neurons need mitochondria positioned where energy demand is high. The study links a small transport failure to large brain effects.
plos-pone-0008410:
André Ouédraogo and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how malaria spreads by mosquito. For a mosquito to pick up malaria, the blood it drinks must hold the sex stage of the germ, called a gametocyte. These stages are most times few and far in the blood. Counts too low for a scope to see may still be high enough to infect a biting mosquito. How much weight such low counts carry was not known.

In a land where malaria comes with the rains, they weighed the share of these faint carriers. Such carriers gave a large part of all the spread to mosquitoes. Plans that find just the cases a scope can see will miss this pool. The work backs the use of more keen tests.
plos-pone-0008510:
Claire Salzer and co-authors map eye change hot spots in fruit flies in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A gene network called the retinal determination network governs early eye growth. It is conserved across the animal kingdom. Switching its members on in the wrong tissue can transform that tissue toward retina. Such ectopic eyes have long fascinated biologists. The team ask which tissues are most prone to transform.

They identify hot spots in developing fly epithelia where transformation occurs readily. Epithelia are sheets of cells that cover body surfaces. Hot spots reveal where the network's signals meet a receptive state. The map helps explain how organ identity can be reprogrammed.
plos-pone-0008610:
Nicole Meyer-Morse and co-authors study a cell defense during listeria infection in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The defense is autophagy, where cells digest their own parts and invaders. Past studies said it helps protect cells from Listeria, a germ that causes foodborne illness. The team find it has no clear role in the germ's escape or growth in macrophages. Instead they focus on a toxin the germ makes, called listeriolysin O.

They show that toxin alone is enough to trigger autophagy. No other germ factor is needed for that effect. The toxin lets the germ escape its compartment in the cell. Autophagy in this infection is thus a response to the toxin itself.
plos-pone-0008710:
Raquel López-Fontal, Miriam Zeini, Paqui Través, and colleagues asked what a thyroid receptor does during liver repair. Their mouse study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. A liver can regrow after part of it is surgically removed. Thyroid hormone T3 was suspected to help that regrowth. Which receptor carries the signal was unclear, though.

The team used mice lacking the beta form of the receptor. After surgery, those livers showed more cell death. They also started their regrowth program later than normal livers. The delay names the beta receptor as a real player in repair.
plos-pone-0008810:
Farhad Karbassi, Veronica Quiros, Vijay Pancholi, and colleagues took apart an eight-piece bacterial enzyme. Their structural study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enolase is a workhorse enzyme in sugar breakdown. Most versions join as pairs of subunits. The Streptococcus pyogenes version stacks eight subunits in a ring of pairs. What held that bigger assembly together was unclear.

Breaking the octamer apart showed its interfaces support each other. Weakening one contact destabilized another contact far away. Cooperating interfaces explain the assembly's toughness. The lesson extends to many multi-part protein machines, including drug targets in germs.
plos-pone-0008910:
Celina Montemayor, Oscar Montemayor, Alex Ridgeway, and colleagues hunted the true target genes of a lonely receptor. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. NR2F1, also called COUP-TFI, is a nuclear receptor with no known natural activator. Such orphan receptors still control many body processes. Finding their direct gene targets in living tissue is hard. Binding alone does not prove control.

The team intersected genome-wide binding maps with gene activity data. Only genes passing both tests counted as direct targets. A verified target list grounds the receptor's role in development. The method itself can be reused for other orphan receptors.
plos-pone-0009010:
Anne-Katrin Rohlfing and co-authors found that salt stress can fool a worm's immune alarms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans lives in soil and is a favourite lab animal. Infection by bacteria or fungi switches on a clear set of defence genes. The team studied genes that respond instead to osmotic stress, meaning water imbalance.

Turning on the salt-stress genes copied much of the infection pattern. The similarity suggests the two alarm systems share wiring. That overlap makes sense for a worm meeting germs and drying soil together. It also warns researchers that a defence signature may not always mean infection.
plos-pone-0009110:
Judith Reinhard and co-authors worked out how honeybees make sense of blended smells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bee meets dozens of complex floral scents on her rounds every day. Each flower's perfume is a blend of many different odorant chemicals. How the bee's small brain unravels those mixtures was still unclear.

Bees, the team found, latch onto a few key odorants within a blend. They learn the whole mixture through those standout parts alone. The rest of the scent simply fades into the background for them. A key-odorant shortcut keeps the bee's crowded world of smells manageable.
plos-pone-0009210:
Ziad Al Tanoury and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines L-plastin, a protein that bundles actin fibers inside cells. Actin bundles give cells shape and help them move. L-plastin was first found in white blood cells and in many cancers, where it serves as a marker.

A phosphate tag on one spot of L-plastin makes it grip actin more strongly. The team measured the speed and strength of that bundling in detail. They also tracked how L-plastin changes the turnover of actin fibers. Those numbers explain how a single small tag can reshape the cell's skeleton, a process that matters in cancer spread.
plos-pone-0009310:
Lisa Rohan and co-authors published this HIV prevention study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tenofovir gel was in clinical trials as a microbicide, a gel women could use to block HIV infection. Oddly, no published pre-clinical testing of the gel existed. The team set out to supply that missing groundwork.

They tested tenofovir in lab dishes and in human tissue kept alive outside the body. In both models, the drug proved effective against HIV-1. Having lab results lets researchers validate what the clinical trials find in people. The study fills the bench side of the record for a leading prevention candidate.
plos-pone-0011410:
Wei Yao and co-authors reported in 2010 a surprising way to raise peak bone mass in female mice. Most of a lifetime's bone strength is built during the growth years, and hormones steer that building. The team blocked the progesterone receptor, a hormone sensor, only during the fast linear growth phase, then measured the adult skeleton.

Mice treated during growth ended with higher peak bone mass than untreated mice. Blocking a hormone signal lifting bone mass was unexpected, since progesterone is usually cast as a supporter of the skeleton. The result uncovers a hidden brake on bone building that acts during youth. If the same brake works in people, easing it at the right age could raise the bone reserve that protects against fractures and osteoporosis decades later.
plos-pone-0011510:
Marc Ancrenaz and co-authors surveyed forests in Sabah, Malaysia, in 2010 and found orang-utans holding on in lightly logged woods. Conservationists had assumed the apes need untouched old-growth forest, which would leave them little room as logging spreads across Borneo. The team surveyed the Ulu Segama Malua forests, where selective logging had taken some trees but left the forest standing.

Orang-utans of the local subspecies persisted in those slightly logged forests at levels suggesting the habitat can maintain them. That softens a doom narrative without removing the threat: heavy logging and clearing remain deadly. Carefully managed logging may buy time and space for the apes while stronger protection is built. For conservation planning, managed forests count as part of the solution, not only as part of the problem.
plos-pone-0011610:
Michelle Carey and colleagues tested common anti-inflammatory drugs during flu infection in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drugs block enzymes called COX-1 and COX-2, which help drive inflammation. Earlier work showed mice lacking COX-1 fared worse with flu, while mice lacking COX-2 fared better, raising questions about drug use during infection.

Carey and colleagues gave flu-infected mice blockers aimed at each enzyme and tracked illness and inflammation. Their results help separate helpful inflammation from harmful excess. For doctors, the findings matter because pain and fever drugs are widely used by flu patients every season.
plos-pone-0011710:
Valentina Neplioueva and co-authors mapped the reach of an RNA-binding protein across the genome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. RNA-binding proteins guide every stage of a message's life and let cells adjust gene activity quickly when conditions change. Their grip on target messages shifts with where the proteins sit inside the cell.

The team studied a double-stranded RNA-binding protein called protein 76, whose levels vary by tissue. They charted its tissue pattern and used genome-wide methods to list the messages it binds. That hit list shows how far one such protein's regulatory reach extends.
plos-pone-0011810:
Ondřej Kott, Radim Šumbera and Pavel Němec tested light perception in underground rodents, in PLOS ONE in 2010. African mole-rats live strictly below ground, are born with tiny eyes and are hardly ever exposed to light. Because they show no obvious reaction to light, they were long considered blind.

The authors examined two strictly subterranean species for any retained light sense. Their tests probe whether the animals live truly in the dark or still register blue light. Whatever vision lingers in such eyes informs how senses decay when evolution stops using them.
plos-pone-0011910:
Britta Muster and colleagues imaged living cells in 2010 to see how the energy machinery is arranged inside mitochondria. Mitochondria supply most of a cell's energy and constantly merge and split. Blocking that movement is tied to several nerve-degenerating diseases.

Inside these shifting organelles, the respiratory chain complexes, the protein machines that make energy, were not spread evenly. They sat in a patchy distribution across the inner membrane. A patchwork layout changes how scientists picture energy production: output may depend on where the machines cluster, not just how many exist. That view matters when explaining why disturbed mitochondrial movement leads to disease.
plos-pone-0012010:
Hideo Matsumura and colleagues combined in 2010 a digital gene-counting method with next-generation sequencing to handle many samples at once. The base method, SuperSAGE, cuts a short tag from each gene message, and counting tags gives a digital readout of gene activity. Sequencing had become fast enough to count tags for whole sets of samples in one run.

Their high-throughput version keeps the counting honest while scaling up to multiple samples. Digital counts avoid some distortions of older analog measures of gene activity. For projects comparing many tissues, treatments, or patients, a scalable counting method is the difference between a pilot and a real study.
plos-pone-0012210:
Scott Heron, Bette Willis, William Skirving, and co-authors modeled coral disease outbreaks on the Great Barrier Reef in PLOS ONE in 2010. White syndrome, a tissue-destroying coral disease, has struck the reef in waves, and hot water stress was already suspected as a trigger. Their model added the other half of the year, asking how winter conditions set the stage for summer outbreaks.

Linking hot snaps with the cold season before them gives forecasters a longer lead time on outbreak years. Reef managers could then watch the most at-risk areas closely or cut other stresses, like pollution, ahead of a predicted outbreak. For a reef under climate pressure, advance warning is one of the few tools left.
plos-pone-0012310:
Jean-Philip Truman, Mónica García-Barros, Matthew Kaag, and co-authors studied how precise radiation treatment interacts with vessel-blocking therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Combining anti-vessel drugs with radiation was a popular hope, yet trials had gained little, mostly because nobody knew exactly how vessel blockade changes radiation's effect. Their setting was radiosurgery, the tightly focused high-dose radiation used on small tumors.

They found the tumor's vessel lining must remodel its membranes for the anti-vessel drug to sensitize the tumor to radiation. A required step like this explains uneven trial results and tells doctors which tumors and timings should benefit. It turns a failed combination into a recipe with conditions attached.
plos-pone-0012410:
Marc Pearton, Sang-Moo Kang, Jae-Min Song and colleagues examined skin immune cells after a flu-like vaccine shot, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Langerhans cells sit in the skin and are first responders when a vaccine enters through it. How they change shape and move right after vaccination in human skin was largely unknown, a gap for teams designing needle-free skin vaccines.

Using human skin samples given virus-like particle vaccines, the team tracked early changes in these cells. The particles stirred the cells and set them moving, a good sign for skin delivery. The work gives vaccine designers concrete early readouts to compare delivery methods before large trials.
plos-pone-0012510:
Jianzhong Ma and Christopher Amos set out the math behind a key fix used in gene studies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When scientists hunt for genes tied to a disease, they compare large groups of people. If the groups differ in ancestry, that gap alone can fake a gene link. A method based on principal components, a way to sum up big data sets, is used to spot and remove that bias.

The authors give the firm math base for how the fix works and when it can be trusted. Gene hunts now use the method as a matter of course, so its limits matter a great deal. Their work helps study teams choose how strong a fix to apply, and when a weaker or stronger one is the right call.
plos-pone-0012610:
Loebig, Klement, Schmoller and co-authors tested a link between body weight and a growth factor called VEGF. VEGF helps blood vessels grow, and its blood level may shift with body mass. Their 2010 study used healthy young men of similar background to keep the test clean.

Each man went through a glucose clamp, a careful lab method that holds blood sugar steady while insulin response is measured. Even after that control, VEGF still tracked with body mass index. That points to a weight link that does not run through insulin alone, a clue for obesity research.
plos-pone-0012710:
Yu, Zeng, Xiong and co-authors warned that some epigenetic cancer drugs may also help cancer spread. Ezrin is a protein raised in many tumours, where it helps them invade new tissue. Their 2010 study asked whether drugs that change gene tags, used to wake silenced genes, also wake ezrin by mistake.

They found such drugs can raise ezrin through changes to its gene control region. A treatment that fights a tumour while feeding its spread would be a bad trade. The warning tells drug developers to screen for this side effect early.
plos-pone-0012810:
Yen, Le, Bansal and co-authors compared ways of measuring fat in the tiny worm C elegans. The worm is a stand-in for human obesity studies because its energy pathways match ours closely. Judging a worm's fat stores, though, needs methods that are exact and fair.

Their 2010 study ran dye-based methods, which stain fat, against label-free methods that need no stain. Stains can mislead, so a checked label-free option strengthens every obesity screen done in worms. The comparison gives labs a clear guide for measuring worm fat.
pmc-1852410:
Gupta, Stamatoyannopoulos, Bailey, and co-authors explain Tomtom, a method for comparing DNA motifs. Motifs are short patterns in DNA that proteins recognise when switching genes on or off. New patterns are found often, but judging whether one matches a known pattern needs sound statistics.

Tomtom measures how similar two motifs are and tests whether that likeness could arise by chance. Users can search a database of known motifs with a newly found one as the query. Reliable matching helps researchers name the proteins likely to bind a site and plan follow-up tests.
pmc-2707010:
Liberati, Altman, Tetzlaff, and co-authors explain the PRISMA Statement for reporting systematic reviews. Systematic reviews and pooled analyses judge whether health care treatments work. Readers can only trust such reviews if the methods are reported fully and clearly.

This long companion paper explains each item of the updated PRISMA guidance and gives examples. It shows authors what to report about searching, selecting, and combining studies. Journals worldwide adopted PRISMA, so the explanation shaped how evidence summaries in medicine are written and checked to this day.  Checklists in the paper show authors exactly which details reviewers will seek.
pmc-2816710:
Larsen, Vogensen, van den Berg, and co-authors compare gut microbes in adults with type 2 diabetes and adults without it. Recent evidence had suggested a link between metabolic disease and the bacterial populations living in the gut. Whether diabetic gut communities truly differ was still an open question.

The team assessed the make-up of intestinal microbes in both groups as controls against each other. Finding real differences would support the idea that gut bacteria play a role in diabetes, not merely reflect diet or drugs. The study helped launch wide interest in microbe-based diabetes care.
pmc-2946910:
Huynh-Thu, Irrthum, Wehenkel, and co-authors test tree-based methods for inferring gene regulatory networks from expression data. Rebuilding the wiring diagram of which genes control which others is a pressing open problem in systems biology. Gene expression measurements from microarrays offer clues, but the network itself stays hidden.

The authors assess their approach within a community benchmarking effort for reverse engineering networks. Tree-based methods treat each gene's activity as something to predict from other genes. Knowing which methods recover real networks best guides the search for drug targets and disease mechanisms.
pmc-3965110:
Finn, Bateman, Clements, and their co-authors described Pfam in 2014, a database of protein families. A protein family is a set of proteins that share a common part and often a common job. Pfam is served from sites in the United Kingdom and the United States and is used worldwide.

Release twenty-seven held close to fifteen thousand entries, each checked by hand by an expert. Users can search a new protein sequence and learn which known families it belongs to. That match gives a strong first clue to what the protein does, which guides lab work on genes, disease, and drug targets.
pmc-4402510:
Ritchie, Phipson, Wu, and their co-authors described limma for RNA sequencing in 2015. Limma is an R and Bioconductor package that gives an integrated way to analyze gene expression data. It handles complex study designs and borrows information across genes to cope with small sample sizes.

The paper shows how limma's methods, first built for microarrays, were extended to RNA-seq counts. Borrowing strength across genes steadies results when only a few samples exist. That is the common case in costly patient studies. Limma became a core tool for finding genes that differ between healthy and diseased tissue or before and after treatment.
pmc-4614810:
Eren, Esen, Quince, and their team presented Anvi'o in 2015, a platform for omics data. High-throughput sequencing and related technologies were transforming studies of natural microbial communities. Full study of microbial lifestyles needs ways to organize and view genetic information interactively.

Anvi'o lets users explore genomes and metagenomes together with their own added data layers. Researchers can inspect, compare, and share analyses through a visual interface. That interactivity helps teams form and test ideas while looking at the data, not after. The platform supports work on how microbes live, interact, and drive processes in oceans, soils, and hosts.
pmc-5715110:
Peter Bankhead and colleagues introduced QuPath, open source software for digital pathology, in 2017. Pathologists now scan whole slides into large digital images, but viewing and measuring them by hand is slow. A free, flexible tool was missing for research use.

QuPath lets users view whole slides, mark regions, and train the software to find tumor areas. It can measure large numbers of cells in a batch and export the results for statistics. Because the code is open, labs can adapt it and share methods. The tool helped make digital slide analysis routine in cancer research.
pmc-6004510:
Godfred Boateng, Torsten Neilands, Edward Frongillo, and colleagues wrote best practices for building survey scales in 2018. Health and social research depends on scales that measure attitudes, symptoms, and behaviors. Building a sound scale takes many steps that are easy to do badly.

The primer walks through item writing, expert review, pilot testing, and checks for structure and reliability. It explains common traps, such as too few items or samples that are too narrow. Each stage has clear advice a small team can follow. New researchers can use it to produce measures that others can trust and reuse.
pmc-8012210:
Jeffrey Granja and co-authors introduced ArchR in 2021, a software package for studying how accessible the DNA is inside single cells. Methods that profile chromatin accessibility one cell at a time can map the regulatory landscape of a tissue in fine detail. The data grew faster than the tools, leaving researchers with huge datasets and slow ways to read them.

ArchR was built to handle that scale, pulling biological meaning out of accessibility data quickly and in an integrated workflow. The authors describe how the package aligns cells, finds marker regions, and links them to genes. For labs working with single-cell regulatory data, it turned an unwieldy analysis into a manageable routine.
plos-pone-0359310:
Jie Wang and co-authors set out a protocol in 2026 for comparing three sets of criteria used to classify antiphospholipid syndrome. This autoimmune condition makes blood more likely to clot and complicates pregnancies, and classifying it consistently is essential for research. The planned study is a systematic review with network meta-analysis, a method for comparing several options across many studies at once.

The criteria under comparison are the Sapporo criteria, their revised version, and the newer 2023 criteria from two major rheumatology bodies. The protocol fixes the questions and methods in advance, so the eventual results can be judged against a public plan. Which set performs best shapes who counts as a patient in every future trial of this disease.
plos-pone-0359810:
Kulthoom Qureish and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about dengue fever in Kenya. It tests vector competence, whether mosquitoes can pick up and pass on dengue-2 virus. The mosquitoes are Aedes aegypti sampled at selected sites in Lamu County, split into groups resistant or susceptible to the insecticide permethrin.

Comparing the two groups matters because spraying programs assume resistance only affects survival, not virus spread. If resistant mosquitoes also differ in how well they carry dengue, control plans need rethinking. Malaria and dengue control teams in coastal Kenya are the readers who must weigh insecticide choices against disease transmission.

plos-pone-0357010:
María Carmen Martínez-González leads a team of eight testing whether needling a deep calf muscle changes how the foot bears weight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tibialis posterior, buried behind the shin, steers the arch when walking, and hidden trigger points in it may distort foot loading. Eighty-two adults with such trigger points were assigned to real deep dry needling or a simulated version, with foot pressure measured on a walking platform before treatment and at three points afterward.

Right after needling, pressure under the heel rose in the treated group. A day later, average pressure rose while contact areas shifted, including less forefoot contact. By seventy-two hours, every difference from baseline had vanished. The authors conclude a single session rearranges foot loading only briefly, which matters for clinicians deciding whether the technique can support longer term gait correction plans.
plos-pone-0348110:
Yangyang Chen leads a team of eight reading ten thousand years of climate from a pillar of black soil in northeast China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Songnen Plain holds one of the world's three black soil belts, vital to national grain supply, yet how its rich layer formed is still debated. The team sliced a sediment profile and combined grain size fingerprinting, chemical weathering measures, and luminescence dating to build a dated history of the whole Holocene.

Five stages emerged. Dust piled up fast in the early Holocene, then a cooling spell arrived near the transition to the middle period, echoing a known global cold snap. The middle Holocene optimum, warm and humid, did the decisive work: weathering peaked and the black soil began in earnest. Late Holocene cold and dryness then slowed the process. The profile ties a farming treasure directly to an ancient climate window.
plos-pone-0357310:
Weirui Zhang and three colleagues studied what Chinese school textbooks teach about the nature of science, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They read senior secondary geography textbooks in light of sustainable development, a theme the books are meant to carry. Textbooks shape whether students see science as fixed facts or as inquiry.

Zhang's team identified gaps between what the books claim about science and how they present it. They also pointed to reforms that would show science as argument and testing, not just lists to memorize. In a country teaching millions of students, textbook wording matters at huge scale. Better books can shape how a generation judges evidence on climate and resources.
plos-pone-0355210:
Tonya Campbell led a team of eight authors charting deaths tied to benzodiazepines in Ontario, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These sedative drugs are widely prescribed, and deaths involving their toxicity have been rising. The team ran a descriptive cross-sectional study of trends and patterns in those deaths.

Campbell's data give coroners and policymakers a clear picture of who is dying and how. Patterns by age, setting, and drug combinations point to where prevention can work, from prescribing rules to safer supply debates. Benzodiazepine deaths often hide inside wider drug toxicity figures, mixed with opioids. Separating them out, as this study does, is the first step toward policies aimed at the right problem.
plos-pone-0357910:
Atefeh Allahbakhshian and three colleagues traced how uncertainty affects heart patients' lives, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People with coronary artery disease live with gnawing doubt about their future. The team ran a pathway analysis linking quality of life in these patients to their coping strategies, perceived stress, and illness uncertainty.

Allahbakhshian's pathways reveal where support could break the chain from uncertainty to poor quality of life. If coping strategies carry much of the effect, teaching better coping becomes a concrete intervention. Cardiac care often stops at the artery; this work insists the mind's burden is part of the disease. Nurses and counselors gain a map of which link to strengthen first for each patient.
plos-pone-0357410:
Rena Hidaka and fellow researchers pilot a monthly program in Tokyo that teaches children about mouths, chewing, and food at community cafeterias. These cafeterias serve local families, and the team added a chewy meal plus a short talk on teeth and balanced eating. About fifty children and thirty parents joined six sessions, answering surveys before and after the program.

Children looked inside their own mouths more often and used fluoride more after the program. Fewer children said they ignored balanced eating, and parents reported serving more meat, dairy, and root vegetables at home. Because there was no comparison group, Hidaka and colleagues treat the gains as promising early signs and call for a fuller trial to confirm them.
plos-pone-0357110:
Sarah Al-Rihaymee leads a systematic review of whether a little-studied mouth bacterium belongs on the list of gum disease suspects. Known gum pathogens do not fully explain why disease severity varies so much between people. The review gathered observational studies in healthy adults that compared the bacterium's presence in people with gum disease against people with healthy gums, in spit or in plaque below the gumline.

Across eight studies from three continents, the bacterium turned up more often, and in larger shares, in disease than in health, with enrichment clearest in advanced stages. The authors rate the certainty as low, since most studies were snapshots rather than follow-ups. Al-Rihaymee and colleagues call for stronger designs before the bacterium earns a firm causal label.
plos-pone-0356910:
Xiaoxia Jia and colleagues model how city firms might cooperate to cut waste when the costs of doing so can be shared. Cities need industry to shrink its waste stream, but each firm weighs its own costs and gains. The study first maps material flows and life cycle impacts. That finds the nodes where cuts matter most. Then it runs a game model in software. Firms linked in a network copy or abandon cooperative moves over time.

Moderate penalties and positive spillovers between neighbors encouraged cooperation most reliably. Cost sharing and fair benefit splits also helped, but only within sensible ranges, and effects shifted with network size. Jia and colleagues advise cities to tune incentives to the local business network rather than copy one national recipe.
plos-pone-0350910:
Vivat Keawdounglek, Anuttara Hongthong, and Warapon Paenkhokuard built a community-run food safety system in Wiang Kaen District, a rural area of northern Thailand, and documented its first steps in 2026. Their mixed-method study surveyed 204 households, interviewed local stakeholders, and tested food from eight establishments for chemical and microbial contamination while residents co-designed the management approach.

Testing found contamination generally low, though pesticide traces turned up in garlic bought from outside markets, beyond local control. Food safety knowledge varied with gender, age, and rice growing. The process's concrete product was a standing Community Food Safety Committee linking households, vendors, and officials. The authors present the model as a workable template for rural districts with informal food systems.
plos-pone-0354510:
Sabrina Al Bukhari and colleagues built a closed-loop pain therapy in which brainwaves drive a virtual reality healer.
