Their 2026 study trained lightweight machine learning classifiers on an open dataset where volunteers rated laser-induced pain. One-second slices of scalp signals became an eleven-step pain scale. The live prediction was then piped into a game engine, where a digital avatar responds with tailored therapy.

The best classifier sorted pain levels with accuracy in the high nineties in cross-validation. It beat comparable published systems. The avatar reacted in real time across slight, moderate, and severe bands. Nothing here treated a real patient yet; the work proves the loop runs. Drug-free, self-adjusting pain care is the stated destination.
plos-pone-0355710:
Theres Mühlberg and three colleagues build a classroom observation tool for identifying which teaching principles a teacher is actually using, in this 2026 German study. Many observation instruments exist, but few are valid, reliable, subject-independent, and rooted in constructivist ideas about learning rather than simple evaluation. The team developed their protocol, called OPTIS, from a comparative review of teaching principles and refined it through expert rounds.

Piloting used both video-recorded lessons and live observation. Two independent observers reached almost perfect agreement with each other, and each stayed consistent over time, as measured by a chance-corrected agreement statistic suited to the data. Expert review supported the tool's foundations and its power to predict what it aims to capture. The authors present OPTIS as a psychometrically sound lens for researchers and school developers studying teaching quality across subjects.
plos-pone-0345910:
Xia Li and Maho Niwa examined how the fat makeup of cell membranes affects stress control in yeast cells. They focused on the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell structure that folds proteins and must pass intact to new daughter cells. Their 2026 study changed membrane fat saturation in a controlled way and watched three linked safety systems.

Changing fat saturation affected whether the stressed reticulum was passed to daughter cells. Yet it affected the other two systems, which repair the reticulum and destroy bad proteins, in different ways. A fat signal also helped trigger the checkpoint that pauses cell division under stress. The findings suggest membrane fats help coordinate how cells protect this key structure during division.
plos-pone-0355410:
Rownak Jahan and colleagues check in 2026 whether fresh fruit skins in their study area carry a gut bacterium that can cause severe infection and resist many drugs. Washed samples from seven fruit types were cultured and tested for the bacterium, its harm related genes, its ability to form slimy layers, and its drug resistance.

More than three in five samples carried the bacterium, most often on oranges. Resistance was high to several common drugs and worrying even for last resort drugs, and most isolates resisted many drugs at once. Harm genes and slime forming were common. Thorough washing and wider monitoring are urged.
plos-pone-0354810:
Yüksel Peker led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study linking a mixed sleep disorder to heart and blood vessel disease in Türkiye. The condition, called COMISA, pairs insomnia with sleep apnea. Drawing on a national sleep registry of nearly thirteen thousand adults sent for sleep testing, they compared four sleep groups.

The mixed disorder appeared more often in patients who had cardiovascular disease than in those without it, even after adjusting for many other factors. The link was modest, though. Peker treats COMISA as a distinct, burden-heavy pattern shaped by both body and behavior.
plos-pone-0354610:
Fahimeh Alsadat Hosseini and three colleagues published this 2026 trial of positive psychotherapy delivered through virtual reality to people with major depression. Seventy-eight patients were split between headset sessions and the same therapy face to face, three sessions each. Mood, life satisfaction, and suicidal thoughts were measured around every session, followed by interviews.

Both formats improved emotions, satisfaction, and suicidal thinking by similar amounts, and patients found the headset version workable. Hosseini calls the trial preliminary and asks for larger groups and longer follow-up before clinics adopt virtual delivery.
plos-pone-0353110:
Amr Sobhy led a team of six authors on this 2026 randomized trial of pain control for young children having penis repair surgery. Thirty children aged one to five received either the standard caudal epidural block or a newer ultrasound-guided block near the sacrum, both using the same local anesthetic. Nurses recorded how long relief lasted and how much rescue medicine was needed.

Children with the newer block waited longer before needing extra pain relief and needed less of it, with similar safety and body readings. Sobhy suggests the technique as a dependable alternative for this surgery.
plos-pone-0353010:
Faith Logan and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol for a pilot trial helping teenagers who live with chronic muscle and joint pain stay active. Many such teens avoid movement for fear of hurting more, which can seed lifelong pain. Their program, called PREP-Y, builds confidence and motivation alongside activity for forty adolescents at a children's hospital in Ohio.

Surveys, activity measures, and pain scales will track functioning, fear of movement, and resilience. As a protocol, the study promises no results yet; Logan's team designed it to shape a later full trial.
plos-pone-0354910:
Ziyang Luo led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of the HIV strain dominant in Ningxia, China. They analyzed just over two hundred local virus sequences of the CRF01_AE recombinant to trace where it travels and who drives its spread. The strain is known for faster disease progression.

Spread radiated strongly from the capital, Yinchuan, toward other cities, carried mainly by people in their twenties and thirties. Transmission remains above the level where the epidemic shrinks, while the virus's mutation pace stays steady. Luo urges prevention aimed at this strain's actual hubs and groups.
plos-pone-0354710:
Michael Getie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of bloodstream infections at a public health institute in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. Four full years of blood culture records, from 2020 through 2023, were reviewed to see which bacteria grew and which antibiotics still worked reliably, using standard lab methods.

Half the suspected cases grew true pathogens, dominated by hard-to-treat Gram-negative and notorious hospital bacteria, hitting males, newborns, and young adults hardest. Getie calls for immediate antibiotic stewardship, refreshed treatment guidelines, and stronger lab testing to track resistance.
plos-pone-0347810:
Hyeonji Song, Yusik Lim, and Jaechul Lim describe a laboratory panel that can tell apart dozens of mouse cell types in one run, in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Flow cytometry sorts cells by fluorescent tags, but overlapping colours and scarce mouse-ready reagents have limited how much can be measured at once. Their panel uses twenty-seven colours across three lasers.

The panel resolves sixteen immune cell families plus several non-immune cell types, and it works across spleen, blood, gut, and other tissues. In a test inflammation model it tracked body-wide shifts in white blood cells and spotted a previously unnoticed cell subset. Such panels speed up immune research in mice.
plos-pone-0342410:
Sabine Pur, Stefan Huesig, and Christoph Schmidhammer trace how online lending marketplaces in three countries grew alike, in this 2026 PLOS ONE case study. These platforms match borrowers with lenders directly online. The authors followed the market leaders in Britain, the United States, and Germany from 2005 onward, comparing who they served and what they promised customers.

All three drifted toward the same shape: funding from institutions rather than small savers, aimed at underserved borrowers such as small firms and the self-employed. Regulation, technology, and institutional money drove the sameness. The authors turn the pattern into a general model of how platform business models standardise across borders.
plos-pone-0353610:
Toqeer Ali Syed and four colleagues propose giving city infrastructure a self-managing digital twin, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. A digital twin mirrors bridges, roads, and water systems in software, fed by live sensors. Their design adds artificial intelligence agents that perceive problems, plan responses, and act through official city systems, while a permissioned blockchain seals every observation, approval, and action against tampering.

Eighteen thousand simulated incidents tested the framework across five designs and three difficulty levels. The paper characterises how the system behaves under stress rather than proving it in a real city. The stakes are accountability: when software orders a road closure or repair, someone must be able to audit why.
plos-pone-0351510:
Brittany Lee Vermeulen and three colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One case study on short online courses, called microcredentials, inside university teaching. The setting was a large undergraduate science subject in 2024, where students also completed a brief sustainability course on thinking, caring, and acting. The authors focused on a smaller group of students and studied their final reflective writing.

Reading those reflections, the team found students understood sustainability more deeply, rethought daily habits, and saw their future science careers differently. Engagement with the self-paced course varied widely, as the authors expected. They offer the case as a workable model for universities that want to build sustainability literacy into existing subjects rather than adding whole new courses.
plos-pone-0351210:
Olanrewaju Onigbogi and four co-authors study how depression drugs link body weight and smoking in American adults. They used a 2023 national health survey. Their model asked whether taking drugs for depression helps explain smoking habits. They compared adults who were underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese.

Use of depression drugs played the largest connecting role in underweight adults. It played the smallest role in obese adults. Underweight adults on such drugs were more likely to smoke than obese adults were. Obese adults on the drugs also showed raised odds of smoking, compared with underweight peers. The authors say weight group should be part of the picture. Clinicians should weigh it when they design quit-smoking support for people treated for depression.
plos-pone-0352110:
Yu Zhao and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One nationwide study of colorectal cancer deaths in China's cancer registration areas from 2005 to 2018, with forecasts to 2035. The team combined trend analysis, an age-period-cohort model, and spatial statistics to separate the roles of aging, calendar time, and birth generation, and to locate high-risk regions.

Mortality rose, then fell significantly for several years, then flattened into a slight rise, with urban rates falling over the later years while rural rates crept up. Risk grew steeply with age, and hotspots concentrated in eastern coastal and northeastern provinces. The forecast shows a slow upward drift ahead. The authors offer the patterns as a basis for targeting screening and prevention where deaths cluster.
plos-pone-0352810:
Josheil Boparai and seven colleagues test a simple fix for weak concussion teaching in medical school. Their 2026 study starts from a known gap. Concussion barely appears in undergraduate medical curricula. Poor knowledge then follows graduates into clinical practice. Students first completed a knowledge survey. Next came a single didactic lecture on concussion.

Knowledge scores jumped sharply right after the lecture. Students were surveyed again within two days. A final survey came two weeks later. Scores at two weeks matched the immediate scores, showing the learning had stuck. No extra teaching happened in between. One focused lecture, the authors argue, earns its place in a crowded curriculum. Better-trained graduates should then recognise and manage concussion more safely in real patients.
plos-pone-0351310:
Jingjing Ma refines how forecasters combine predictions about a country's energy mix. The 2026 study works with compositional data: shares of coal, oil, gas, and renewables that must sum to a whole. Single forecasting models shine at different times. Combining them helps, but only if the weights adapt. Ma proposes an aggregation method built on an ordered weighting operator, informed by each model's recent accuracy. A genetic algorithm searches for the weight set that minimises error against the real series.

Two combination schemes resulted: one with time-varying weights, one built on the new operator. Both were tested on China's primary energy production structure. The varying-weight model beat the benchmark on prediction accuracy. Energy planners live and die by share forecasts: grid investment, import contracts, and carbon budgets all hang on them. A demonstrably better way to blend rival forecasts is a quiet but consequential upgrade.
plos-pone-0352310:
Mengxuan Liu and five colleagues search public gene data for shared sparks between sepsis and diabetes. Their 2026 bioinformatics study concerns pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death that bursts cells open. Both diseases kill many people, and they worsen each other in practice. Two gene expression datasets supplied the raw material. The team filtered for genes that change in both conditions and belong to the pyroptosis machinery. Network and pathway tools then mapped their neighbourhoods.

Seven genes survived the sieve. Most specialise in killing cells or sounding immune alarms. Their pathways centred on cell bursting and an inflammatory signal family. A separate enrichment pass flagged another immune signalling route. Immune cell mixtures in blood correlated with the genes' activity too. None of this treats a patient yet. It nominates molecular markers where two major diseases overlap, giving laboratory researchers concrete suspects for the crosstalk clinicians see at the bedside.
plos-pone-0345710:
Jorge Quiroga-Canaviri and colleagues argue that standard measures of output misjudge Latin American economies. Those measures ignore the limits of nature. They also ignore the slow loss of natural wealth. The team proposes a bioeconomy frame rooted in Andean and Amazonian thought. It joins an entropy-aware view of production with ancestral knowledge. Six countries were studied across three decades. Human development stood in for well-being.

The new model explained far more of the well-being pattern. It also surfaced a paradox. Saving the shared fund of ecosystems and cultures predicted higher well-being. Normal accounts book that saving as a pure cost. In these results, care for nature reads as an investment that pays in human development.
plos-pone-0349610:
Alba Roldan and colleagues examined how shaky movement affects learning in adults with severe cerebral palsy of the athetoid or ataxic types. Thirteen adults with the condition and eighteen without practiced motor tasks that taught through two channels: correcting errors and chasing rewards. Extra movement noise might open exploration, or it might drown the signals learning needs.

The cerebral palsy group moved far more variably, made larger absolute errors, and adjusted less precisely within tasks. Yet the two teaching channels were not equally blocked. Error-based practice produced substantial improvement after training, while reward-based learning lagged further behind. For therapists, the split is practical guidance: build drills around clear error feedback, where these learners demonstrably gain, rather than around reward signals their motor noise obscures.
plos-pone-0350510:
Chidozie Ezechukwu and colleagues interviewed the people charged with delivering Nigeria's new HPV vaccine in Kano, Kaduna, and Lagos states, asking what keeps the program from running steadily. The vaccine prevents cervical cancer, and Nigeria added it to the national schedule recently, but early rollout stumbled. Policymakers, immunization officers, agencies, community groups, and partners described the friction from their seats.

The analysis organizes the barriers by the machinery of delivery: how policy is implemented, how the program is financed, and how services reach girls in practice, with community-level obstacles woven through each. Interview studies like this cannot weigh the barriers, but they name them in the words of the people hitting them, which is where fixes start. Sustaining a vaccine program is a systems problem, and this is a systems map.
plos-pone-0351110:
Jaya Kshatri and colleagues lay out a planned trial of joined-up primary care for older adults in urban India. The patients live with several chronic diseases at once, plus growing frailty. Indian primary care still tends to treat one disease per visit. Ten public health centers in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, will take part. Whole clinics will be assigned by lot. Half will give a monthly package of combined care. Half will give standard care as usual.

The trial will judge health-related quality of life and well-being. It is built from parts a public system could truly staff and fund. As a protocol, it reports no results. If the package works, its design is the point. It shows other cities a model that does not depend on private money or rare specialists.
plos-pone-0349410:
Breast cancer that starts young tends to behave worse, and Le-Wei Zheng and colleagues searched tumor DNA for why, focusing on the hormone-sensitive luminal type. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined gene fusions, mutations, and missing DNA segments across many tumors.

One pairing stood out: a fused gene joining two partners, together with deletion of a gene called KDM6B, marked tumors with aggressive traits and shorter survival. Young patients' tumors also carried more fusions overall and distinct mutation patterns. The authors propose the pairing as a warning marker that could help doctors single out young patients needing closer watching and stronger treatment.
plos-pone-0351410:
American law reviews are edited by students who must pick a few articles from thousands, and they lean on the author's school as a quality shortcut. Chad M Topaz simulated that market with a computer model, in this 2026 PLOS One study, and compared it with centralized matching like the system placing medical residents.

More than sixty percent of top placements differed from what quality-based matching would give, and article quality lined up only loosely with journal rank. Partial fixes such as longer deadlines barely helped; the scattered structure itself caused the waste. The model also shows prestige bias persists even between equally strong articles, an inequity built into the system.
plos-pone-0351610:
Editorial Note: PLOS One corrects a greenhouse tomato study after data from another institution was included by mistake. This 2026 note replaces the wrong figure and fixes sentences describing the test of micro-fog systems, which cool greenhouse air by spraying fine mist during summer heat.

The corrected values describe midday conditions with and without fog: the fogged section ran cooler and far more humid, with much lower dryness stress on the plants. The original paper argued the gentler air improved leaf photosynthesis, growth, and yield. Readers should rely on the corrected figure and numbers given here rather than those first printed.
plos-pone-0350810:
Medical students in Tunisia will soon treat people living with HIV, and Imen Mlouki and colleagues tested whether hands-on workshops can cut the stigma those patients face from health workers. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered all fifth-year students at the Monastir medical faculty across two academic years.

Two hundred sixteen students completed anonymous questionnaires before and after each workshop, using validated knowledge and stigma scales. Most already knew the facts about HIV well. The team measured how far attitudes moved after active sessions, and which student traits traveled with lingering stigma. Findings should help faculties design training that changes behavior, not just knowledge.
plos-pone-0349510:
Kaleab Fikre, Abeje Berhanu Kassegne, and Getnet Tadele interviewed forty one people in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: cancer patients, family caregivers, and religious leaders. In depth talks explored how faith shapes what cancer means and what care people seek. Beliefs in Ethiopia had drawn little study despite their central place in daily life.

Illness was often read as divine or supernatural in origin: a punishment, a test of faith, Gods will, or spiritual attack. Views shifted over time with teaching, custom, and reflection. Faith brought comfort and strength while also steering treatment choices, sometimes toward prayer first. Clinicians who grasp those frames, the authors argue, can plan care patients will actually follow.
plos-pone-0350610:
Ika Saptarini and colleagues in Indonesia followed dengue patients through fever and early recovery in 2026, measuring immune signals in blood. Severe dengue often declares itself as fever fades, and doctors lack early warnings of who will worsen.

Paired blood samples from more than one hundred patients at five hospitals were tested for a set of messengers and complement parts. Two signals ran higher in the severe form during early recovery, while none separated the groups during fever. Links among the signals also shifted. Tracking how immune signals move, not just their level on day one, may sharpen dengue care.
plos-pone-0350110:
Marleen G A M van der Velde and co-authors introduced a new Dutch registry tracking urgent internal medicine care in 2026. The registry follows how hospitals handle urgent medical admissions, so units can compare themselves with a shared benchmark and find bottlenecks.

The report covers a single centre pilot at one teaching hospital, drawing records for more than six thousand emergency patients aged sixty-five and over between late 2019 and mid 2023. Data cover complaints, ward organisation, and measures like time in the emergency department. The pilot proves the dashboard works locally before national use, and shows the case mix such registries must handle.
plos-pone-0348510:
Aboa Paul Koffi and co-authors carried out a huge hunt for yaws, a poverty-linked skin infection that mostly strikes children in the humid tropics, across fifteen districts of Côte d'Ivoire. The country is one of the few where yaws remains endemic, and planners needed its true extent before attempting eradication. Their 2026 campaign visited nearly four thousand villages and targeted close to half a million children in schools and homes.

About fifteen percent of examined children had skin lesions of some kind. Blood tests flagged two hundred ninety-one possible yaws cases, and a confirmatory test verified about half, mostly in children aged five to fourteen. Confirmed cases received a single antibiotic dose. Teams also catalogued other common skin conditions, giving health authorities a fuller map for the eradication push.
plos-pone-0350010:
Xue Zhang, Xiaoya Ba, and Bo Li studied seven major cyberattacks that spread through supply chains, hitting sectors from retail and logistics to energy and health care. Attackers in these cases slipped in through trusted third-party connections instead of breaking front-door defenses. The team mapped how each attack entered, spread inside, and was eventually stopped.

Across the cases, four spread patterns kept recurring, including flattened networks that let intruders roam and alert overload that paralyzed defenders. Damage grew worst when systems were tightly linked and teams failed to coordinate. Recovery worked only where firms shared information early and were organized before the crisis, which the authors call synergy dependency.
plos-pone-0341210:
Xiaocui Yuan and colleagues built an automated system that both finds defects in railway fasteners and measures their parts precisely. Fasteners hold rails in place, and worn or broken ones threaten train safety. Inspectors can spot defects with cameras, but careful measurement of each part still relies on slow hand work.

A 3D line laser scanner captures color images and matching depth maps of each fastener. One neural network spots defects and locates sound fasteners, while a second segments the parts so the system can compute block sizes, pad thickness, and bolt height. In tests the defect finder reached very high precision, pointing toward faster and more consistent track inspection.
plos-pone-0349310:
Jean-Marc Perone and colleagues mined data from a large cataract surgery trial to learn why eye pressure falls after the cloudy lens is removed, even in eyes without glaucoma. The drop is well known but unexplained, and knowing its drivers could sharpen glaucoma care. They tracked pressure at one, three, and twelve months, sorting eyes by starting pressure into high, middle, and low bands.

A wide set of eye measurements and surgical details was tested for what predicted the size of the drop at three months, in the whole group and each band. A literature review checked the regression approach against prior traps in this kind of analysis. Since cataract surgery is the world's most common operation, its pressure side effect is a therapeutic lever hiding in plain sight.
plos-pone-0347210:
Zhichao Jiang, Xiaorun Wang, and Pengling Liu ask whether digital tools can raise the quality of farm goods that China sells abroad. Their 2026 study uses yearly data from thirty-four Chinese provincial regions covering more than two decades. They build an index of farm digital growth and track how it lines up with export quality over time.

Digital growth did go with better export quality, and the link held up under extra checks. The gains ran through faster farm technology, better trained workers, and smoother shipping. Effects were stronger in eastern regions, big grain areas, and places with more open markets. Government support and trade openness made the link stronger still.
plos-pone-0348610:
Zhiqi Huang, Yizhang Jiang, and Kaijian Xia present a fuzzy logic classifier that learns from several views of the same data at once. Fuzzy systems sort items by degrees of belonging rather than hard lines, which suits messy real-world data. Their 2026 model lets each rule's center shift to fit the data and weighs rules by importance for each new sample.

Across five public datasets, from handwriting to brain signals, the model beat strong rivals at sorting accuracy. Removing either new part hurt results, and using both helped most. Brain signal sorting gained the most from the pairing. The design offers a clearer, more flexible way to classify when information arrives from mixed sources.
plos-pone-0349110:
Yingjie Kuang and co-workers train machine learning models to predict which leg vein clots confined to the calf will fail to clear. Such clots are common, and doctors lack good tools for judging their course. Their 2026 study gathers records for sixteen hundred patients, builds six competing models, and tests the best on patients the models never saw during training.

All six models sorted outcomes acceptably to strongly. A boosted-tree model won overall, pairing high accuracy with honest probability estimates. An explanation method then ranked which patient features drove its calls. A tool like this could help doctors decide who needs closer watching or longer treatment, and who can safely be left to heal.
plos-pone-0343610:
Ada R. Miltz and her team tested a chain of harm for people with HIV in the UK. The chain runs from slights in daily life to shame, then to lone days, then to low mood. They used a UK-wide survey from 2022 and 2023. It held more than twelve hundred straight men and women with HIV.

More than half felt shame about their state. Slights in health care fed that shame the most. Next came fear of public spots and slights from kin. Lone days were the top link to low mood. Cash strain hurt too, while grit helped. The chain fit the data well, the team says.
plos-pone-0347410:
Long Zhou, Litao Zhu, and Faming Zhang ran pot experiments to free phosphorus locked in iron-rich red soils, where maize often starves despite fertiliser. They combined organic phosphorus with two helpers: phytase, an enzyme that releases phosphorus from plant residues, and bacteria that dissolve mineral phosphorus. The 2026 study measured plant growth, root shape, and how much phosphorus the maize actually absorbed.

The combination outperformed either addition alone, and the enzyme proved the stronger partner, raising phosphorus uptake by more than half in one comparison. Roots grew longer, thinner, and more branched where phosphorus flowed better. The authors offer the recipe as a sustainable way to farm phosphorus-poor red soils.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Israel's pull-out from south Lebanon reshaped this force renewal of 2000. On 27 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1310 without dissent. Six weeks before, the Secretary-General had confirmed the pull-out. It met the terms of Resolution 425 from 1978. Lebanon asked the force to stay while Beirut sent its own troops south.

The text backs the plan for UNIFIL to spread through its whole zone. Lebanon will add troops and police in the south at the same time. The mandate then runs six months, to 31 January 2001. Strong backing for Lebanon's land, freedom, and self-rule is restated. The force stayed an interim one, the text stresses, even after twenty-two years.

Latvia followed its Baltic neighbor through the same door in 1991. On 12 September, the Council adopted Resolution 710 without a vote. The same meeting handled Estonia's bid. The Republic of Latvia had declared its freedom restored in August. The Soviet Union was falling apart around it. Most Western states had never called the 1940 seizure lawful.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Latvia. Admission followed days later, with Estonia and Lithuania as well. Latvia framed its return as a state restored, not a state born. That claim rested on the view that its 1918 republic had never died in law.

Spain under General Franco troubled the young United Nations in 1946. Many members saw his regime as a leftover of Europe's fascist era. The Council had kept Spain's situation on its active list. Resolution 10, adopted unanimously at the Council's 79th meeting, changed the handling of that question.

The members took Spain off the Council's list of seized matters. All records and papers on the case went to the General Assembly. The Secretary-General had to notify the Assembly of the transfer. The question of Franco's Spain thus moved arenas. It became an Assembly debate, where pressure on the regime continued through resolutions on membership and diplomacy.

Should the UN Charter itself be rewritten? Ten years after its birth, that debate came due. The Charter said a review meeting must be held if both big UN bodies agreed. On 21 November 1955 the General Assembly voted for such a meeting, at a fit time. Resolution 110 gave the Council's answer on 16 December 1955.

Nine members backed the Assembly's choice. The Soviet Union voted no. France held back. The Council thus agreed that a review meeting should take place one day. In the end, no such meeting was ever held. The Charter stayed as written in 1945, barring small tweaks. This text preserves the one formal step ever taken toward a full review.

Kabul alone had UN-backed guards after the Taliban fell. The force called ISAF watched the capital and its edge. By 2003, Afghan leaders wanted that shield spread wider. Their foreign minister wrote to ask for help on 10 October. NATO, which ran the force, wrote too. Resolution 1510 passed with no dissent on 13 October 2003.

The Council let ISAF work past Kabul, as means allowed. Its task was to keep the peace so aid and rebuilding could go on. The force's mandate grew by twelve months. States in ISAF could use all steps needed to do the job. Reports were due each three months. The move marked the first big growth of the Afghan mission.

Resolution 1410, adopted unanimously on 17 May 2002, designs the UN mission that would stand beside a newborn Timor-Leste. East Timorese voters had chosen a constituent assembly in August 2001 and a president in April 2002, completing the road to independence set for 20 May. The Council praised their courage and vision, and the UN administration that had run the territory since 1999.

In place of that administration it established a successor support mission, UNMISET, for an initial twelve months from independence day. The new mission's job was narrower: help fragile young institutions with administration, policing, and defense capacity while Timorese officials took command. The resolution frames independence not as an ending but as a handover.

Resolution 1610, adopted on 30 June 2005, sets the endgame for the UN mission in Sierra Leone. Security was steadily improving, and the Secretary-General's April report laid out a drawdown schedule for UNAMSIL, with a strong UN presence to remain after the troops left. The Council praised the truth and reconciliation commission's work and urged the government to spread its report widely.

UNAMSIL's mandate was extended for a final six months, to the end of 2005, so the withdrawal could be completed in order. The Special Court trying Sierra Leone's war criminals was called essential work, and all states were urged to make sure its indictees actually appeared before it. Peace in Sierra Leone, the text insists, also depended on calm next door in Liberia.

The border dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea drives Resolution 1710, adopted on 29 September 2006. The UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, watched the Temporary Security Zone between them. A boundary commission had ruled on the border under the Algiers Agreements, but marking the line on the ground had stalled, and Eritrea was limiting the mission's movement.

The Council extends UNMEE for four months, until 31 January 2007. It demands that Eritrea lift all limits on the mission at once and that Ethiopia accept the boundary ruling fully and let marking begin. It warns that if no progress is shown by the deadline, it may reshape or change the mission, and it plans a review before 30 November 2006.

Keeping weapons of mass destruction away from armed groups is the aim of Resolution 1810, adopted on 25 April 2008. It builds on Resolution 1540 from 2004, which ordered every state to block non-state actors from getting nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons. A committee, the 1540 Committee, tracked how states were doing, but many had not yet filed their first reports.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council repeats that all states must fully carry out Resolution 1540. It extends the 1540 Committee, with expert help, for three years until 25 April 2011. States that have not reported must do so without delay. The committee is told to match offers of help with states that need it, run outreach events, and deliver a full review of progress by set dates.

AMISOM is extended and pressed to reach full strength in Resolution 2010, adopted on 30 September 2011. Mogadishu's security had improved, the Kampala Accord of June 2011 had deferred Somali elections to August 2012, and a September roadmap set the transitional institutions twelve months of tasks. Drought and famine were at their worst.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes African Union member states to maintain AMISOM until 31 October 2012. It urges the AU to raise it to its mandated 12,000 uniformed personnel. The Secretary-General must keep providing the UN logistical support package for up to 12,000 troops. The package includes a guard force for UN and international staff in Mogadishu and counter-IED and ordnance disposal work. Future Council support for the transitional institutions is made contingent on completing the roadmap's tasks, and the Council signals it will review AMISOM's troop levels once the mission reaches 12,000.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 10, adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-seventh plenary meeting, is one brief procedural sentence. The Assembly asked the Secretary-General to send the provisional rules of procedure of the Trusteeship Council, drawn from the Preparatory Commission's report, to that Council as soon as it was set up.

General Assembly Resolution 410 (V), adopted at the fifth session in 1950, created the United Nations Korean Reconstruction Agency for the relief and rebuilding of Korea. The Assembly noted the vast ruin left by the fighting. It held that a United Nations programme was needful both for lasting peace and for the groundwork of a united, free Korea.

The agency, known as UNKRA, was placed under an Agent General answerable to the Assembly. He worked beside the unification commission. Its policy put food, clothing, and shelter first. Then came farm output and the repair of transport and power. Aid was shared fairly across the whole population, with no political strings attached.

Resolution 69/10 of the General Assembly, from its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns cooperation between the United Nations and the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Commonwealth has held observer status since 1994. The Assembly notes the Commonwealth's regional work in trade, health, environment, crime, and drug control. It asks the Secretary-General to consult regularly with its leadership. He is to report to the seventy-first session. It invites United Nations agencies and financial institutions to deepen their cooperation with it.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Somalia had a weak interim government and an ongoing armed conflict when the Council adopted Resolution 1910 on 28 January 2010. The resolution concerns AMISOM, the African Union Mission in Somalia. Its soldiers, mainly from Uganda and Burundi, were protecting the interim authorities in the capital, Mogadishu.

The Council allowed African Union member states to keep AMISOM in Somalia until 31 January 2011. It asked the Union to build the force up toward its planned strength of eight thousand troops. United Nations logistical support for the mission would continue. Donor countries were urged to pay for the force. The text also pushed for more training of Somali police and security forces, and it set reports to the Council every four months.

India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir in September 1965, and the fighting was spreading. A cease-fire call two days earlier, in Resolution 209, had not stopped it. The Council adopted Resolution 210 unanimously on 6 September 1965. It said the wider fighting made the crisis far more serious.

The Council called on both sides to stop all hostilities at once, across the whole area of conflict. Every soldier was to pull back to the positions held before 5 August 1965. The Secretary-General was told to push hard to make the cease-fire take effect. He also had to strengthen the United Nations observer group in the area and keep the Council informed without delay.

African contract workers in Namibia went on strike in early 1972, and South Africa answered with harsh repression. South Africa was still occupying Namibia, although the United Nations had ended its mandate years before. Leaders of African states and of the United Nations Council for Namibia addressed the Council. Resolution 310 was adopted on 4 February 1972.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's refusal to obey the United Nations decisions on Namibia. It restated that the occupation was illegal and harmful to the Namibian people. The repression of the workers was condemned as well. South Africa was told to end it and to scrap any labor system that clashed with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It also had to pull its police, military forces, and civilian staff out of Namibia at once. Further steps would follow if it refused.

Cyprus in 1977 was calm in part, but its peacekeeping force still could not move freely in the north of the island. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 7 June, called the force essential. It helped maintain quiet and made the continued search for a settlement easier. Talks between the two communities offered the best hope. Resolution 410 was adopted on 15 June 1977.

The Council extended the force's stationing to 15 December 1977. It repeated its call for urgent progress on a settlement. That call rested on the General Assembly's plan for Cyprus and on Resolution 367. Both sides were urged to show restraint. The Secretary-General was to continue his mission of good offices between the communities. He had to report on this resolution by 30 November 1977.
un-sc-res-1310:
Israel had pulled its forces out of southern Lebanon weeks earlier. On 27 July 2000 the Security Council extended UNIFIL, its Lebanon force, for six months. The new term ran until 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General had confirmed that Israel had cleared the withdrawal line. Lebanon now planned to send more of its own troops south.

The Council backed the force deploying across its whole area. It restated Lebanon's sovereignty and independence. It condemned every act of violence, above all attacks on the force itself. It also pressed armed groups in the south to stop fighting. The aim was a calm border while Lebanon rebuilt its authority there.
un-sc-res-110: The United Nations Charter faced its ten-year review moment in 1955. Article 109 allowed a general conference to revise the Charter. The General Assembly had decided such a conference should meet at a fitting time. On 16 December 1955 the Security Council stated its agreement with that decision. The whole resolution is that single act of concurrence. In the end, no review conference was ever held.
un-sc-res-1510:
Afghanistan's security force outgrew Kabul in the autumn of 2003. On 13 October 2003 the Security Council let ISAF expand across the country. Until then the force had guarded the capital and its surroundings. Now it could support Afghan authorities in other areas, as resources allowed. The aim was to let the United Nations and aid groups work safely nationwide. Afghans themselves held the chief duty for security, the text notes.

The Council also extended ISAF's mandate for twelve months. Member states in the force could take all needed measures. The force had to keep working closely with Afghan leaders. It also had to coordinate with the United States-led coalition. The expansion marked a turning point in the war.
un-sc-res-1410:
Independence for East Timor brought a successor mission from the Security Council on 17 May 2002. The people of East Timor had chosen a constituent assembly in August 2001 and a president in April 2002 by peaceful vote. The transitional administration, UNTAET, had led the territory to the point of statehood. The Secretary-General warned that the new institutions were still fragile.

The Council created the United Nations Mission of Support in East Timor, UNMISET, from 20 May 2002 for an initial twelve months. Its mandate covered help with administration, law enforcement, and security while Timorese bodies took over. Under Chapter VII, the mission could take the actions needed to do its work. Over two years it would hand all operational duties to the East Timorese authorities as milestones were met. The drawdown was reviewed against real progress, not a fixed date.
un-sc-res-1610:
UNAMSIL received its final extension on 30 June 2005. The Secretary-General's report of 26 April set out the drawdown schedule he advised. A strong United Nations presence was still needed after the peacekeepers left. The Council praised the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's work and thanked the Special Court. Sierra Leone's forces would take full charge of security when the mission closed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for a final six months, to 31 December 2005. The Secretary-General had to finish planning for a follow-on United Nations office to start in January 2006. UNAMSIL and the country team were encouraged to work as one in the mission's last phase. Sierra Leone's army and police had to be ready to guard the country alone. The Council underlined the need to keep the Special Court's premises secure. The government was urged to keep building its forces with outside help.
un-sc-res-1710:
UNMEE was extended for four months as the border deadlock deepened on 29 September 2006. The Secretary-General's report of 19 September lay before the Council. Both parties had accepted the Boundary Commission's rulings as final and binding, yet marking the line had not begun. The mission was praised for doing its duties in hard conditions.

The Council extended UNMEE's mandate for four months. It restated its demands from resolution 1640 (2005): Eritrea had to lift its limits on the mission, and Ethiopia had to accept the border ruling without delay. Both parties had to give UNMEE full access, help, and protection. The Council voiced regret at the lack of progress on demarcation. It called on both sides to cooperate with the Commission and start the work of marking the border. If it found no real movement, the Council meant to review the mission's future at the mandate's end.
un-sc-res-1810:
The 1540 Committee gained three more years on 25 April 2008. Resolution 1540 (2004) had ordered every state to bar non-state actors from weapons of mass destruction. Resolution 1673 (2006) had kept the committee working. The spread of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons was restated as a threat to international peace. Peaceful uses of the same science had to stay open, the Council stressed.

The Council restated every decision and duty in resolution 1540. States that had not yet filed a first report were called again to do so without delay. States that had reported were urged to add fresh detail whenever asked. Voluntary summary action plans were encouraged. States needing help were told to send their requests to the committee. The Council extended the 1540 Committee's mandate for three years, to 25 April 2011. A full report on states' compliance was due.
un-sc-res-2010:
Somalia reached the Council's table and drew Resolution 2010, adopted on 30 September 2011. Famine gripped the country that summer. Al-Shabaab had pulled out of most of Mogadishu, yet attacks went on. The African Union force, called AMISOM, still stood below its authorized strength of 12,000 troops.

The Council keeps AMISOM deployed until 31 October 2012. The African Union must raise the force to its full 12,000 level fast. United Nations logistical support runs for the same period. Somali leaders must follow the new road map of tasks, or future support is at risk. A guard unit will shield the growing number of officials working in Mogadishu.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The fourth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/4210, covers the force in 1958 and 1959. UNEF was still a young experiment, holding the line between Egypt and Israel after the Suez Crisis. Its camps and patrol routes were now set, and its routines were taking shape.

The report describes the force's strength, its observation work, and talks with both parties. It also takes up the thorny question of who should pay. The document belongs to the years when peacekeeping was being invented in practice, one report at a time.
europmc-pmc10225110:
Guan, He, and Xu review recent progress and future prospects in gastric cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Gastric, or stomach, cancer is among the most common cancers worldwide. Most patients are found at a late stage, because early symptoms are vague and screening is rare in many countries.

The review covers the main systemic treatments: chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immune therapy. It explains which patients gain from each approach and how biomarkers guide the choice. It closes with trials and ideas that may improve the still poor outlook for advanced disease.
europmc-pmc10240810:
Yang and colleagues review amino acid metabolism in immune cells in a 2023 paper. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and immune cells consume them in large amounts when they respond to threats. Inside tumors, cancer and immune cells compete for the same supply, which can blunt the immune attack.

The review explains how amino acid use steers what immune cells can do. It shows how tumors exploit that dependence to evade destruction. It then surveys ways to retune the supply so that immune therapy against cancer works better.
europmc-pmc10481210:
Rao and colleagues tested ChatGPT across a full run of clinical work in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool trained on vast text sets. Past tests gave it single questions, not linked chains of choices. Real care needs step-by-step thought, like a doctor at work. The team fed it 36 standard case stories from a clinical manual.

Each case asked for likely diagnoses, tests, a final call, and a care plan. Human scorers marked each reply. Rao reports an overall score of 71.7% across all cases. Final diagnosis scored best, at 76.9%. The first list of likely causes scored worst, at 60.3%. Scores rose as the tool gained more case facts.
europmc-pmc10499610:
Zhang and a large team gave an algorithm in 2023 that designs better mRNA for vaccines. mRNA is a message strip that tells cells to build a target protein. Such messages break down fast, which hurts storage and strength of a vaccine. A tighter fold and smart word choice in the code can slow that decay.

The snag is scale: the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 allows a vast sea of code variants. Their tool, LinearDesign, borrows a trick from language parsing to search that sea. It found a top design for the spike in just 11 minutes. Zhang reports far longer message life and more protein made. Antibody levels in mice rose up to 128-fold over a standard design.
europmc-pmc10533410:
Wang and a large team asked in 2023 what marks tumours that respond to immune therapy in triple-negative breast cancer. Some patients gain from checkpoint drugs, which free immune cells to attack. Others gain nothing, and no firm test split the two groups. The team mapped proteins in place inside tumours from a trial.

They read 43 proteins in tumour samples taken before, during, and after therapy. Two shares stood out as top predictors of response. Wang names growing CD8 T cells with a TCF1 mark, and cancer cells that show MHCII. On therapy, tumours that responded filled with a killer T cell type. Tumours that resisted showed CD15-marked cancer cells. Early biopsies may help steer care as it unfolds.
europmc-pmc11609310:
Ma and colleagues review liquid biopsy for cancer detection and monitoring in this 2024 paper. Tissue biopsy, cutting a tumour sample, remains the gold standard for diagnosis, with stable samples and high accuracy. It is also invasive and limited for repeated checks. Liquid biopsy reads tumour signals from blood and other fluids instead.

Its advantages include being non-invasive and quick, the authors note. Components now assayed include circulating tumour cells, circulating tumour DNA, exosomes, microRNA, other circulating RNA, tumour platelets, and tumour endothelial cells. The review covers the current status of each marker class for early diagnosis and prognosis. Challenges include low signal levels in early disease and lack of standardisation. Future prospects are mapped, with the field described as undergoing rapid progress.
europmc-pmc1183210:
Galperin took a 2005 census of signal proteins in bacteria and archaea. These proteins sense the world and pass messages inside the cell. Parasites in stable homes tend to carry simple signal kits. Free-living microbes in changing places carry far richer kits.

The census covered 167 complete genomes checked by hand. It counted sensor kinases, chemotaxis receptors, and related switch proteins. Larger genomes held many more signal proteins, roughly with the square of size. Galperin calls this spread a kind of bacterial IQ. The catalog helps compare how microbes read their surroundings.
europmc-pmc1215510:
Ryan, Barry, Murphy, and Mahon explored a puzzle about stem cells in 2005. Mesenchymal stem cells come from adult bone marrow. They can help rebuild cartilage, bone, muscle, and tendons. Normal immune rules should reject cells from another person.

In practice, these stem cells often avoid rejection. Lab dish studies back that pattern. The cells show few alarm flags to the immune system. They also calm killer cells and reshape nearby immune activity. Ryan compares this tolerance to how a mother tolerates a fetus. The trait could make donor cell therapy far simpler.
europmc-pmc1560110:
A small score change on a health survey can mean two unlike things. de Vet and co-authors untangled them in 2006. One is the smallest change a tool can reliably detect, beyond noise. The other is the smallest change patients count as important.

Methods that use score spread alone tend to find the detectable change. Methods anchored to patient judgment find the important change. de Vet argues the two should not be merged into one number. Knowing both tells clinics whether a tool is sharp enough to catch changes that matter. Anchor-based methods, they say, deserve preference for importance.
europmc-pmc1637810:
When a child meets a chemical can matter as much as how much. Selevan, Kimmel, and Mendola compiled what was known in 2000 about critical windows of exposure, from before conception through adolescence. A workshop weighed evidence for five body areas.

Broad windows of sensitivity exist for the breathing, reproductive, nervous, and hormone systems, and for cancer. But detailed data stay thin. Comparing dose at the target tissue across species needs work. The panel also flagged neglected topics: exposures around puberty, adult effects of early exposure, and gene-environment interplay. Selevan argues window data sharpen risk assessment and protect the most sensitive ages.
europmc-pmc1769410:
Smoke and indoor air pollution raise tuberculosis risk, a pooled analysis confirms. Lin, Ezzati, and Murray reviewed observational studies in 2007: 33 papers on smoking, five on passive smoke, and five on indoor pollution from biomass fuels.

Smokers faced higher risk of a positive TB skin test, of active disease, and of dying from TB. Passive smoke and biomass smoke also pointed to higher disease risk, though on thinner evidence. The exposures persist or grow exactly where TB burden is highest. Lin suggests TB control programs add tobacco and indoor air measures to their plans.
europmc-pmc1820610: Enhancement of SMN2 exon 7 inclusion by antisense oligonucleotides targeting the exon. — a 2005 science paper on SMN2 exon tricks. It boosts exon 7 inclusion. The paper is the SMN2 study: the findings on antisense tricks, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1852410: Quantifying similarity between motifs. — a 2005 science paper on motif likeness math. It quantifies the motif similarity for labs worldwide. The paper is the motif-math study: the findings on motifs for labs, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1931610: Intense sweetness surpasses cocaine reward. — a 2005 science paper on sugar beating cocaine. It finds sweetness tops the reward for labs. The paper is the sweetness study: the findings on cocaine reward, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2025310: Design and analysis of randomized clinical trials requiring prolonged observation of each patient. II. analysis and examples. — a 2005 science paper on trial design stats. It guides the trial design. The paper is the design guide: the findings on clinical trials, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2222610: A role of TRPA1 in mechanical hyperalgesia is revealed by pharmacological inhibition. — a 2005 science paper on TRPA1 and pain. It reveals the TRPA1 role. The paper is the TRPA1 study: the findings on hyperalgesia, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2235210: Blood lead concentrations < 10 microg/dL and child intelligence at 6 years of age. — a 2005 science paper on low lead and kid smarts. It links the lead concentrations. The paper is the lead study: the findings on child ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2289810: The Dutch version of the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score: a validation study. — a 2005 science paper on a Dutch knee-score test. It validates the knee score. The paper is the validation study: the findings on knee ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2363610: Information needs of patients with cancer: results from a large study in UK cancer centres. — a 2008 science paper on cancer patients' info needs. It surveys the information needs. The paper is the need study: the findings on cancer, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2543010: Health-related quality of life in breast cancer patients: a bibliographic review of the literat — a 2008 science paper on quality of life in breast cancer. It reviews the bibliographic literature. The paper is the quality review: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2633610: Dengue virus type 2 infections of Aedes aegypti are modulated by the mosquito's RNA interferenc — a 2008 science paper on dengue in mosquitoes. It modulates the RNA interference. The paper is the dengue study: the findings on dengue ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2642810: Acute exercise and oxidative stress: a 30 year history. — a 2008 science paper on exercise and oxidative stress. It reviews the 30-year history. The paper is the history study: the findings on exercise ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2654510: Assembly and development of the Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm matrix. — a 2008 science paper on slime-city building. It studies the slime-city building for labs. The paper is the slime study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2687710: Gene expression profiling of the tumor microenvironment during breast cancer progression. — a 2008 science paper on tumor microenvironments. It profiles the gene expression. The paper is the profile study: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2707010: The PRISMA statement for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies that evaluat — a 2008 science paper on the PRISMA statement. It reports the systematic reviews. The paper is the PRISMA guide: the findings on reporting ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2781110: An abundance of ubiquitously expressed genes revealed by tissue transcriptome sequence data. — a 2008 science paper on ubiquitous genes. It reveals the tissue transcriptome. The paper is the gene study: the findings on gene ills, filed here in session.
plos-pone-0004910:
Simon Reinke and colleagues studied influence of recovery and training phases on soccer players body composition and immunity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Professional soccer players endure lengthy seasons with high physical stress maintained throughout. The recuperation period before next pre season is generally considered short but sufficient. The team tracked peripheral vascular function and immune system markers across recovery and retraining in elite athletes.

Recovery restores most markers but not all equally. Short off seasons may accumulate fatigue across careers. Monitoring guides individualized load management. Elite sport science informs occupational health. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005010:
When a cell dies by apoptosis, its DNA is chopped into pieces. The first cuts were thought to land randomly. Miriam Di Filippo and Giorgio Bernardi showed otherwise in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used an entirely new approach on chicken liver cells. Their focus was early apoptotic DNA fragmentation.

The early cuts strike only a few specific regions. Those regions are open chromatin, where DNA is loosely packed. The precision suggests a programmed first strike. Random shredding comes later, if at all. The finding rewrites the opening chapter of cell death. It raises new questions about how the cutting machinery chooses its first targets.
plos-pone-0005110:
Dried bloodstains hold DNA that forensic scientists prize. Ancient DNA researchers prize it too. A worry was that aging hemoglobin damages that DNA. April Marrone and Jack Ballantyne tested the worry in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hemoglobin is the iron-carrying protein of red blood cells. In the dry state, it changes over time.

Those changes did not increase oxidative DNA damage. Dried blood keeps its DNA safer than feared. The finding reassures anyone reading genes from old stains. Crime labs can trust aged samples a bit more. Ancient DNA work gains the same reassurance. The study turns a plausible fear into a tested non-issue.
plos-pone-0005210:
Macrophages are immune cells that swallow invading bacteria, a process called phagocytosis. Staphylococcus aureus can survive that swallowing, turning the macrophage into a refuge. Koziel and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the swallowing also changes the macrophage itself.

After taking in the bacteria, macrophages raised their levels of anti-death factors that keep the cell alive. A living host cell shelters the bacteria inside it. That bargain helps explain why staph infections can persist, and it points to the host cell's survival program as a treatment target. If the host cell stays alive, the germs inside it stay safe too, so drugs that break that truce could clear infections that now come back.
plos-pone-0005310:
For a synapse to release its message, vesicles must dock at the membrane in a precise molecular embrace. Camoletto and colleagues studied one docking partnership in PLOS ONE in 2009, between the proteins syntaxin1 and Munc18. A lipid called sphingosine turned out to regulate it.

Mice lacking an enzyme that breaks down sphingolipids model a disorder with mental retardation, making them useful for this question. The work shows lipids are not passive packing in synapses. They actively tune docking, which links lipid balance to healthy brain signaling. Fat and sugar signals share the stage at the synapse, so a fault in fat balance could dull the mind in ways that pure protein views would miss at first glance.
plos-pone-0005910:
Liz Allen and co-authors compared in 2009 two ways of judging which research papers truly matter: expert review and citation counts. Funders need to know which outputs were landmarks. Shortly after publication in 2005, nearly seven hundred Wellcome Trust papers were rated by experts.

The team checked how well bibliometric indicators matched those expert judgments of quality and importance. Agreement was imperfect, which matters when money follows metrics. Counts are cheap and experts are costly, so the trade-off needs evidence. This study supplies it for a large, real cohort of biomedical papers.
plos-pone-0006010:
The eye sharpens an image before the brain ever sees it. Jacques Demongeot, Yannick Fouquet, Muhammad Tayyab and colleagues borrowed that skill for image processing in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies how natural vision works, in healthy eyes and in failing ones, and turns those mechanisms into contrast and contour operators for pictures.

Their models rest on neural networks with lateral inhibition, where active cells quiet their neighbors and edges stand out. Such flows can raise contrast and trace outlines in an image. By copying the retina's own tricks, the work links biology to software and may help both: better image tools, and a clearer model of vision itself.
plos-pone-0006110:
What a young rat eats can echo in its adult pancreas. Nicolas Theys, André Clippe, Thomas Bouckenooghe and colleagues followed that echo in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies rat islets, the pancreas clusters that make insulin. These islets start life with a weak antioxidant defense. They hold plenty of one guard enzyme and too little of the two that finish its work.

An early low-protein diet worsens that imbalance, and the islets falter. A defense left lopsided leaves insulin cells open to oxidative harm for life. The work links early nutrition to later diabetes risk by a named mechanism, giving the broad idea of developmental programming a concrete, testable chain.
plos-pone-0006210:
Smoking makes Crohn's disease worse, raising the risk of narrowed bowel, abnormal tunnels, and surgery. Ole Haagen Nielsen and colleagues asked what smoking does to gene activity in the colon, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of Crohn's patients. Genes and environment together drive the disease, and smoke is its best-known environmental harm.

The team profiled which genes were switched on or off in smokers versus non-smokers with Crohn's. Those shifts point to the pathways through which smoke aggravates the bowel. Knowing the pathways strengthens advice to quit with hard biology. It may also reveal drug targets that mimic the benefit of quitting.
plos-pone-0006710:
Liang-I Lin, Shih-hui Chao, and Deirdre R. Meldrum built a simple device for isolating single cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microfabricated devices are powerful for cell-level studies. Building them, though, requires clean rooms and special training. Most biology labs cannot make or afford them easily. The authors wanted high-throughput single-cell analysis without microfabrication.

Their device is called the Microscale Oil-Covered Cell Array, or MOCCA. It is low-cost and simple enough for ordinary labs to assemble. Cells settle into an array where each can be studied alone. Single-cell work reveals differences that mixed samples hide. A practical device like MOCCA widens access to that kind of analysis.
plos-pone-0006810:
Mojgan Rastegar and colleagues designed gene therapy vectors for Rett syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rett syndrome is an autism spectrum disorder. It is the leading cause of intellectual disability in females. Mutations in the MECP2 gene cause the condition. No treatment exists.

The team built viral vectors carrying the MECP2 gene. Their vectors are isoform-specific, matching particular versions of the protein. Expression from the vectors can be regulated. Control matters because too much MECP2 is also harmful. Regulated, specific delivery is a step toward safe gene therapy for Rett syndrome.
plos-pone-0006910:
Rikke Bæk Sørensen and colleagues found the immune system attacking a cancer-helping enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, or IDO. IDO suppresses immunity inside tumors and their draining lymph nodes. It helps establish tolerance toward the cancer. That makes IDO a villain in tumor immunology.

Patients nevertheless carried cellular immune responses against IDO itself. The immune system strikes back, as the title puts it. Such spontaneous responses suggest IDO can serve as a vaccine target. Turning a tolerance promoter into a target is an elegant reversal. The finding supports vaccines designed around IDO-derived peptides.
plos-pone-0007010:
Rudolph Spangler, Noel Goddard, and David Thaler fine-tuned a detection test in PLOS ONE in 2009. PCR can in principle detect a single target DNA molecule. In practice, stray bacterial DNA hiding in reagents sets the real limit. That contamination plagues efforts to find sparse bacteria in environmental and health samples.

The team varied the amount of Taq polymerase in the reaction. Their aim was the best signal-to-noise for broad range detection. A cleaner test matters for water safety and hospital screening. When bacteria are rare, cutting background noise is the difference between detection and a false answer.
plos-pone-0007110:
Oliver Baumann and Mark Greenlee studied attention and eye tracking in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smooth pursuit lets the eyes follow a moving target. Older views treated it as nearly automatic. Newer evidence showed attention matters for accurate pursuit. What attention does during pursuit, though, was unsettled.

The pair had subjects attend to moving sounds while tracking with their eyes. They measured the resulting activity in the cortex. Attention to auditory motion changed pursuit-related brain responses. The study shows the senses cooperate during tracking, rather than the eyes working alone. That matters for understanding attention disorders.
plos-pone-0007210:
Anna T. Reinicke, Kyla D. Omilusik, Genc Basha, and colleagues studied immunity to a foodborne bacterium in 2009. The bacterium is Listeria monocytogenes, which can cause serious illness. Dendritic cells can start CD8 T cell responses by cross-presentation, showing outside material in a special way.

That process lets a small number of dendritic cells start primary immune responses. The authors ask whether cross-priming by dendritic cells is essential against Listeria. Their PLOS ONE paper tests the requirement in living infection. The result matters for vaccine design, where dendritic cell pathways are a common target.
plos-pone-0007310: Mihaela E. Sardiu, Joshua M. Gilmore, Michael J. Carrozza, and colleagues presented a proteomics method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is protein complexes, groups of proteins that work together as machines inside cells. Knowing which proteins connect within a complex is essential for mapping cell function. The authors build a probabilistic deletion network from quantitative proteomics data, using protein removal patterns to infer how complex members connect with each other.
openalex-w1969593010: In Europe and Asia, genes track language and geography — but not in South America. Roewer and colleagues' 2013 study found continent-wide decoupling of Y-chromosomal variation from language and geography in Native South Americans. The result rewrote assumptions about the continent's peopling.
openalex-w1978700210: Ebola returned — this time in West Africa. Bausch and Schwarz's 2014 paper on the Ebola outbreak in Guinea examined where ecology meets economy, with over 350 cases and 69% fatality at the time. The analysis traced the Zaire ebolavirus's deadly emergence.
openalex-w1987104810: Lung scarring in IPF may replay embryonic programs gone wrong. A 2008 paper by Selman, Pardo, and Kaminski argues the disease involves aberrant recapitulation of developmental programs. The authors linked embryonic signaling pathways to the lung's runaway scarring process.
openalex-w2007400810: Amazon frogs mostly descend from Andean ancestors. A 2009 study found the rainforest's frog diversity comes mainly from Late Miocene Andean lineages. The work traced the frog boom to ancient mountain radiations millions of years back.
openalex-w2010506910: Vivax strikes the youngest — falciparum waits. Lin and colleagues' 2010 study mapped differential infection and disease patterns of P. falciparum and P. vivax in young Papua New Guinean children. The work showed immunity to vivax arrives faster.
openalex-w2053689710: Can blue light keep us alert? A 2011 study tested blue-enriched light's effects on melatonin, alertness, and thinking skills. The experiments asked whether short-wavelength light beats ordinary lamps for wakefulness at work and school desks.
openalex-w2057099110: Schizophrenia changes the brain's signal complexity. A 2014 study measured complexity of brain fMRI signals in schizophrenia during a social exclusion task. The entropy and Hurst scores separated patients from peers at rest and under stress.
openalex-w2076407210: Dengue hit Machala in waves — maps caught them. Stewart Ibarra and colleagues' 2014 study analyzed spatiotemporal clustering, climate periodicity, and social-ecological risk factors for dengue during the 2010 Machala outbreak. The work pinpointed where and why the virus surged.
openalex-w2110745710: The rarest B decays got measured. The CMS team's 2013 paper measured the Bs0→μ+μ− rate and hunted B0→μ+μ− in collisions. The results pinned the ultra-rare decays against Standard Model predictions — a precision test, passed with flying colors.
plos-pone-0006310:
Brain responses to food pictures differ between lean people and those who have lost weight. Marc-Andre Cornier and colleagues tested short-term overfeeding in thin and reduced-obese volunteers in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Energy intake is regulated by body signals mixed with sensory input from the outside world.

The study examined how overfeeding changes the neuronal response to visual food cues in both groups. Comparing people who were never heavy with those who slimmed down isolates weight history effects. Such effects may explain why keeping weight off is so hard. The work maps appetite circuits under deliberate excess.
plos-pone-0009710:
Glaucoma slowly steals side vision, which can make driving risky. David Crabb and colleagues tracked eye movements in glaucoma patients as they viewed a driving scene. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eye movements show where a driver looks and what they might miss.

Where the gaze goes matters when part of the visual field is gone. The team mapped scanning patterns and compared them with safe driving needs. Patterns like these could inform fitness-to-drive checks. They also matter for designing road scenes that are easier to scan.
openalex-w2155573710: Do strong boards and shareholder rules lead to more honest financial reporting in Latin America? A 2013 study in the Journal of Business Ethics tackles that question. American and European research says good corporate governance improves the quality of reported earnings, but Latin American firms often have controlling owners who can override such rules. The paper measures whether governance reforms actually curb earnings manipulation across Latin American markets.
openalex-w2171812510: In 2006, hundreds of scientists descended on Mexico City to chase its pollution downwind. This 2010 overview paper describes MILAGRO, the Megacity Initiative that tracked the Mexico City metropolitan area's emissions as they traveled, transformed, and aged in the atmosphere. The campaign's goal: understand what one of the world's largest megacities exhales — and what that means for air and climate far beyond its borders.
openalex-w2423333910: Between September 2015 and January 2016, Advanced LIGO heard the universe's darkest collisions for the first time. This 2016 Physical Review X paper presents the full results of the search for binary black hole merger signals in that first observing run. Beyond the headline detections, it details the analysis that turned faint spacetime ripples into confirmed discoveries.
openalex-w2594421110: Losing your sense of smell erodes quality of life — and predicts neurodegeneration and even death. This 2017 Rhinology position paper tackles olfactory dysfunction, arguing the field is held back by inconsistent methods. It calls for standardized approaches so research on smell loss can translate into real help for patients.
openalex-w2918495910: Getting to sustainable electricity doesn't require one giant leap — it can happen through evolutionary steps.
