arxiv-2606-16310: Transformer attention has a costly memory footprint from caching keys. MLA (multi-head latent attention) shrinks that cache, and this paper adds QK normalization — stabilizing the query-key math — without needing the full key cache back. The result is a more stable, memory-light attention variant for engineers training large language models.
arxiv-2606-16410: Some flakes spit volts when warmed — a boon for small sense gear and heat cash. This paper feels that warm-volt trait in CuInP2S6, a peel-thin layered flake, down at dot scale. For flake pros who chase wee power skins.
arxiv-2606-16710: Multi-agent AI systems are supposed to be benign — but false claims can still spread between agents like a rumor. This paper studies misinformation propagation in benign multi-agent systems: how wrong beliefs travel even when no agent means harm. It targets AI safety researchers worried about emergent deception.
arxiv-2606-16910: Teen talk online swims with mind-benders — pushy peers, slick ads. IMPACTeen charts the wiles in teen chat: aims, twists, sway-moves, marks, and fallout. It is for teen-guard researchers. Know the wiles, shield the young. Wiles mapped, youths safer. Every trick named.
19893-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
The Great Events by Famous Historians retells world-shaping moments through noted writers. Volume ten covers an age dominated by Spain's Philip the Second. Philip succeeded his father Charles the Fifth on Spain's throne. American conquest wealth poured into his coffers without end. His domains' vast extent made him his age's central figure. The absoluteness of his authority matched his wealth. Famous historians narrate such peaks and falls in turn.

Rossiter Johnson edited the set in 1905 for home libraries. Each volume pairs events with historians who wrote memorably on them. Philip's Spain brings Armada, Inquisition, and Dutch revolt. The series sold history as literature to general readers. Its selections show what 1905 thought great. Volume ten is a fair cross-section of the set.
arxiv-2601-06910:
Huihui Huang ♢ \diamondsuit and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers PenForge. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Penetration testing is essential for identifying vulnerabilities in web applications before real adversaries can exploit them. Recent work has explored automating this process with Large Language Model (LLM)-powered agents.

But existing approaches either rely on a single generic agent that struggles. In complex scenarios or narrowly specialized agents that cannot adapt to diverse vulnerability types. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07210:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Angshul Majumdar and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Quantum-Compatible dictionary learning via doubly sparse models. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Dictionary learning (DL) is a core tool in signal processing and machine learning for discovering sparse representations of data.

In contrast with classical successes, there is currently no practical quantum dictionary learning algorithm. We argue that this absence stems from structural mismatches between classical DL formulations and the operational constraints of quantum computing. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07910:
Marc Klinger, Jonah Kudler-Flam, and Gautam Satishchandran work on entropy in quantum gravity. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the second in a series, studies observables outside a steady black hole. It also covers the static patch of de Sitter spacetime, a model of an expanding universe.

Earlier work showed that graviton backreaction shifts the horizon area at second order. That shift places a real constraint on which observables count as physical in the region. The authors use this setup to argue that generalized entropy acts as von Neumann entropy. They also work out the full symmetry group and its edge modes.
arxiv-2601-08110:
Reza Arablouei presents a faster back-end for incremental SLAM, the mapping task robots use to locate themselves. His 2026 arXiv paper claims batch-level accuracy at much lower computational cost. The method rests on two ideas that work together.

Information-guided gating uses a log-determinant criterion on the information matrix. It measures how much new data adds and triggers global optimization only after a real gain. Selective partial optimization then updates only the parts that need it. Skipping needless relinearization saves time on every step. For robotics readers, the paper offers a path to accurate maps without paying full batch cost.
arxiv-2601-08610: Wenxuan Guo, Panos Toulis, and Yuhao Wang develop permutation inference for regressions with multi-way clustering. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such applications often have few effective clusters or heavy-tailed data. Standard cluster-robust and bootstrap inference then prove unreliable in finite samples. Missing data add a further complication in the same settings. The authors build finite-sample valid permutation inference under conditional exchangeability of errors. Economists with clustered panel data gain tests whose stated error rates can be trusted at real sample sizes.
arxiv-2601-07010:
Yi Chen, Yue Ban, Qi-Biao Zhu, and Xi Chen wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on light that leaks through a pair of prisms. A thin sheet of graphene sits in the path of the light. Graphene is a sheet of carbon one atom thick. The setup is a case of frustrated total internal reflection, where light that should bounce back can cross a small gap.

At low terahertz rates, the graphene can host surface waves called plasmons. Those waves let light pass through in a sharp peak. They also shift the beam to the side as it leaves. That side shift is called the Goos-Hanchen shift, and here it grows large. The paper works through when the peak and the shift show up. The results may guide small parts that steer light by touch with a sheet of carbon.
arxiv-2601-07310:
Zhongming Liu and Bingbing Jiang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on two ways a model can focus. Deep learning models use what is called attention to weigh parts of their input. One form weighs which channels of data count most. The other form weighs which spots in the input count most. Teams must fuse the two forms into one block.

Most teams fuse them in one of two ways: one after the next, in a chain, or side by side at the same time. To date, teams pick by trial, with no firm rule to guide them. Liu and Jiang study the full range of picks in one work, on the same terms. The aim is a clear set of rules for how to order the two forms of focus.
arxiv-2601-08710:
Franz Baader and Oliver Fernandez Gil study how to join terms in formal logic. To join two terms, one must swap in values for their free parts so both sides match. The type of a rule set tells how hard that join task is. That type rests on how we rank the swaps we use.

The pair shows the rank rule can change the type. If we count all free parts, we may get one type. If we count only parts in the task, we may get a next type. They then lift results from single rule sets to whole classes of sets. A reader in logic gets a sharp warn. A claim about join type must state which rank rule it used.
arxiv-2601-09110:
Kai Hu and four co-authors mark farm plots in space shots with just a few marked cases. Plot marks guide crop counts and land checks. In poor zones, marked shots are few and dear. Top tools need vast marked sets and fall hard when marks are thin. Past shots over time can help, but time adds its own noise.

Their tool borrows priors from SAM, a broad mark tool. Priors here are shape sense learned from vast past data. With that sense, a few marks can guide a full mark of a time set. A reader in farm tech gets a way to map plots where hand marks will stay rare.
arxiv-2601-09510:
Sebastian Tim Holdum, Frederik Ravn Klausen, and Peter Michael Reichstein Rasmussen take up an open problem about central binomial coefficients. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether the coefficient 2n choose n is always divisible by 4 or 9 once n passes 256. Nobody knows the full answer yet.

The authors prove a related density result in prime bases. For a fixed odd m, the share of exponents k for which m fails to divide the coefficient at 2^k tends to zero. Density results like this show the stubborn cases grow ever rarer. The work chips at the open problem from the side of powers in prime bases.
arxiv-2601-09910:
Gergely Kiss, Ádám Markó, Zoltán Lóránt Nagy, and Gábor Somlai study point sets in a finite field space. A set is called p-divisible when each flat plane cuts it in a count that p divides. Such sets link pure math with code and design work.

The team looks at sets of p squared points in three dims. A known guess by Ball says each such set must be a cylinder. A cylinder is built by lifting a plane set along one line. The paper probes when this guess holds. It sorts sets by type and tests which shapes can occur.
arxiv-2601-10310:
Jan Christian Blaise Cruz, David Ifeoluwa Adelani, and Alham Fikri Aji treat a new tongue as a shift in sense, not just new words. A model that knows one tongue must adapt to the next. Past work leans on shared weights and scale. Sense may still drift twixt tongues.

The team made SENSIA, a sense based align plan. It starts from a Backpack model in one tongue. It lines up sense mixes and context states on paired text. It trains a tongue model loss at the same time. That keeps speech fluent in the new tongue. The aim is sense that stays put across tongues.
arxiv-2601-10610:
Jean Bertoin, Armand Riera, and Alejandro Rosales-Ortiz study self-similar Markov trees, random branching shapes used in probability theory. Each tree carries a decoration, a value assigned across the tree that can grow or shrink along branches. Their work builds on a recent monograph that set up this class of trees. The focus here is on local times and excursions.

Local times measure how much a process lingers near a level. Excursions capture the stretches of a path between returns to a base state. For these decorated trees, both notions need fresh care. Results of this kind feed models of growth, fragmentation, and random search. The paper gives probabilists new tools for a class of trees with wide use.
arxiv-2601-10710:
Cheng Chen and co-authors tackle a weak joint in vision-language models. These models link a vision encoder to a large language model. In most designs, only the encoder's final output feeds the language model, through one crude link. That single bridge forms a bottleneck for visual detail.

Fine detail lives in early vision layers, while broad meaning sits in late ones. A static link cannot blend both well. The authors propose dynamic cross-layer injection, feeding visual features at many depths into the language model. The aim is tighter alignment between words and image structure. Better fusion could sharpen how models describe and reason about what they see.
arxiv-2601-12210:
Alexander Medvedev and Anton V. Proskurnikov ask when pulse-modulated feedback can keep a system's output in a set corridor. The system is positive, time-invariant, and has one input and one output. The output must stay in a fixed band of values.

For third-order plants with a set form, they prove the task can always be solved in steady conditions. Pulse feedback switches the input in bursts in place of a smooth signal. A proof of solvability guides safe control in such plants. The work is in control theory.  The proof is for plants with a set third order form.
arxiv-2601-12310:
Jennifer Dodgson, Alfath Daryl Alhajir, and Michael Joedhitya build a self-training system whose only reward is survival. Self-training often degrades, since no outside gauge judges data quality. That leads to reward hacking and drift in sense.

Their proof-of-concept system trains under sparse outside feedback and bounded memory. Selection is mediated by the environment, not by a learned reward. They chart its learning dynamics and its failure modes. A stable self-trainer could learn in open settings with less oversight.  Bounded memory is part of the design from the start.  Its failure modes are part of the report, not hidden.
arxiv-2601-11210:
Li Wang, Wenyu Chen, Ning Yu, Zheng Li, and Shanqing Guo test privacy in video models. Their 2026 preprint is called VidLeaks, on attacks for text-to-video systems. These models train on vast sets of clips scraped from the web. That scale raises sharp risks for copyright and private rights.

An attack of this kind asks if a clip was in training. That test can audit what a lab used to build its model. Old tests were made for still images or plain text. They miss the mix of space and time that drives video. VidLeaks is built for that mix. It aims to give owners and auditors a tool that fits video.
arxiv-2601-11310:
Antoine Carreaud and five coauthors segment vast aerial images with care. Their 2026 preprint uses stage-wise attention for the task. Semantic segmentation labels each pixel by what it shows. Ultra-high-resolution images are key in mapping and land monitoring.

Transformer models are strong at this task but hit a wall. Memory use grows with the square of the token count. Big images force a bad choice on the model. It must shrink either context or fine spatial detail. The team's stage-wise attention works through the image in steps. That design aims to keep both wide context and fine detail. Remote sensing work needs that pair to map land well.
arxiv-2601-11510:
Letitia Li and five coauthors report on formal methods in real defense code. Their 2026 experience report covers an electronic warfare codebase. Formal methods prove code traits rather than just test cases. That power beats unit testing for some kinds of assurance.

The catch is a steep learning curve for developers. That curve blocks wider use in industrial workflows. A tool must give useful output with minimal user effort. The team applied such tools inside a real engineering flow. They report what helped and what hindered in practice. The lessons aim to ease adoption by working teams. High-assurance fields like electronic warfare gain the most.
arxiv-2601-11710:
B. Draine studies resonant scattering of helium light in H II regions. The 2026 preprint is accepted by The Astrophysical Journal. H II regions are clouds of ionized gas around hot stars. The line in focus is the He I triplet at 1.0833 micrometers.

Metastable helium atoms scatter those triplet photons on resonance. The team studies optical depths typical of H II regions. Regions with large metastable column densities stand out. They are predicted to show unusually broad emission spectra. Multipeaked line shapes are the other predicted trait. Such spectra can diagnose the gas in star-forming clouds. Observers can test the forecast with infrared telescopes.
arxiv-2601-13410:
Aditya Acharya, Auguste Gezalyan, and David Mount classify points in a high dim space bent by the Hilbert metric. That metric grows the Cayley-Klein hyperbolic span to any convex body. It has wide use in learning and convex shape work. Classify is a core task, to split points by kind in such a bent space.

The team works in the polygonal form of the metric, where the body is a polygon like form in many dims. They give rules to classify points there with care for cost as dims grow. Bent spaces fit data whose ranks bend, so sound rules there aid real tasks. The work links pure shape to a stock learning act.
arxiv-2601-13510:
Kazuki Nakazawa and co-authors read the spin weave of a Fermi surface from a wavy magnet mark. Spin orbit links tie a bit's spin to its path. That tie is a must for many next tech plans. Yet to probe its strength and form is hard, most of all in layered stacks.

The team's probe is the Shubnikov-de Haas effect, a wave in magnet drag as field grows. In its non linear form it can hold marks of the spin weave on the Fermi surface. That surface is the edge of filled states in a metal. A probe that reads spin weave with a lab mark aids stack design for spin tools.
arxiv-2601-12910:
Tim Baumgartner and Iryna Gurevych, at TU Darmstadt, present SciCoQA, a dataset for paper and code alignment. Scientific papers often ship with code that should implement their methods. Discrepancies between paper and codebase can hide bugs or changed claims. Detecting those gaps is key to faithful implementations and reproducibility.

They construct SciCoQA from GitHub issues and reproducibility papers. Real reported mismatches give the dataset grounded examples. To scale it, they propose a synthetic generation method for paper code discrepancies. Quality assurance of this kind helps readers trust published code. It also gives tool builders a benchmark for alignment checkers.
arxiv-2601-13610:
Hansika Weerasena, Matthew Randall, and Prabhat Mishra work on keeping chip traffic safe from spies in 2026. In a system-on-chip, many parts talk through a network-on-chip. Rogue parts can listen in on that traffic, a stealthy and common attack. Strong coding can guard the data, but it can cost too much for small, tight chips.

The team uses multi-path routing, which splits a message across paths. They pair it with an all-or-nothing transform, a trick that makes partial data useless alone. A spy who grabs one path gets nothing of worth. The plan seeks strong safety with costs a small chip can bear.
arxiv-2601-13710:
Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury and co-authors predict who gains from sinus surgery in 2026. Chronic rhinosinusitis is a long-term swelling of the sinuses that burdens daily life. Surgery helps some patients much and others far less. The team defines success as a set drop in the SNOT-22 score six months after surgery.

They compare generative AI with supervised machine learning for this forecast. Both use clinical data from before surgery, not scans alone. A sound forecast could guide patients and doctors to better choices. It could also spare some patients surgery that would not help them.
arxiv-2601-14310:
Nay Myat Min, Long H. Pham, Hongyu Zhang, and Jun Sun attack hallucination detectors in this 2026 paper. Single-pass detectors scan a model's internal signals for signs of made-up text. Those signals include uncertainty, hidden-state geometry, and attention. The method rests on one quiet assumption. It assumes false text leaves traces that stand apart in those signals.

The team tests that assumption with a white-box, model-side adversary. It fine-tunes small LoRA adapters on the model while the detector stays fixed. Their procedure, CORVUS, learns to camouflage the signals a detector can see. It even adds an embedding-space stress test on attention. The study shows how such detectors can be fooled.
arxiv-2601-14410:
Debanjan Roy and four co-authors study a quantum guessing task in this 2026 paper. Quantum state exclusion means naming at least one state from a known set that was not used to prepare a system. It is the mirror image of state identification. A set of states is said to admit the task under certain conditions, which the abstract begins to spell out.

The team's twist is scale: they study exclusion with many copies of the system. More copies give more data per test, but the rules of the game change too. Readers get a study of how copy count affects a basic quantum task, with exact phrasing of the setup cut off in the evidence pack.
arxiv-2601-15510:
Dev Pradeepkumar Nayak, Muhammad Saif Ullah Khalid, and Ali Tarokh model a swimming robot fish in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fish swim by pairing body undulation with tail fin flapping. The two motions interact in complex ways. The team builds a computational framework for a swimmer inspired by the jackfish. In their model, the tail fin sits on its own mount.

That fin pitches passively as fluid forces push it. A nonlinear torsional spring links it to the body. The setup lets the authors probe the body-caudal fin joint itself. They study its dynamic traits and its effect on the flow around the swimmer. Such work guides the design of underwater robots. A well-tuned tail joint can mean faster, cheaper swimming with less energy spent.
arxiv-2601-15210:
Mathys Le Grand, Pascal Urard, and co-authors speed up the design of metasurfaces, flat optics with tiny patterned features. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with inverse design: start from the light behavior you want and find the shape that gives it. The link from shape to behavior is nonlinear and complex.

Classic optimization is slow here and often lands on poor shapes. The authors boost posterior sampling with diffusion models. Sampling many candidate shapes from the learned distribution makes the search richer. The method aims at designs that older tools would miss.
arxiv-2601-15410:
Alex Wright explains a modern way to say a space is negatively curved at large scales. His 2026 arXiv explainer deals with hierarchical hyperbolicity. Curvature is defined locally, yet negative curvature has coarse effects that ignore local detail.

In 1987, Gromov isolated one such effect from which many others follow. His hyperbolic spaces are geodesic spaces where every triangle is thin. Hierarchical hyperbolicity extends that idea to spaces built from many hyperbolic pieces. Wright's piece asks what the notion is and why geometers now use it so widely in their daily work.
arxiv-2601-16710:
P. Noterdaeme and a team of thirteen co-authors report a rare find in deep space. They caught the mark of hydrogen gas in light from a far quasar. The gas sat at a vast span, from when the cosmos was young. Just one such unit showed in ten million plain atoms. Their 2026 preprint lays out the catch and its import.

A big scope in Chile, with a sharp eye tool, took the light. The mark hints at cold, dense clumps in thin gas. These clumps are less than a light span wide. Such finds test tales of how gas clumped early on. They also show how much cold fuel stars had to form.
arxiv-2601-16810:
Nacho Añez-López and a large team map a dark cloud where stars are born. The cloud, G14, sits far off and blocks star light. In such clouds, gas falls in to form stars. Pull, churn, and magnet fields all fight in that fall. Their 2026 preprint uses ALMA to trace the magnet side.

Fine maps show threads of gas and field in the cloud. The team weighs if fields can hold back the fall. That fight sets how fast stars form. It also sets the mass of stars that form. Clear maps help sort which force rules in cold clouds.
arxiv-2601-16910:
Michael Kapralov, Luca Trevisan, and Weronika Wrzos-Kaminska hunt hidden crowds in chance graphs. Some graphs are built with crowds sewn in by chance. Links in a crowd come oft, links across crowds come rare. The task is to find those crowds from the graph. Their 2026 preprint works on graphs with extra shape built in.

That shape can help or hide the crowd hunt. The team gives ways to find crowds in such graphs. Crowd hunts serve fraud, bio, and social net work. Firm proofs on chance graphs guide real-world hunts. They show when crowds can be found at all.
arxiv-2601-17210:
Nyi Nyi Aung, Bradley Wight, and Adrian Stein tackle control of systems whose traits are not known in advance. They study second-order systems, a broad class used for motion and vibration. Their method shapes input signals so switches happen at precise times. It pairs that shaping with live estimates of the system traits.

Because the traits are learned while the system runs, no prior knowledge is needed. The design treats the system as a black box. It still aims for exact switching and smooth motion. For engineers, that means one tool can fit many machines. It cuts the need for long hand tuning on each new setup.
arxiv-2601-17510:
David L. Donoho and co-authors publish the full record of a 2024 town hall on statistics in the age of AI. The session ran at the Joint Statistical Meetings. Top statisticians debated how AI reshapes their field. Topics spanned culture, infrastructure, and training. Foundation models and large-scale empirical work drove much of the talk.

A full record lets readers hear the debate as it was. It shows where the field agrees and where it splits. Training the next cohort is a core concern. So is who owns the data pipelines science now needs. The record serves as a primary source. Future historians of statistics can cite what leaders said, not summaries.
arxiv-2601-17610:
A. Nigoche-Netro and co-authors trace galaxy evolution through dark matter's role. They use a sample of about 126,000 late-type galaxies. The data come from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The team analyzes stellar mass as a function of dynamical mass. Dynamical mass includes the dark matter halo's pull. Late-type galaxies are spiral systems still forming stars.

That mass link shows how visible growth tracks dark scaffolding. Nearby galaxies give the clearest view of the link. A huge sample smooths out odd cases. The study helps sort which traits dark matter drives. It serves models of how spirals grow over cosmic time. The journal record is the Astronomical Journal.
arxiv-2601-17710:
Huy Trinh and three co-authors detect falls with low-cost millimetre-wave radar. Aging populations strain long-term care homes across North America. Falls need fast response, yet false alarms exhaust staff. Alarm fatigue is a real safety risk in itself. The team targets post-fall floor occupancy. They ask if a person stays on the floor after a fall, in a quasi-static state.

Radar guards privacy better than cameras in bedrooms. Low cost lets homes deploy it widely. A reliable post-fall read cuts false dispatches. It also speeds help for true falls. The work fits care settings where staff time is scarce. Quiet, sure sensing is the goal.
arxiv-2601-18010:
Jingyao Wu, Grace Lin, Yinuo Song, and Rosalind Picard build an emotion reader that takes doubt seriously. Their 2026 preprint presents AmbER 2. Emotion is ambiguous by nature. Human raters often disagree on what a voice or a face shows. Speech and text can also point to different feelings in the same moment. Much work models the rater side of that doubt, using label distributions. The cross-modal side has been handled mostly by fusing features, without naming the conflict.

AmbER 2 is aware of both kinds of ambiguity at once. It works across speech and text. Naming the conflict lets the system stay honest when signals clash. That honesty matters in health, education, and support tools that react to feelings.
arxiv-2601-18310:
Hadyan Luthfan Prihadi and co-authors study entanglement across time in a deformed holographic theory. Their 2026 preprint deals with a thermal conformal field theory changed by a relevant scalar operator. The dual picture is a hairy black hole in anti-de Sitter space. The team computes the holographic timelike entanglement entropy and the timelike subregion complexity for this setup. Scalar hair means the black hole carries a scalar field profile, which leaves marks on both quantities.

Timelike entanglement is a young probe of quantum gravity. How it reacts to a deformation tests the holographic dictionary itself. Complexity adds a second lens on the same state. The work extends both tools to a less symmetric, more realistic setting.
arxiv-2601-19410:
Ahrii Kim and Seong-heum Kim test whether longer context truly helps models fix translations. Automatic post editing refines machine translations by correcting the errors that remain. New language models are strong translators, but how well they post edit, above all with whole document context, is little understood.

The pair compare closed and open weight models under a simple document level prompting setup. They grade edit quality, use of context, and toughness against odd inputs. If long context does not pay in edits, translation pipelines can save the tokens for steps that do pay.
arxiv-2601-19510: Vitor Gaboardi dos Santos and five colleagues present ALRM, a system that puts a large language model in charge of a robot's actions. Recent language models can reason and plan in steps, and agentic frameworks build on that skill. ALRM applies those ideas to robotic manipulation, the task of moving and handling objects with a robot arm. The work sits where language models meet hands-on robot control.
arxiv-2601-19810:
Octavio Pappalardo studies how reinforcement learning agents can teach themselves before facing real tasks. Unsupervised pre-training gives an agent prior knowledge that speeds later learning. One promising idea mirrors human development: agents that set and pursue their own goals. The hard part is generating goals, choosing among them, and learning from them effectively.

The paper proposes a method for learning efficient exploration through self-imposed goals. An agent that explores well in pre-training starts downstream tasks with a head start. The approach needs no external reward during the exploratory phase. That makes it usable where rewards are sparse or undefined. The work speaks to robotics and game agents that must adapt quickly to new worlds.
arxiv-2601-20210:
Huan Yang, Bing Liu, Houdun Zeng, and Xiaoyuan Huang analyze gamma-ray emission from the region of S147, a middle-aged supernova remnant. They use about sixteen and a half years of data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope. Spatially, they find a new extended source of gamma rays, distinct from the emission tied to the remnant's glowing shell filaments.

The new component points to cosmic rays that escaped the remnant and now strike nearby molecular clouds. When cosmic rays hit gas, they produce gamma rays that reveal their path. The study helps trace how the particles scattered by an old explosion spread into the space around it.
arxiv-2601-20310:
Xin Zhang and five colleagues present SemBind, a defense for watermarks placed inside AI-generated images. Latent watermarks are built into the generation process of diffusion models, which makes detection and attribution easy. But black-box forgery attacks can lift a provider's watermark from one real image and stamp it onto images the provider never made.

That forgery breaks trust in provenance, since a watermark would no longer prove origin. SemBind binds the watermark to the meaning of the image itself, so copying it onto other content fails. The work matters as platforms rely on watermarks to sort real media from fake.
arxiv-2601-20510:
Robin Singh and five colleagues evaluate how well detectors catch audio deepfakes made by modern text-to-speech systems. Speech synthesis has grown so realistic that telling fake from real audio is now a serious challenge. The authors compare three leading systems: Dia2, Maya1, and MeloTTS, which stand for streaming, language-model-based, and non-autoregressive designs.

By testing detectors against all three families, the study shows where detection keeps up and where it fails. The result matters for fraud prevention, since voice clones already fuel phone scams, and for any court or newsroom that must trust a recording.
arxiv-2601-20610:
Ting Li builds a way to draw cause-and-effect claims from brain scans and other medical images. The aim is to learn how features of an organ, seen in a scan, change health outcomes. That kind of claim is key for research and for care, but it is hard to make with care.

The model she proposes is a functional linear structural equation model. It links three things: health outcomes, the scan data treated as smooth curves, and plain facts about the patient, such as genes, sex, and age. Keeping the scan as a curve keeps where in the organ a signal sits. That care is what lets the model aim at causes, not just at guesses about who will do well.
arxiv-2601-18510:
Yibo Li and seven colleagues give language model agents a way to learn on the job with no new training runs. An agent's weights freeze once it ships, so it cannot learn from its own past wins and slips in the plain way. Full re-training is dear and can wipe old skills. The team skip the weight change and learn in a leaner way.

Their plan feeds the agent fresh cues drawn from its own past runs, right at the time of need. Those cues steer its next steps while its weights stay put. In time the agent acts as if it had learned, with no risk of a bad train run. The trick could let field agents grow with use at low cost. It also keeps the base model whole for the next user.
arxiv-2601-18910:
A lab report checks how well the count of doubt in a space scope's shots holds up when the shots are near dark. The scope is a tool on a famed space eye that reads light past the hue our eyes can see. Some of its marks are so faint that a shot may hold just none or one count of light in each dot. At that floor, the plain maths of doubt can go wrong.

The report tests the scope's own count path on such near-dark shots. It asks if the doubt the path states is the doubt the shots truly hold. A wrong doubt count can bend all claims made from faint shots. The check serves all who use the scope to read the most faint stars and clouds. It is part of the care that keeps space data sound.
arxiv-2601-18710:
Azra Bano and Larry Liebovitch test if quantum learn tools can spot a kind of blood cancer in shots of blood cells. The cancer, named in the title, is found now by staff who read cell form by eye. That read is slow and takes rare skill. A smart tool that helps could speed care. But quantum tools face hard caps: their states break when read, so the plain way to train a net will not run on them.

The pair try two paths that fit those caps. One learns by a push-pull of stored force, with no need for the banned train trick. The next is a small quantum chain whose dials are tuned by a plain tool. Both are graded on real shots with just two calls: cancer or not. That would show such tools can do real work now.
arxiv-2601-21410:
Erica Zhang, Naomi Sagan, Danny Tse, Fangzhao Zhang, Mert Pilanci, and Jose Blanchet blend language model knowledge into classic statistics with guardrails. Language models hold broad facts that could sharpen data analysis. Past attempts either trusted that guidance without checking it, which invites made-up facts, or locked it inside one fixed learner.

Their framework, Statsformer, validates the guidance before use. It also spreads the knowledge across an ensemble of learners rather than one. Checked guidance keeps the gains of outside knowledge while limiting harm from errors. The design suits fields where a wrong fact can spoil a serious analysis.
arxiv-2601-21510:
David Valle, Alexandre Wagemakers, and Miguel A.F. Sanjuán review how machine learning reads chaotic systems through their basins. In a chaotic system, the basin of an outcome is the set of starts that end there. Mapping those basins once took heavy computation, and acting on the map in real time was out of reach.

Learning methods from image networks to transformers now chart phase space far faster. They also mark out safe sets, regions where a system can be kept under control. The review ties these tools to live action on chaotic systems. Faster maps could help steer ships, circuits, and other systems that sit near chaos.
arxiv-2601-22210:
A team of algebra scholars sort out a class of modules over twisted affine Lie superalgebras. Their 2026 preprint deals with the zero-level, integrable, finite-weight case. These are abstract structures used to study symmetry in math and physics.

The main result gives a full account of what such modules look like. Each one is built, in a set way, from a module over a simpler algebra. That base algebra takes one of two named forms. The result gives peers a clean map of this corner of the field. It can anchor later work on these algebras.
arxiv-2601-22310:
Paula Mellado studies what happens where a sheet of graphene meets a topological insulator. In her 2026 preprint, a moiré pattern — a large-scale beat pattern from two grids — reshapes the surface states. The pattern tunes the Rashba effect, which links an electron's motion to its spin.

With no spin-orbit link, the folded bands come out flat and spin-paired. Turn the link on, and the pairing breaks. The repeat scale of the spectrum then shrinks by half. The result shows a neat knob for spin control. Such knobs are prized in thin-device design.
arxiv-2601-22410:
Imene Kolli, Kai-Robin Lange, Jonas Rieger, and Carsten Jentsch track how word senses shift over time with graphs a human can read. Their 2026 preprint builds, for each target word and time slice, a web of nearby senses. Two signals feed the web: word-vector closeness and how well words swap in real text.

The graph form keeps the result open to inspection, unlike black-box scores. Scholars can watch a sense split, fade, or be born across decades of text. The method suits history, media, and language study. It turns a vague drift into a map.
arxiv-2601-22510:
Xingyu Zhao, Darsh Sharma, Rheeya Uppaal, and Yiqiao Zhong trace how transformers learn arithmetic, skill by skill. Their 2026 preprint notes that models make odd errors even at large scale. Past work showed a gap between model and human skill blending; this work hunts the cause in the learning path itself.

They watch how part-skills form, clash, and settle as training runs. The name for their find is shattered compositionality: skills that should stack cleanly instead break apart. Knowing the cause can guide fixes in training and data. It also warns users where sums may silently fail.
arxiv-2601-22710:
Jaehee Kim and Pilsung Kang built AlienLM, a privacy layer that scrambles text before it reaches a black-box model API. Users must send prompts and data to outside providers, which puts private text at risk at that border. Their 2026 preprint translates the text into an alien tongue by a fixed word swap.

The swap is a bijection, so the text can be restored on return. The provider sees only the scrambled form. A deployable, API-only layer needs no change at the provider's end. The work seeks privacy without losing the model's use. That balance is the hard part.
arxiv-2601-21910:
Sofia Giampietro, Ralf Sasse, and David Basin work on the tools that check cryptographic protocols for flaws. Diffie-Hellman groups sit at the heart of secure key exchange, and symbolic verifiers model them to prove protocols safe. But the tools support only some of the math these groups allow.

In particular, they lack support for exponent addition. The reason is deep: the tools reason by unification, and unification becomes undecidable in the full theory of Diffie-Hellman operators. The team's 2026 preprint pushes beyond the finite variant property, a limit that has bounded what verifiers can handle. Extending these models would let automated checkers cover more real protocols, including ones whose security rests on the missing operations.
arxiv-2601-22010:
Dongxuan Zhu and co-authors help language models give more varied answers. Models often default to a narrow set of responses, even when many good answers exist. That sameness limits brainstorming, tutoring, and any tool where diversity of output is the point.

Their 2026 preprint explores diverse generation paths through activation steering done at inference time. Steering nudges the model's internal activations, here using a construction tied to the Stiefel manifold, a space of orthonormal frames. The aim is diversity without retraining and without wrecking quality. Practical steering methods matter for a simple reason. They can be applied to deployed models today. Users get several genuinely different drafts. They do not get near-copies of one safe answer.
arxiv-2601-20810:
Shahd Seddik and five co-authors work on making AI write better code for hard problems. Their 2026 paper notes that large language models excel at code generation but stumble on complex tasks. Retrieval-augmented generation helps by fetching outside knowledge. Yet the fetch can miss key context, and the model may hallucinate when fed irrelevant data.

The authors propose Programming Knowledge Graphs, or PKG. A knowledge graph stores code and text as linked facts with clear meaning. That structure supports fine-grained retrieval: small, precise pieces of context. The aim is to hand the model only what it truly needs. The paper targets software tasks where a wrong guess is costly. It shows one way to ground code models in curated knowledge.
arxiv-2601-20910:
Mao Fabrice Djete and Nizar Touzi study near-perfect play in games with huge crowds. Their 2026 paper concerns approximate Nash equilibria in mean field games. A mean field game models a large population of similar players. Each player reacts to the average behavior of the whole group. An approximate equilibrium is a strategy profile no one can gain much by leaving. The authors define it through the mean field solution itself.

The key measure is the gain from one player deviating alone. Under the mean field strategies, that gain shrinks to zero as the population grows. This gives a rigorous bridge between the finite game and its limit model. Such bridges justify using mean field math for traffic, finance, and crowd systems. The paper firms up the theory behind those uses.
arxiv-2601-21010:
Xiaomin Cao, Mohammadali Mohammadi, Hien Quoc Ngo, and Michail Matthaiou cut the power bill of giant antenna arrays. Their 2026 paper studies extremely large antenna arrays, or ELAAs, for integrated sensing and communication. Such arrays give high-resolution near-field sensing. That power comes at a price. In conventional digital designs, activating every element leads to prohibitive power demands.

The authors seek the same sensing skill with far less energy. Turning off or idling parts of the array is the natural lever. The challenge is to keep resolution while spending less. Integrated sensing and communication systems must do two jobs on one platform. Power discipline decides whether such systems leave the lab. The paper speaks to designers of future wireless networks that both talk and watch.
arxiv-2601-21110:
Jaden Pieper and Stephen Voran hide datasets on purpose to test speech quality models honestly. Their 2026 paper introduces Dataset Concealment, or DSC. It is a rigorous new procedure for evaluating objective speech quality estimation models. Such models predict how good a voice call sounds. Research results often fail to match real-world performance. DSC quantifies and decomposes that gap. It also interprets what the gap says about models and datasets.

Concealment means evaluators cannot tune to the test data. The procedure then breaks the performance gap into parts. Each part points to a cause: model weakness or dataset quirks. That honesty helps buyers of quality tools trust lab numbers. It also guides researchers toward fixes that matter. The paper upgrades how the speech field grades its own rulers.
arxiv-2601-21210:
Paul He, Yinya Huang, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Zhijing Jin check whether language models reason causally better than scores suggest. Their 2026 paper studies LLM causal reasoning. Current benchmarks often rely on string matching or surface-level metrics. Those metrics miss whether an output is formally valid. A chain can sound right while breaking the semantics of causal reasoning. The authors use symbolic verification to look deeper.

Symbolic checks can certify each step against causal rules. That reveals hidden correctness: valid reasoning that crude scoring marked wrong. It can also expose fluent but invalid chains. Fair measurement matters as these models enter science and policy work. The paper upgrades the field's ruler for causal skill. It shows that some models know more causality than their scores confess.
arxiv-2512-01310:
Yanteng Zhang and co-authors ask if models trained on photos help with brain scans. Big brain scan sets could train strong base models. But brain scans vary a lot in quality. Some are crisp, while others are warped or cut off.

Photo data from daily life is far more clean and even. That gap can hurt a model moved from photos to brains. The team studies the gap by training models for age guesses from scans. Their work shows what breaks in the move. It also points to steps that make base models for brain data more sound.
arxiv-2512-01510:
Franz Thaler and co-authors teach scan models to work across scan types. A model trained on CT scans often fails on MR scans. In real care, the new scan type comes with no labels. Retraining is not an option at test time.

Their method trains on one source type alone. Random convolution with semantic care varies the training images. Source matching aligns traits across styles. The net then segments the new type cold. Cross-type skill would save huge labeling costs when clinics switch scanners or protocols. No target-domain images are used at all in training, which matches clinics that cannot share scans across sites for legal reasons.
arxiv-2512-01710:
Stefano Zeppieri adds mixed memory to language model generation. Models write coherent text in one prompt. Across long chats they lose relevance, personal fit, and continuity. Human talk rests on many memory types at once. Past chats, traits, and context all guide each reply.

MMAG mixes those memory forms for the model. Recalled chats ground facts. Trait memory tunes tone and choice. Context memory tracks the present scene. Mixed memory aims for replies that stay on thread over long use, like a good human partner in talk. Mixed forms also degrade gracefully, since a lost trait memory still leaves chat recall to keep the exchange on solid ground.
arxiv-2512-01810:
Sarah Segel and co-authors present DeepCAVE, a visual tool for automated machine learning. Hyperparameter tuning drives AutoML gains. Its process is complex and hard to debug. Users often cannot tell why a search stalls or picks odd values.

DeepCAVE gives interactive views into that process. Users can inspect runs, compare configs, and spot waste. Clear views help teams fix searches early. Better debugging of tuning saves compute and lifts final model quality across AutoML pipelines. Views cover cost and quality jointly, so a tuner can see when extra trials buy nothing but a larger cloud bill at month's end.
arxiv-2512-00710:
Ryan French and eight coauthors report new solar observations in a 2025 paper on flare ribbons. Solar flares are sudden bursts of energy on the Sun, and ribbons are bright bands that mark where energy lands. The team used the Solar Orbiter spacecraft's Extreme Ultraviolet Imager for fast, sharp views.

They used short-exposure images from the high resolution imager to catch fine detail. Inside a hook at the end of one ribbon, they found small blob-like or bead-like shapes moving along it. The sighting came during the impulsive phase of a mid-sized flare. Such beads may show how energy is released in small, quick bursts.
arxiv-2512-00810:
Saeed Hedayatian and Stefanos Nikolaidis wrote a 2025 paper on a kind of optimization that values variety. Quality-diversity algorithms do not hunt for one best answer. They build a set of answers that are both strong and different from each other, covering many styles of solution.

Most current methods keep variety by cutting the behavior space into fixed boxes and filling each box. Hedayatian and Nikolaidis propose a softer version of that idea. A softer rule could keep diversity without forcing solutions into rigid bins. Such sets are useful in design and robotics, where having good options matters more than one winner.
arxiv-2512-01210: Ruiyu Wang, Carl Yang, and coauthors from several universities in the United States and Britain wrote a 2025 paper on disease prediction. Their approach augments a large language model with a knowledge graph, a structured store of facts and the links between them. The model can then draw on organized knowledge when it predicts disease. The author list spans computer science, medical sciences, and nursing, which fits the paper's place between computing and clinical practice.
arxiv-2601-22910:
Giovanni Manfredi, Jean-Louis Rouet, and Bruce Miller explore a universe that holds equal amounts of positive and negative mass. The masses follow the Bondi idea, in which negative mass still obeys the equivalence principle and momentum rules. In such a universe, gravity's grip changes character at the present era.

The authors link that change, from a loose to a strongly coupled regime, with the shift from steady expansion to faster expansion. The match mirrors the known dark-energy coincidence, but needs no dark energy. It offers a fresh, testable story for why cosmic expansion speeds up.
arxiv-2601-23110:
Niels Lauritzen and Jesper Funch Thomsen study when maps of Weyl algebras can be lifted to higher precision. The Weyl algebra captures the algebra of variables and their derivatives, central to quantum mechanics. They work over a perfect field of positive characteristic, modulo a prime squared.

An endomorphism, a self-map of the algebra, may or may not lift from the mod prime setting. Knowing which maps lift sharpens the picture of these algebras in positive characteristic. The question ties algebra to long-standing conjectures about polynomial maps. Positive characteristic shapes the whole question, since lifting behavior there differs sharply from the familiar characteristic-zero setting.
arxiv-2512-00210:
Jet tagging sorts the sprays of particles produced in collider collisions, and transformer models now lead the field. Timothy Legge and a team of co-authors ask why attention in the Particle Transformer is so sparse, in a 2025 study. Its attention pattern is nearly binary, which is striking.

The team investigates where that sparsity comes from and whether it encodes physically meaningful correlations. The Particle Transformer is a leading model at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. Understanding its inner behavior helps physicists trust its decisions and may point to simpler, faster models that keep the same physical insight. Sparse attention is cheaper to compute, so the pattern may be a feature, not a bug.
arxiv-2512-00310:
Finding disease in chest X-rays without labeled examples is the goal of unsupervised anomaly detection. Qinyi Cao, Jianan Fan, and Weidong Cai present ART-ASyn in 2025, a framework that synthesizes realistic anomalies for training. Synthetic anomalies come with known masks, which enables explicit supervision.

Older synthesis methods often produce anomalies that look unlike real pathology and ignore anatomical structure. ART-ASyn is anatomy-aware and texture-based, aiming for irregularities that blend with real tissue patterns. More realistic fake lesions could train detectors that miss fewer real ones, a direct concern for hospital screening programs. Chest X-rays are among the most common medical images, so gains here scale widely. Anatomy-aware synthesis respects ribs and lung boundaries that naive fakes ignore.
arxiv-2512-00410:
Planning paths for a team of drones means avoiding collisions while sharing work fairly. Hongzong Li, Luwei Liao, Xiangguang Dai, and Yuming Feng present an iterative exchange framework for multi-UAV cooperative path planning in 2025. Efficiency means minimizing total mission cost, while fairness means balancing workload across aircraft.

A plan that is merely efficient can overburden individual drones, draining batteries and risking failures. The exchange framework trades tasks between aircraft step by step to balance both goals. Balanced, collision-free planning matters for delivery fleets, mapping missions, and search operations run by cooperating drones. Collision-free trajectories are the non-negotiable constraint underneath the efficiency and fairness goals. Iterative exchange improves the plan in small trades instead of one global solve.
arxiv-2512-00510:
Unauthorized transmitters increasingly interfere with shared radio spectrum. Nazim Bicer presents data-driven methods for locating multiple emitters from distributed power measurements in 2025. Dynamic spectrum sharing needs fast detection using low-cost sensors without precise time synchronization.

Two convolutional neural network approaches detect and localize emitters from sparsely sampled power maps. Sparse, cheap sensing keeps deployment realistic for regulators and network operators. Reliable localization from power alone could help authorities find interference sources quickly, before they disrupt communications that share the band. Power maps are cheap to collect, since receivers only report signal strength. Multiple emitters are harder than one, because their power patterns overlap. For the folks who guard the airwaves, the gain is speed. A cheap net of small ears can flag a rogue source and point crews to the right street fast.
arxiv-2512-03310:
Language models can memorize private details from training data. Kunj Joshi and David Smith propose a way to reduce that risk in this 2025 work. Memorized personal information, such as names and numbers, poses security and privacy threats.

Their method, randomized masked fine-tuning, hides random parts of the data during training. The aim is to cut memorization of personal details while keeping performance loss small. Safer fine-tuning matters for firms that train models on customer text. It could also help meet privacy laws. Masking during fine-tuning is cheap to add, which makes the privacy gain practical for teams.
arxiv-2512-02010:
Very low precision number formats make large language models faster and lighter, but squeezing every part of training into four-bit arithmetic often breaks learning. Jack Cook and co-authors present Four Over Six in 2025, a method that makes the NVFP4 format more accurate through adaptive block scaling.

To gain NVFP4's speed, weights, activations, and gradients all have to be stored in that tiny format, in both the forward and backward passes. Careless rounding then causes training to diverge and inference quality to sag. Adaptive block scaling adjusts the scale factor block by block to keep values representable. The method aims to keep four-bit training stable and faithful.
arxiv-2512-03010:
Svenja Strobel and four co-authors fill the holes that LiDAR scans leave behind. LiDAR point clouds are the gold standard in active 3D reconstruction, exact in flat regions. Scanners miss small structures, though, and fail on dark, absorbent materials that swallow the beam.

Photogrammetry from multiple photos can infer those missing details, since they often sit in feature rich regions. SurfFill completes point clouds using Gaussian surfel splatting to merge both sources. Complete scans matter for heritage preservation, construction checks, and robot maps that must not omit thin obstacles. Two eyes beat one in the field once more. What the beam skips, the lens can catch, and the blend of the two is the scan crews can sign.
plos-pone-0010010:
Roy Malka, Eliezer Shochat, and Vered Rom-Kedar offered a math-based study of bacterial infection in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infections take hold when invading bacteria overwhelm the body's defenses. Neutrophils, a front-line white blood cell, do much of that defense, so low counts or poor function raise risk sharply.

The authors used bistability, an idea where a system can settle into one of two stable states. In their framing, a body can sit in a healthy state or tip into an acute infection state. That view helps explain why similar exposures can end very differently, and why early treatment can matter so much.
plos-pone-0010210:
The authors were Biaoyang Lin, Anup Madan, Jae-Geun Yoon, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study profiled glioblastoma, the most deadly common brain tumor. Better treatments need a full picture of which molecular pathways go wrong in this cancer. The team applied a next-generation sequencing method called massively parallel signature sequencing to tumor samples.

Combining those reads with bioinformatics, they found two genes turned up in tumors. The genes, TGFBI and SOX4, were up-regulated compared with normal tissue. Each up-regulated gene is a candidate marker or drug target for a cancer with few good options.
plos-pone-0010310:
Thierry Baron, Anna Bencsik, and Eric Morignat studied prion spread in sheep-like mice in 2010. Prion diseases, such as scrapie and BSE, are caused by misfolded prion proteins. Agents differ in how they target brain regions and lymphoid tissues, and the pattern depends on the host. Their PLOS ONE model used transgenic mice carrying sheep prion genes.

They analyzed resistant prion protein in the spleen of those mice. Ruminant prions showed distinct splenotropisms, distinct tastes for spleen tissue, by strain. Such patterns can help identify which prion strain is present in an animal.
plos-pone-0009910:
A growth pathway inside cells can be switched on by bringing two proteins together. Zhiyong Ding and colleagues tested whether that contact alone is enough to fire the pathway. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The proteins are PDK1 and AKT1, both key links in cell growth signaling. Their physical association proved sufficient for pathway activation. That held independent of membrane localization and of phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase, two steps long thought required. AKT pathways help control cell survival and growth. The result simplifies a famous pathway's wiring diagram. Each partner is a kinase, an enzyme that switches other proteins on.
